subject: english
source: JAMB UTME Use of English syllabus (IBASS 2025)

topics.name: Answering Comprehension Questions
topics.description: How to read a passage for answers: find the topic sentence, tap the evidence, then choose. Covers inference, mood, attitude, figures of speech and idiom in context.

topics.name: Summary Writing
topics.description: One passage, five questions, one summary. How to compress without losing the point, and how JAMB marks a summary.

topics.name: Description Passages
topics.description: Description gives a detailed picture of a person, place or thing. Recognising it tells you where to look for the topic sentence and the details.

topics.name: Narration Passages
topics.description: Narration tells a sequence of events. Plot, turning point and the narrator’s attitude carry most of the answers.

topics.name: Exposition Passages
topics.description: Exposition explains a process, a cause or a comparison. Signposting words carry the logic, and the answers hide inside them.

topics.name: Argumentation and Persuasion
topics.description: Argumentation defends a position. Learn to spot the claim, the concession and the rhetorical question, and to read the writer’s opinion rather than your own.

topics.name: The Cloze Test
topics.description: Ten questions from one gapped passage. The gaps are grammar questions wearing a passage costume — learn to read the gap, not the story.

topics.name: Synonyms
topics.description: Words with the same or nearly the same meaning. Also covers the trap: near-synonyms are not interchangeable in every context.

topics.name: Antonyms
topics.description: Opposites — and the harder grade question: which word is the opposite in this context, not in general.

topics.name: Clause and Sentence Patterns
topics.description: Simple, compound and complex sentences; clauses and their functions; subject-verb agreement and inversion. The patterns JAMB tests by asking you to rebuild a broken sentence.

topics.name: Word Classes and Their Functions
topics.description: Nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs and the rest — what each does in a sentence, and how function beats form when they disagree.

topics.name: Mood, Tense and Aspect
topics.description: Three tenses, three aspects: past, present and future, and whether the action is finished or ongoing.

topics.name: Number, Agreement and Concord
topics.description: Making the verb agree with the right noun, including the phrases and prepositions that come between them.

topics.name: Degrees of Comparison
topics.description: Positive, comparative and superlative — including the irregular forms and the one-word rule that catches most candidates.

topics.name: Question Tags
topics.description: The tag that closes a statement. Same tense, opposite polarity, and the fixed expressions that never change.

topics.name: Mechanics: Spelling and Punctuation
topics.description: Correct spelling and the punctuation marks JAMB tests — the apostrophe, the comma, the full stop, the colon.

topics.name: Ordinary, Figurative and Idiomatic Usage
topics.description: The same word can be literal or figurative. Idioms tested are formal ones in Standard British English.

topics.name: Vowels: Monophthongs, Diphthongs and Triphthongs
topics.description: One glide or two or three in a single vowel sound, and what changes when you add a suffix.

topics.name: Consonants and Consonant Clusters
topics.description: Place and manner of articulation, and the clusters that English stacks together without a vowel between them.

topics.name: Rhymes and Homophones
topics.description: Words that sound alike but are written differently, and words that rhyme but are not homophones.

topics.name: Word Stress
topics.description: Which syllable carries the stress in a one-syllable or many-syllable word, and how suffixes move it.

topics.name: Emphatic Stress in Connected Speech
topics.description: Emphasis places stress on a word in an utterance for the purpose of emphasis. Learn to hear where the stress lands and what it signals.

topics.name: Comprehension and Summary
topics.description: Three-passage set structure, coherence and multi-passage synthesis.

topics.name: Lexis and Structure
topics.description: Clause and sentence patterns.

topics.name: The Lekki Headmaster
topics.description: Kabir Alabi Garba's approved reading text, chapter by chapter. What happens in each chapter, who said what, the money and the morals — so a Section A candidate can sit the ten novel questions without rereading the book.

lessons.title: Comprehension Tips
lessons.objective: Read a passage for the questions that follow, locate textual evidence and eliminate options that the passage does not support.

content.heading: Comprehension tips
paragraphs: A candidate reads a passage twice, then discovers that every question points to a line they did not mark. Reading with the questions already in mind prevents that waste.

content.heading: Read the questions first
paragraphs: Do not read the passage first. Read the five questions in one sweep, because they tell you what to look for and which parts of the passage are likely to matter.

Notice the question verb. 'What' asks for a fact, 'why' for a reason, 'whom' for a person, 'how' for a manner, and 'infer' for a conclusion the text supports without stating. The verb tells you the kind of evidence to hunt.
Every answer must be supported by the text, not by real-world knowledge. A statement can be true in life and still be a wrong option because the passage never makes it.
bullets: Read the questions before the passage.
Let the question verb set your purpose.
Every answer needs textual support.
content.takeaway: The questions turn the passage from a text into a search space.

check.question: A question asks 'Why did the council fail?' What should you look for?
check.why: 'Why' asks for a cause or reason, so the answer must explain the failure rather than name a time or person.

content.heading: Read with a map
paragraphs: Read each paragraph for its topic sentence, usually the first. Note what the paragraph contributes: a claim, an example, a contrast or a conclusion.

Circle proper nouns, dates and figures, because questions reuse them. Slow down at signal words: however and but mark a turn, therefore marks a conclusion, because marks a reason, and for example marks support.

If a word is unfamiliar, keep going. The surrounding sentence usually supplies a definition, an example or a contrast that lets you infer the meaning without a dictionary. The map also tells you where an answer is likely to sit.
bullets: Find each paragraph's job.
Mark names, dates, figures and signal words.
Infer unfamiliar words from their surroundings.
content.takeaway: A paragraph map turns a second reading into a quick lookup.

check.question: In 'The scheme was cheap; however, it failed', what does 'however' signal?
check.why: 'However' marks a turn against the previous clause, so the second idea contrasts with the first.

content.heading: Answer by evidence
paragraphs: Match the question type to its tactic. Main idea wants the option that covers the whole passage, tone wants the writer's attitude rather than the topic, and vocabulary wants the option that fits the surrounding lines. Reference wants the nearest earlier noun that fits grammatically.

Inference is the hardest: the answer must follow from the text, while a distractor may feel plausible but is not implied. Eliminate options with extreme words such as always, never and everyone, options that are true in life but absent from the passage, and options too vague to be checked.
Budget about two minutes per question. Leave a hard item, answer the others, then return with a clearer mind.
bullets: Match each question type to its tactic.
Inference must follow from the text.
Eliminate extremes, absent truths and vagueness.
content.takeaway: When two options survive, the one with the stronger textual support wins.

check.question: Which option should you reject in a comprehension question?
options: an option supported by a quoted sentence
an option that is true but not stated in the passage
an option that restates the main idea
an option that matches the writer's tone
check.why: Comprehension answers must come from the passage; a true statement the passage never makes is still unsupported.

visual.caption: Work from the question to the evidence before you touch the options.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Never leave a comprehension question blank. If stuck, choose the option with the strongest textual support, not the one that sounds most like your own opinion.

content.problem: In the Kolo Creek passage, why did the village council fail to solve the water problem?

steps.reason: The question asks about the council, so scan for the sentence that names it. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, circle where the stem's key noun first appears.
steps.result: Paragraph 1 says the council met several times but had no money for a borehole.
steps.predictPrompt: Does that show ignorance, indifference or a lack of resources?

steps.operation: Separate the cause from the excuse
steps.reason: The passage says the council knew about the problem, so awareness was not the failure. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, list what the passage blames and cross off what it clears.
steps.result: The failure was money, not knowledge or concern.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you choose between the possible routes?

steps.reason: The answer must restate the evidence without adding to it. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, mark every detail the answer ignores outside the text and cross them off.
steps.result: The correct option is 'resources, not awareness'.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.heading: Go deeper: Why reading the questions first saves time
paragraphs: Picture someone looking for a shop on Allen Avenue with a clear list in hand. They walk straight to it. A person without the list walks every street hoping to stumble on it. That is the difference a question paper makes.

A question tells you what to look for in the passage — a name, a date, a reason, a feeling. Once you know the target, your eyes move to it the way a torch beam moves to a coin. You are no longer reading the whole stall; you are looking for one small thing.

That is also why teachers say to read quickly the first time and slowly the second. The first reading is a search. The second confirms. A candidate who reads the questions first does both jobs, because the questions mark the lines that matter.

Try it with a short paragraph about a flood in Sokoto State. The questions may ask where, when, who and why. Circle the place, the time, the person and the reason as you read, and the answers begin to build themselves.
The method is not cheating. It is reading with a purpose. The examiner wants you to find understanding, and a purpose is the fastest way the brain finds anything.
bullets: Read the questions before the passage
Search for the exact lines the questions want
Confirm with a slower second look

content.heading: Go deeper: Words that show where a passage turns
paragraphs: Every passage has a heartbeat. It sets a mood, then changes it, then lands a point. Signal words are the pulse marks of that rhythm: they tell you that something new is starting.

But and however mark a turn — the writer switches idea. Therefore and so mark a rounding-off — the writer is wrapping up. Because tells the reason. For example introduces a case. Learning these five means you hear the writer change gear without hearing every word.
A passage that praises a scheme and then turns with however is usually tested at the turn, not at the praise. The turn is where the writer hides the point. Your job is to go straight to the turn.

Practice alone will teach your eyes. Write three paragraphs yourself and mark the signals in red. Then read your own marks and notice how they carry you past the unimportant lines straight to where the meaning sits.
In the hall, underline however, therefore, and because as soon as you see them. They are the lamps over the important tables.
bullets: Five words do most of the work: but, however, therefore, because, for example
Turns usually carry the answer
Mark the signals as you read

content.heading: Go deeper: Why a wrong option is often extreme
paragraphs: One option in every set is the opposite of the passage — but they rarely look opposite. They look harmless: too strong, too absolute, too confident. Extremes are their costume.

Always, never, everyone and must are suspicious words. A passage about a school that improved in many ways will not say that every student changed or that no teacher ever failed. If an option overpromises, it is usually the trap.

The opposite trap is vagueness — an option that is true but would fit almost any passage. That option is wrong for this passage because it avoids the key detail. Passages have fingerprints; the right option must match them.

Time also matters. Two minutes per question keeps you moving. If one question fights you, skip it and return. A finished paper that never gets stuck is a stronger showing than three perfect answers and twenty blanks.
Remember: inference means reading what is there, not adding what you wish were there. If the answer needs outside knowledge to be true, the passage is not the source — so it cannot be the answer.
bullets: Beware always, never, everyone and must
True but vague options usually fail
Give each question two minutes

content.question: A question asks what 'it' refers to in 'The committee rejected the plan because it was too costly.' What do you check first?
hints: Reference questions look backwards for a noun.
The pronoun must fit grammatically and in meaning.
'It' cannot refer to the committee here, because the committee was not costly.

content.title: Kolo Creek
content.purpose: what changed the village — and what the chairman really means

questions.question: In paragraph 1, “there was no money for a borehole” shows that the council’s failure was mainly one of
questions.explanation: The council met “several times to discuss the problem” — they knew about it. What stopped them was money, not ignorance or indifference.

questions.question: The word “fate” as used by the chairman in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: He contrasts “fate” with “a problem waiting for a plan” — the village had treated the shortage as something that could not be changed, when it could.

paragraphs: For many years, the residents of Kolo Creek depended entirely on a single hand-dug well. When the well ran dry each March, women and children walked over four kilometres to the next village to fetch water. The village council met several times to discuss the problem, but every meeting ended the same way: there was no money for a borehole.

Everything changed when a team of engineers visited the community as part of a rural water scheme. They tested the soil, sank a borehole near the primary school, and trained three young people to maintain the pump. Within a year, cases of water-borne illness reported at the health centre fell by more than half, and school attendance rose because children no longer spent their mornings fetching water.

The chairman of the council later admitted that the community had grown used to managing scarcity instead of solving it. “We treated the shortage as fate,” he said, “when it was only a problem waiting for a plan.” The borehole did not just bring water; it changed what the village believed was possible.

content.title: Rain at the Bus Park
content.purpose: the mood of the waiting passengers — and what the writer admires

questions.question: The writer’s attitude towards the stranded passengers is best described as
questions.explanation: Clues: “no grumbling”, “good humour”, “as though the delay had been a small festival”, and the closing praise of “a patience … no timetable can teach”.

paragraphs: The rain had been falling since dawn, drumming steadily on the zinc roof of the bus park. Passengers huddled under the narrow shed, watching the road turn slowly into a brown river. A hawker moved among them, balancing her tray with practised ease, calling out prices that nobody answered. Yet there was no grumbling; strangers shared umbrellas, and a boy laughed as his paper boat spun away down the gutter.

When the downpour finally eased, the driver clapped his hands and shouted that the journey would continue. People climbed aboard with damp clothes and good humour, as though the delay had been a small festival rather than an inconvenience. There is a patience in such moments that no timetable can teach.

content.prompt: You just answered with evidence tapped first. On Saturday, will you read the passage first or the questions first — and which sentence from Kolo Creek would you point to as proof your method works?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names one method (“questions first, so I know what to hunt for”), one reason tied to evidence (“because my taps on the council sentences decided Q1 before I read the options”), and one fallback (“if the passage is narrative like the bus park, I read for mood first”). If your answer has all three, your method is exam-ready; if not, borrow the missing piece.

content.title: The Blackout Proposal
content.purpose: whether the writer supports the shutdown — and where he places the blame

options.text: a punishment of the innocent that misses the cause
the only way to stop cheating centres
unfair only to traders and patients

questions.question: The writer’s position on the social media shutdown is that it is
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 calls it punishing “millions of innocent users” while syndicates “switch to offline methods”; paragraph 3 demands securing presses instead. The writer opposes it because it misses the cause.

options.text: unable to control the officials within their own system

questions.question: “It cannot police its own gates” (paragraph 3) implies that the authorities are
questions.explanation: The sentence follows the call to “prosecute the officials who sell” papers and closes with “the gatekeepers did” break the exam — the failure is internal, not technical.

paragraphs: Every examination season brings the same proposal: shut down social media until the last paper is written. Its supporters argue that leaked questions and coordinated cheating spread through phones faster than any invigilator can respond. They point to cancelled results and withheld scripts as proof that the examination system is bleeding, and they insist that a temporary blackout is a small price for credibility.

The proposal sounds decisive, but it mistakes the channel for the cause. Questions leak because printing and distribution chains are compromised long before candidates open an app; cheating centres operate with or without a network signal. A shutdown would punish millions of innocent users — traders, patients, emergency responders — while the syndicates simply switch to offline methods they used for decades.

The honest fix is narrower and harder: secure the printing presses, rotate question sets, and prosecute the officials who sell them. A society that reaches for a blackout every time it faces malpractice is confessing that it cannot police its own gates. The phone did not break the examination; the gatekeepers did.

content.title: The Water Filter
content.purpose: the correct order of the layers — and what filtering alone cannot do

options.text: between the sand and the gravel
at the very top of the bottle

questions.question: According to the passage, the charcoal layer comes
questions.explanation: Order from the neck upward: cotton wool, then charcoal (“add crushed charcoal”), then sand, then gravel. Charcoal sits directly above the cotton wool.

options.text: makes water clear but not germ-free

questions.question: “Only heat sterilises” means that filtering
questions.explanation: The passage says filtered water “will look clearer, but it is not yet safe” and must be boiled — filtering clarifies appearance; boiling kills germs.

paragraphs: To make a simple water filter, you need a clean plastic bottle, gravel, sand, charcoal, and cotton wool. First, cut off the bottom of the bottle and turn it upside down so the neck points downwards. Place a layer of cotton wool in the neck to stop fine particles escaping, then add crushed charcoal to remove odour and taste. Above the charcoal, pour a thick layer of fine sand, and finish with a layer of gravel to trap the largest impurities.

Pour the dirty water slowly through the wide opening and collect what drips from the neck. The water will look clearer, but it is not yet safe: boiling it for at least five minutes destroys the germs that filtering cannot remove. A filter clarifies; only heat sterilises. Anyone who drinks the filtered water without boiling it has completed only half the task.

content.title: Blue Dusk
content.purpose: the mood of the closing market — and what Alaba takes home

questions.question: The dominant mood of the passage is one of
questions.explanation: Despite the day taking “his money, his patience, and very nearly his temper”, Alaba feels “oddly repaid” and “slightly mended” — loss resolved into calm, not anger or fear.

paragraphs: The market did not close so much as dissolve. Lanterns bloomed one by one above the stalls while the last daylight thinned into a violet haze, and the bargaining — fierce at noon — softened into banter. A woman folded her remaining peppers into a basin with the tenderness of someone putting children to bed, and the scent of roasting corn drifted through the lanes like a rumour.

Alaba lingered at the gate, unwilling to break the spell. The day had taken his money, his patience, and very nearly his temper, yet standing there in the blue dusk he felt oddly repaid. Some places do not merely sell you things, he thought; they return you to yourself, slightly mended.

lessons.title: Summary Writing
lessons.objective: Compress a passage into the exact number of sentences or words the question demands, keeping the main point of every paragraph.

content.heading: Summary writing
paragraphs: A summary question gives a passage and a hard limit: one sentence, two sentences, or ten words. The limit is part of the task, not a suggestion.

content.heading: The instruction is a hard limit
paragraphs: Section A gives a passage of about two hundred words and five questions. One asks for a summary, and its instruction names a number: one sentence, two sentences, or not more than ten words.

That number is a hard limit, and JAMB marks against it. The marks come from four things: the right number of sentences, the right length, the main point of each paragraph, and accurate wording in your own words.
Writing three sentences when one was asked for loses a mark for free. So does writing one when two were asked, because a skipped paragraph is a skipped point.
bullets: The number of sentences is a hard limit.
Marks reward coverage and accurate wording.
Too many or too few sentences both cost marks.
content.takeaway: Treat the sentence or word count as part of the question.

check.question: The instruction says 'in one sentence' and you write two. What is the result?
options: full marks if both sentences are correct
a lost mark for breaking the limit
no effect, because length is a guide
check.why: The instruction is a hard limit, so exceeding it loses a mark even when the content is accurate.

visual.caption: A summary is judged by different rules from an ordinary comprehension answer.

rows.right: The main points of the passage

content.heading: Build it in three moves
paragraphs: First, mark the main point of each paragraph in the margin as a single phrase, never a quotation. Second, decide which paragraph carries the passage; it is often the last, because the passage usually ends by saying what it has argued towards, but not always.

Third, write one sentence per main point in your own words, using exactly the number you were given. For a one-sentence summary, a subordinate clause carries two points: 'The market grew because it is cheap, but its future is uncertain because the land is needed for a road.'
Compress by naming the subject once and attaching the cause, the consequence and the qualification to it. Do not list every detail; keep what the passage would lose if it were removed.
bullets: Mark one phrase per paragraph.
Find the paragraph that carries the passage.
Attach causes and qualifications to one subject.
content.takeaway: A summary keeps the skeleton and drops the decoration.

check.question: Which detail belongs in a summary of a passage about a market's growth and possible closure?
options: the colour of the traders' stalls
the reason for the growth and the threat to the land
the price of a single item
check.why: The cause of growth and the threat to the land carry the passage's argument; the other details are decoration.

content.heading: What loses marks
paragraphs: Four errors lose marks reliably: quoting instead of paraphrasing, listing every detail, adding your own opinion, and adding information the passage does not contain. The last two are marked the same way because both go beyond the text.

A fifth trap is reporting a character's final quotation instead of what the passage is about. If the last paragraph is a quote, ask what the quote is doing in the passage's argument, then summarise that.
Check the sentence count before you submit. Most lost summary marks are counting errors, not comprehension errors.
bullets: Do not quote; paraphrase.
Do not add opinion or outside facts.
Summarise the quote's function, not the quote.
content.takeaway: Every sentence in a summary must earn its place.

check.question: Which habit most reliably loses summary marks?
options: quoting long phrases from the passage
check.why: A summary must be paraphrased; long quotations repeat the passage instead of compressing it.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Count the sentences in your summary before you submit. If the instruction said one and you wrote two, cut the weaker one; if it said two and you wrote one, add the paragraph you skipped.

content.problem: A passage describes a night market: how it grew, why it grew, and its uncertain future because the land is needed for a road. Summarise it in one sentence.

steps.reason: You cannot choose what to keep until you know what each paragraph contributes. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, write one line on what each paragraph contributes before choosing.
steps.result: Growth, cause, and threat: three points.
steps.predictPrompt: Which point carries the passage's argument?

steps.reason: The last paragraph usually states what the passage has been driving at. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, ask which paragraph the earlier ones build towards and why.
steps.result: The threat to the land gives the passage its point: the market may not survive.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.reason: One subordinate clause can carry the cause while the main clause carries the threat. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, mark every detail you added outside the text and cross them off.
steps.result: A fast-growing night market has drawn traders because it is cheap, but its future is uncertain because the land is needed for a road.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.heading: Go deeper: How to read a summary instruction
paragraphs: A summary question is not free writing. It comes with a limit, usually from the instruction: write in one sentence, write in three sentences, or write about some part of the passage in a third of the words. The instruction decides what shapes your answer, and ignoring it costs marks even when the ideas are right.

That is why reading the instruction first is the smartest thing you can do. It tells you the number of points to find, the form to use and the slant to take. Most papers want three or four points from one paragraph or a section of the passage.

Your summary must not add new ideas. Anything you cannot match to a line in the passage is not a summary — it is your opinion, and it is rejected. A good summary sounds like the passage with less crowd, not like you.
Be ruthless with words. Two points share one line of grammar when possible. Strike 'very', 'really', 'just', 'the fact that', 'in my opinion'. Keep the bone. No decorations, no fillers.
Before you finish, count the instructions again: Did I cover all the points? Did I keep the same order? Did I leave out my side of the argument? If the answer is yes, the summary is done.
bullets: Read the instruction before writing
Pull points out of the passage; never add your own
Delete every decorative word

content.heading: Go deeper: Where the points hide in a paragraph
paragraphs: Every paragraph has bones: a topic sentence, one or two supporting points, and sometimes a closing statement. The topic sentence tells you what the paragraph argues. The supporting points give the evidence. The closing line may be the conclusion itself.
The easiest clue is the first sentence. Most paragraphs argue from there. If the first sentence does not argue, it tells you where the argument is building to. That is the second-best clue.
Enumeration words are also bonuses — first, secondly, finally, also, moreover. When you see a list, you have a list of points. Each item in the list can become one point in your summary.
Definitions are gifts. When the passage defines something, the definition is always point one. A passage defining 'erosion' in three sentences has given you one complete point you can use.

Sentence-by-sentence, mark only the lines that give full information. Skip the intro and pleasantries. The summary of an exam paragraph is usually three or four facts; writing down everything is a trap for candidates who cannot dare to omit.
bullets: The topic sentence tells you what the paragraph argues
Look for lists and definitions
Mark only full-information sentences

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the last sentence matters
paragraphs: The last sentence of a paragraph is the sentence examiners read most closely. It is almost always one of these: a conclusion, a caution, a reason, or a prediction. If the paragraph set a problem, the last line tells you what the writer thinks of it.
That is why 'therefore', 'thus', 'hence' and 'so' are priceless. They announce that a summary point is being finished. When you see one, stop and ask yourself what the writer wants you to notice.

The last sentence also reveals the writer's attitude. If the writer praised an idea and then said it would not last, the writer's attitude is the opposition — not the praise. In a summary, the attitude matters.

Go back after writing every summary and ask: does my last sentence give the writer's conclusion? Does it give the strongest point, not the first point? Does it sound like the writer and not like you? If all three answers are yes, the technique is working.
Never treat the last sentence as decoration. It is the exit door. The point you take from it is the one the examiner wanted.
bullets: The last line usually carries the conclusion
Therefore, thus and hence mark it
Capture the writer's position, not just the facts

content.question: Here is a one-sentence summary: 'The passage describes a night market, its traders, its growth and its problems.' Which summary error does it commit, and how would you fix it?
hints: Does the sentence report the passage or summarise its argument?
It lists topics instead of stating what the passage says about them.
Rewrite it with the market's situation and its uncertainty.

content.title: The Return of the Night Market
content.purpose: what the market is, why it grew, and what could end it

options.text: A night market has grown quickly because it is cheap, but its future is uncertain because the land is needed for a road.
The council's road plans are being obstructed by traders who have refused to move.
Traders at the market pay more for space than they would pay for a shop on the main road.
Night markets are a common feature of Nigerian cities and cannot be regulated by councils.

questions.question: Which of the following best summarises the passage?
questions.explanation: A summary must carry the passage's main points in order: the market exists and is large, it grew because it is cheap, and its future is threatened by the road project. B misstates the passage — the council has not been obstructed, the traders have asked for an agreement. C inverts the rent figures. D is a generalisation the passage never makes.

options.text: the landowner who owns the land

questions.question: The daily fee at the market is collected by
questions.explanation: Stated directly, and with a deliberate contrast: 'collected by a rotating committee of traders rather than by the landowner'.

options.text: the number of stalls trading on that Friday
the market's income for the month

questions.question: The figure 214 in paragraph 1 refers to
questions.explanation: 'A count by the market association found 214 stalls trading food, tailoring, phone repairs...' The count is of stalls, and the list that follows are the kinds of trade at those stalls.

options.text: annoyed that something appeared before they had planned for it
amused by the traders who built the market
relieved that the market will move on

questions.question: The phrase 'slightly ruefully' in the last paragraph suggests that the planners are
questions.explanation: 'Ruefully' means with regret. The regret is at being outmanoeuvred: the market 'showed up before they did'. The planners are not amused by the traders — they are rueful that a market arrived without their plan.

options.text: set aside for a particular purpose

questions.question: In paragraph 3, 'earmarked' most nearly means
questions.explanation: 'The land is earmarked for a road project' means the land has been set aside for the road. The context — the council has said so, and the traders have asked for a formal agreement — confirms it.

paragraphs: In the last four years, a night market has appeared on an unused strip of land behind the neighbourhood's old bus depot. It opens at seven in the evening and closes around two in the morning. On a Friday in March, a count by the market association found 214 stalls trading food, tailoring, phone repairs, hairdressing and second-hand clothes.

The market's organisers say its growth has been driven by the cost of rent elsewhere. A trader who paid forty thousand naira a month for a shop on the main road in 2023 pays six thousand for a table at the market. The market charges a small daily fee, which is collected by a rotating committee of traders rather than by the landowner, who has so far declined to sell the land.

Whether it lasts is unclear. The council has said the land is earmarked for a road project, and the traders have asked for a formal agreement. For now the market continues, and the planners have begun referring to it, slightly ruefully, as the thing that showed up before they did.

content.prompt: Take the summary question in The Return of the Night Market. Write your own one-sentence summary now, before you look at the option. Then compare: which of your facts did option A carry that yours missed, and which did yours carry that A left out? An option that is correct is usually slightly longer than a candidate's first attempt — what was missing from yours?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer identifies one specific missing element — usually the uncertainty ('the land is needed for a road') or the cause of the growth ('because it is cheap') — and explains why it matters: without the third paragraph, the summary reports a success story instead of the passage's actual subject, which is a market whose success may be temporary. If your summary was longer than the option, that is not a fault; but if it was longer and still missed the uncertainty, the summary was drifting into detail instead of tracking the passage's argument.

lessons.title: Description Passages
lessons.objective: Recognise a description passage, find its topic sentence and choose answers that match what the passage shows rather than what it mentions.

content.heading: Description passages
paragraphs: A description passage makes you see a person, place or thing. It has no plot and no argument, so its centre is the topic sentence.

content.heading: A picture, not a story
paragraphs: Description paints a person, place, thing or moment. It does not tell a story or argue a case; its job is to make you see and feel something accurately. The order of details, the sensory words and the exact measurements all serve that one purpose.
Because there is no plot or argument, the centre of gravity is the topic sentence: the sentence doing the describing. Everything after it is detail hanging from that sentence.
Ask what the passage is showing and which details make the showing precise. That question answers main-idea items before you read the options.
bullets: Description shows rather than tells.
The topic sentence carries the main idea.
Details sharpen the picture.
content.takeaway: Find what the passage is showing, not what it merely mentions.

check.question: What is the main job of a description passage?
options: to tell a sequence of events
to make a subject vivid and precise
to explain a process step by step
check.why: Description aims at vivid, accurate presentation; sequence belongs to narration, proof to argumentation and process to exposition.

content.heading: Recognise it by its movement
paragraphs: Description usually opens wide and narrows: the whole subject first, then its parts. The first sentence gives the subject and scale, and each later sentence tightens the focus.
It leans on precise sensory language: colour, texture, temperature, sound, size and number. Precise is not the same as decorative; a detail earns its place by making the picture sharper.

Contrast the signals. A sequence of events means narration, signposting such as first, next and as a result means exposition, and a claim with reasons means argumentation. Description has none of those.
bullets: It moves from the whole to the parts.
It uses exact sensory detail.
It lacks a plot and a thesis.
content.takeaway: Description holds one scene still and makes it exact.

check.question: Which detail most strongly signals a description passage?
options: a claim followed by three reasons
the colour, texture and temperature of a place
a character's decision and its consequence
check.why: Sensory precision is the signature of description; the other options signal exposition, argumentation and narration.

visual.caption: The movement of the passage tells description and narration apart.

content.heading: Where the answers sit
paragraphs: Whole-passage questions ask for the main point, and the answer is the topic sentence or the idea it supports. Part questions ask for a detail, and the answer is stated flatly; scan for the noun in the question.
Inference questions ask for something not stated outright. The answer is the option the passage makes more likely, not the option that is merely plausible.

JAMB sets about two hundred words from some discipline and five questions. The discipline is there to tempt you into answering from prior knowledge, so check the passage even when the subject looks familiar.
bullets: Main idea answers to the topic sentence.
Detail answers are stated outright.
Inference answers follow from the text.
content.takeaway: Match each question to the part of the passage that can settle it.

check.question: A question asks for the passage's main point. Where should you look first?
check.why: The topic sentence states what the passage is showing, so it is the best guide to a main-idea answer.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In a description, read the first sentence for the subject and the last for the writer's attitude. Those two lines settle most questions.

content.problem: A passage opens: 'The old market hall is a wide, low building of red brick, its roofline broken by a row of small ventilator turrets.' A question asks what the passage mainly describes.

steps.reason: There is no sequence and no argument, only a building being shown. Reach for the passage-type key because the stem tips you off to a description. If stuck, re-read the first sentence and name its role.
steps.result: It is description.
steps.predictPrompt: Which sentence names the subject?

steps.reason: The sentence that names the subject and its character carries the main idea. Reach for the topic-sentence test because it carries a description's main idea. If stuck, underline the subject and list what is said about it.
steps.result: The first sentence gives the hall's size, material and shape.
steps.predictPrompt: Which part of the question does this step answer?

steps.operation: Match the option to the topic sentence
steps.reason: History and supervision are details or absent; the main point is the hall's physical character. Reach for detail pairing because the correct option restates the topic sentence and nothing else. If stuck, cross off options that add or omit a detail.
steps.result: Choose 'the physical and sensory character of the market hall'.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.heading: Go deeper: What a descriptive passage looks like
paragraphs: A descriptive passage paints a scene like a camera never moves. It gives you light, colour, sound, smell and texture — the beach at dawn, a market stall at noon, a hospital ward at night. Your job is not to judge, just to see.

Descriptive passages are usually about places, objects, people or processes that have strong visible features. A mosque with arches, a rainy city street, a masquerade dance, a mother braiding hair — all give the writer rich material.

They do not have a plot. Nothing really 'happens' in a story sense. The movement is outward into the details, not forward in time. If a passage ever tells you what happened first, second and third, it has moved into narration.

The language is heavy with adjectives. Every noun comes dressed: the tall, thin, sweating man in the blue cap. The narrow, winding, muddy road. Once you count those adjectives, you know you are reading description.

Examiners set descriptive passages to test how well candidates can locate specific details and manage vocabulary questions on descriptive words. They also use them to test how well you avoid confusing description with story.
bullets: No plot, just a painted scene
Rich with adjectives and sensory words
Moves outward into detail, not forward in time

content.heading: Go deeper: How to answer the description questions
paragraphs: Questions in a descriptive passage ask you to identify details: what colour was the cloth, where was the object placed, who was present, what was the weather. They usually give the answer straight from the passage.
Architecture-of-the-passage questions ask for the main idea or title. These test your ability to see the scene as a whole. 'A market in the afternoon' is a title; 'Tuesday shopping' is a storyboard.

Vocabulary questions test the exact words the author used. 'Glistening' does not mean 'shiny' as much as 'wet and bright'; 'feeble' does not mean 'small' as much as 'weak'. The context tells you the exact word the writer wanted.

Some questions ask for purpose: why did the author describe the scene this way? The answer sits in the topic sentence — usually the first or last sentence — which tells you whether the writer wanted to praise, compare, warn or explain.
Solve these by searching for the key noun in the question, then locating the sentence that uses it. The answer is almost always in the same sentence or one line away.
bullets: Find the key noun from the question in the passage
Some answers make vocabulary questions about descriptive words
The whole scene is easier to name than a chain of events

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap of confusing description and narration
paragraphs: The biggest trap in these passages is mistaking description for story. A descriptive passage may mention a market, a crowd, then a woman selling fish. That is not a story because nothing changed. A narration says the fishwoman argued with a customer and won. That is story.

Words that mark narration: suddenly, then, afterwards, next, finally. Words that mark turns: however, but, yet. Words that mark conclusions: therefore, thus, hence. Words that mark description: walls, colour, shape, texture, smell, small, big. Notice the difference by reading the first few sentences closely and asking yourself whether anything moved.

Questions are designed to catch candidates who confuse the two. They will ask who the main character is — but there is no character, no journey. The right option is the one that names the scene, not the one that invents an event.
If you are lost, underline every noun in the first two sentences and ask whether the writer is listing things or telling things. Listed things point to description; told things point to narration.
Practice this on any two passages side by side. Descriptions in one column, narrations in another. The side-by-side test is the fastest way to build the reflex.
bullets: Description shows; it does not happen
Narration tells things that changed
Underline every noun to see which type it is

content.question: A passage describes a workshop as 'long and narrow, every surface grey with dust'. A question asks about the writer's attitude. What do the details suggest?
hints: The details are exact but not admiring.
Grey dust and narrowness create a cramped, worn impression.
Choose the option supported by those details, not by your own reaction.

content.title: The Termite Mound
content.purpose: what the mound looks like, and what the old man meant by 'a process'

options.text: show that a mound is far more complex than its appearance suggests
warn readers against disturbing termite mounds on farmland
explain step by step how termites build their mounds
compare termite mounds with the houses of the village

questions.question: The writer's main purpose in describing the mound is to
questions.explanation: The passage is not a warning and not a comparison. The third paragraph drives the point home: the mound is 'not a thing but a process'. Everything from 'four metres high' to 'a nursery where the young are tended' builds the contrast between plain appearance and hidden complexity.

options.text: air drawn in through openings near the base cools as it descends
the outer walls reflect the heat of the sun away from the interior
the queen controls the temperature of the whole colony
the tunnels are dug deep enough to reach damp ground

questions.question: According to paragraph 2, the temperature inside the mound stays steady because
questions.explanation: The passage gives the mechanism explicitly: air enters low and cools on the way down. There is nothing about reflection, a regulating queen, or damp ground.

options.text: regards the colony's capacity to rebuild as more important than the structure
had never seen a termite mound before the writer arrived
wanted the writer to move on so that the mound would not be disturbed
believes termite mounds are dangerous to village farmland

questions.question: The old man's remark that the mound was 'not a thing but a process' suggests that he
questions.explanation: He had just described his grandfather taking clay and the colony replacing it within a season. 'Not a thing but a process' is the conclusion he draws from that rebuilding — the point is what keeps happening, not what stands there.

questions.question: The word 'furrowed' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
questions.explanation: The sentence continues 'into vertical ribs that catch the light'. Ribs are grooves, and grooves catch light on their edges.

options.text: setting the plain appearance against the complexity underneath
hiding the writer's opinion behind plain words
claiming the mound is literally a town

questions.question: The writer's phrase 'What looks like a lump of earth is a city' works by
questions.explanation: It is a contrast, not a literal claim: 'looks like' sets up the plain appearance, and the second half reveals what it actually contains. The following paragraph supplies the evidence for that contrast.

paragraphs: The mound stands at the edge of the farm like a small hill, four metres high and wider at the base than a two-storey house. Its walls are grey-brown and fired hard by the sun, and the surface is furrowed into vertical ribs that catch the light. Inside, the temperature holds steady at around thirty degrees whatever the weather outside, and the air moves in slow currents through vents near the top.

What looks like a lump of earth is a city. It holds thousands of workers, a queen who may live for a decade, and a nursery where the young are tended. There are no doors and no corridors in the ordinary sense; the tunnels widen into chambers and narrow again, and the whole structure breathes. Air drawn in through lower openings at the foot of the mound cools as it descends, which is why the temperature at the base can be twenty degrees lower than on the bare ground outside.

An old man in the village told me that his grandfather used to break open a small mound to take the clay for his walls, and that the colony rebuilt what was taken within a season. He was not boasting about the termites. He was telling me that the mound was not a thing but a process — something that keeps happening as long as nobody stops it.

content.prompt: In The Termite Mound, you had to infer what the old man meant by 'not a thing but a process'. Write down the exact sentence you tapped as evidence, and the exact sentence you would have needed instead if your tap had been wrong. Which one did you find faster — the evidence sentence or the answer option?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names the sentence you tapped ('the colony rebuilt what was taken within a season'), the reason that sentence settles the question (it shows rebuilding, so the mound is an ongoing activity), and a fallback — what you would look for if the tap had failed (the phrase 'not a thing but a process' itself). If you also noticed that you read the options faster than the passage, that is worth knowing: it means you are at risk of choosing the option you recognise rather than the one the passage supports.

lessons.title: Narration Passages
lessons.objective: Follow a narration passage's timeline, narrator and turning point, and answer questions from what the events show.

content.heading: Narration passages
paragraphs: A narration passage reports what happened. Its questions usually turn on why a character acted, what a moment reveals, or how the story changes.

content.heading: A sequence with a turn
paragraphs: Narration tells what happened in time. It has a sequence, usually a complication and a resolution, and its questions often turn on why a character acted or what a moment reveals.
Time markers carry the order: at dawn, by the time, later, finally. A flashback deliberately breaks the order, so note when the passage moves backwards before you answer a sequence question.
The narrator matters. A first-person narrator reports only what they know, so a question about another character's feelings may require inference rather than a direct statement.
bullets: Events move in time.
Time markers and flashbacks control the order.
The narrator limits what can be known.
content.takeaway: Read narration as a timeline with a turning point.

check.question: A passage begins 'Years later, he still remembered the morning...' What does this signal?
check.why: The phrase moves from the present of the telling back to an earlier morning, which is a flashback.

content.heading: Recognise it
paragraphs: Narration strings events together. Look for verbs of action, time adverbials and a change between the beginning and the end.
Dialogue is common but not decisive; a description can contain speech. The test is whether the passage moves from one event to another rather than holding one scene still.

Distinguish narration from exposition: exposition explains a process or idea, while narration reports what someone did. A passage that says first, next and as a result is explaining, not narrating. A paragraph of pure scene-setting may still belong to a story, but the narrative question will turn on the event that follows.
bullets: Action verbs and time markers signal narration.
Dialogue alone does not make a story.
Events change; explanations do not.
content.takeaway: If the passage moves from event to event, it is narration.

check.question: Which sentence is most likely from a narration passage?
options: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy.
First, heat the water, then add the powder.
She left at dawn and returned after dark.
Cities are more efficient than villages.
check.why: It reports two events in time; the others explain, instruct or argue.

visual.caption: Both passages move, but only one moves through time.

content.heading: Where the answers sit
paragraphs: Detail questions ask what happened or who did it, and the answer is stated in the timeline. Sequence questions ask for the order, so track the time markers rather than the paragraph order when a flashback appears.
Inference questions ask why a character acted or what a remark suggests. The answer must be supported by behaviour, dialogue or consequence, not by your sympathy for the character.
Main-idea questions ask what the passage shows about a person or situation. The answer usually names a change, a lesson or a tension, not a single event.
bullets: Detail questions follow the timeline.
Inference rests on behaviour and consequence.
Main idea names the change, not one event.
content.takeaway: A narration answer must be earned by something a character did or said.

check.question: A character gives away his last money and then walks home hungry. What does the passage most likely show?
check.why: The two events together show a generous act and its consequence, which is the kind of change a main-idea question rewards.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: When a narration question asks why, find the sentence just before the action. Motive is usually shown by what the character has just seen, lost or remembered.

content.problem: A passage says the lorry was due at dawn, the driver arrived after the market had started, and he unloaded what he had and went home. A question asks what the ending suggests about his feelings.

steps.reason: The delay is the event that changes the day. Reach for the passage-type key and a timeline tracker because narration moves through events in order. If stuck, note each time marker and order them.
steps.result: He was due at dawn but arrived after trading began.
steps.predictPrompt: What does he do after arriving late?

steps.reason: In narration, feelings are shown through what a character does. Reach for the action-over-dialogue filter because narration shows feeling through what characters do. If stuck, list the last action and what it avoids doing.
steps.result: He unloads and leaves instead of staying to sell.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.reason: The action must support the inference without contradicting the text. Reach for detail pairing because the inference must rest on what the text shows. If stuck, cross off any option the final action contradicts.
steps.result: He is resigned or defeated, not cheerful about the delay.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.heading: Go deeper: What a narrative passage feels like
paragraphs: A narrative passage tells you a story with movement: someone did something, something happened, or something changed for someone. It is the passage that feels like reading a small chapter of a book.

Time moves forward in narrations. That is the first thing to notice. Words like then, after, next, later, before, finally, suddenly all signal that something changed over time. If you see none of those and the passage seems to list nothing but features, it is probably a description.

The story can be about anything — a girl leaving for school, a farmer facing drought, a young man starting a business, a child winning a prize. The size does not matter. What matters is that something happened and that the outcome is visible.

Narrative passages test your ability to follow order. 'What did the woman do before she left?' 'Which event was the turning point of the passage?' These are about sequence, not about descriptive detail. They want the storyline, not the furniture.

Keep one hand on the timeline. Read the passage with one eye on the steps: what first, what next, what last. Mark the sequence with arrows. Most narrative questions are answered by seeing the timeline clearly.
bullets: Something happened; something moved forward
Words like suddenly, then, after mark it
Reading narrative means reading a timeline

content.heading: Go deeper: How the story unfolds in its sentences
paragraphs: Narratives are built in four moves: setting the scene, introducing the problem or event, moving through the action, and reaching a result. Almost every narrative passage follows this skeleton, even the shortest ones in exams.

Setting: 'On the morning of the market fair, the fields were dry and cracked.' That line tells you where we are; you are now a witness. Problem/event: 'The river had not risen.' That line is why the story matters; without it, nothing happens.

Action: 'Women argued at the borehole. Men walked the long road carrying water.' That line is life unfolding. Result: 'That day, the fair opened with rows of empty stalls.' That line is the punchline.

Examiners often ask you to identify one of the four moves by name — setting, complication, climax, resolution — or to identify the problem or the outcome. All are answered straight from the sentences that carry them.

Scan for transition phrases to locate each move quickly. It saves reading every line. If you must find 'the turning point', it is usually the sentence with 'however', 'but', 'when suddenly', or 'then'.
bullets: Setting, problem, action, result: the four moves
Transition words mark the turning points
Identify which move a sentence belongs to

content.heading: Go deeper: Answering about character and feeling
paragraphs: Narratives always involve someone who does something. The 'someone' is the character, and the character feels, wants, struggles, wins or loses. The examiner will ask you to name the character's feeling or goal.

Feelings are often shown through actions, not stated plainly. 'She wiped her forehead and let out a sigh' signals exhaustion and relief. 'He clutched his book and walked without looking up' signals focus and seriousness. Feelings live in behaviour.
Goals are usually visible in the first few lines of any narrative: why is this story being told? A man travelling to the city — why? A woman striking a bargain — why? The answer is the goal.

The outcome is saved for the last few sentences. That is where you confirm whether the goal was reached. Winning or losing, the result matters to the examiner, because it tells you the author's position on the story.

To answer feel and goal questions, first find the verb in the question (feel, want, hope, wish, strive), then find those verbs in the passage. They often sit close together, and the answers live there.
bullets: Feelings live in behaviour, not in labels
The goal is stated early; the result is stated last
Search for the verbs asked about

content.question: A story says a boy laughed as his paper boat spun away down the gutter. What does the detail suggest about the mood?
hints: The boy's reaction is playful, not distressed.
The boat is lost, yet he laughs.
The mood is light despite the rain.

content.title: The Night the Road Flooded
content.purpose: why the writer remembers that night, and what the final image means

options.text: the family sets out walking in the failing light
the pickup arrives at nine o'clock
the transformer fails during the afternoon

questions.question: The turning point of the narrative comes when
questions.explanation: The transformer failing is what made the walk necessary, and the pickup only reverses the difficulty. The moment the situation actually changes for the family is the decision to walk, which is also the last thing they can control.

options.text: to carry more than she could hold
to keep the books out of sight
to weigh the bag down against the wind

questions.question: Why did the mother put the books in a plastic bag over her head?
questions.explanation: The bag goes over her head in heavy rain, and at the end the books inside it are wet. The intention is unambiguous even though the outcome fails.

options.text: the family's preparation has been damaged, and something larger is at stake
the books were of little value to the family
the family did not care about the coming examination
the rain will stop before Thursday

questions.question: The final image of the wet books mainly suggests
questions.explanation: The narrator calls the worry about Thursday's exam 'absurd', and the mother says nothing while gripping the bag. The books being wet is the concrete loss; the 'absurdly' and the silence are what tell you the real subject of the passage is not the exam.

questions.question: The writer's attitude towards the mother's silence at the end is best described as
questions.explanation: He notices exactly what she did and did not do, calls his own worry 'absurdly', and remembers the image. That is fondness looking back, not resentment.

questions.question: In paragraph 2, 'a ragged orange light' is used to suggest the light was
questions.explanation: 'Ragged' is the giveaway, and the cause is given in the previous clause: many generators starting one after another, each throwing a slightly different light.

paragraphs: The rain started at four in the afternoon and did not stop. By six, the road out of Ijebu-Ode had become a shallow river running brown between the grass verges, and the buses had stopped climbing it. My mother decided we would walk. She tied my books in a plastic bag, put the bag over her head, and told me to hold her sleeve.

We got perhaps two hundred metres before the light went. The transformer had failed earlier in the day, and the whole street sat in the dark while the rain hammered the zinc roofs. Then the generators started, one after another, and the street filled with a ragged orange light that made everything look like a photograph of itself. We waited under a woman's awning for an hour, watching the water carry a plastic chair past us.

At nine o'clock my father came back for us in a borrowed pickup, and we rode home with the water breaking around the wheels. I remember thinking, absurdly, that the exam on Thursday was the problem to be worried about. My mother said nothing. She was holding the plastic bag very tightly, and the books inside it were already wet.

content.prompt: In The Night the Road Flooded, the writer says the exam was 'the problem to be worried about' — absurdly. Write the ending of the story in one sentence, as you would summarise it, and say whether your summary kept or lost what the final image is really about. Then name one question you would ask if you were the examiner.
content.modelResponse: A strong answer summarises the events in order (flood, walk in the dark, rescue, wet books), then admits which part the summary lost — the fact that the narrator's worry was 'absurd' because the real worry was his mother's silence and the family's preparation. A strong examiner question would ask which detail in paragraph 1 is the writer's judgement rather than the scene, because that tests whether the candidate can hear a narrator's voice inside a narration. If your summary kept the emotional turn, your examiner question will be sharper.

lessons.title: Exposition Passages
lessons.objective: Map an exposition passage's process, cause or comparison, and answer from the explanation rather than from prior knowledge.

content.heading: Exposition passages
paragraphs: An exposition passage explains how something works, why it happens, or how two things differ. Its questions test whether you followed the explanation.

content.heading: Explanation, not story
paragraphs: Exposition explains how something works, why something happens, or how two things differ. Its purpose is understanding, so it organises information rather than events.
Common patterns are process (first, next, finally), cause and effect (because, therefore, as a result), comparison (similarly, unlike, whereas) and classification (types, kinds, categories).

Find the pattern and you have found the passage's skeleton. A question about why a step comes before another is a process question, not a memory test. The pattern also predicts the wrong options: a process question rarely rewards a definition, and a comparison question rarely rewards a cause.
bullets: Exposition organises information, not events.
Process, cause, comparison and classification are the main patterns.
The pattern tells you where an answer sits.
content.takeaway: Name the pattern before you answer the question.

check.question: A passage says 'First the water is heated, then the powder is added.' Which pattern is this?
check.why: The steps follow one another in time, which is the process pattern.

content.heading: Recognise it
paragraphs: Exposition signposts its structure. Sequence words mark a process, causal words mark an explanation, and comparison words mark a contrast.

It often defines its subject before developing it: 'Photosynthesis is the process by which...' The definition is usually the topic sentence and the best answer to a main-idea question. Read the first two sentences together: the definition names the subject, and the next sentence usually begins the explanation.
Unlike argumentation, exposition does not try to persuade you to agree. It may recommend a step, but its main job is to make the mechanism clear.
bullets: Signpost words reveal the pattern.
A definition often opens the passage.
Exposition explains; it does not take sides.
content.takeaway: Exposition wants you to understand, not to agree.

check.question: Which word most strongly signals a cause-and-effect explanation?
check.why: 'Therefore' marks a result, which is the core of a cause-and-effect explanation.

visual.caption: Explanation and persuasion can share a topic but not a purpose.

content.heading: Where the answers sit
paragraphs: Process questions ask what happens at a stage or why the order matters; the answer is in the sequence, often in one sentence.
Cause questions ask why something happens; the answer is the stated cause, not the result. Comparison questions ask for a difference; the answer is usually the clause after 'whereas' or 'unlike'.

Main-idea questions ask what the passage explains. Choose the option that names the whole mechanism, not one stage of it. A detail question may quote a single stage, so check that the option names the stage the question asks about.
bullets: Process answers sit in the sequence.
Cause answers name the cause, not the result.
Main idea names the whole mechanism.
content.takeaway: Answer from the explanation's own structure, not from the topic's general facts.

check.question: A question asks why the water rises in the tube. Which answer is correct?
options: the result of the water rising
the stated cause earlier in the process
a fact about water in general
the last stage of the process
check.why: A why-question asks for the cause, which the passage states before or alongside the result.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Underline the signpost words as you read. They mark the steps, causes and contrasts that the questions will ask about.

content.problem: A passage explains: 'First, the tube is filled with water. Next, the flame is placed beneath it. As a result, the water rises.' A question asks why the filling step must come before the heating step.

steps.reason: The words first, next and as a result mark a process with a cause. Reach for the passage-type key because the stem tips you off to an exposition. If stuck, re-read the first sentence and name its role.
steps.result: This is a process explanation.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the flame do to the water?

steps.reason: The result clause tells you what the earlier steps produce. Reach for the cause-and-effect chain because expositions explain how one step produces the next. If stuck, underline each verb and ask what it makes happen.
steps.result: Heating causes the water to rise, so the water must already be there.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you choose between the possible routes?

steps.operation: Choose the option that states the dependency
steps.reason: The answer must explain the order, not merely repeat it. Reach for detail pairing because the answer must state the dependency the passage shows. If stuck, cross off options that repeat the order without explaining it.
steps.result: The filling must come first because there is nothing to heat otherwise.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.heading: Go deeper: What an expository passage explains
paragraphs: An expository passage explains something — a process, a concept, a system or a problem. It is the passage that can be read aloud in class and the class nods along. It teaches, not persuades, not tells.
The topic is usually stated at the top. 'How elections work in Nigeria.' 'Why deforestation is a problem.' 'How to treat a fever at home.' 'The danger of plastic waste.' Each of those is expository.

The passage is organised logically, not emotionally. Cause first, then effect. Problem first, then solution. Step one, then step two. Numbering helps: first, secondly, thirdly. Comparison helps: on one hand, on the other hand. Time helps: before, during, after.
Vocabulary is technical and precise. Words like therefore, because, as a result, consequently, thus — these words mean the writer is explaining, not arguing. The tone is dry, steady, instructional.
Read the first two sentences and the last sentence. Between them is almost always the full weight of the passage. The body expands the opening claim with evidence and examples.
bullets: Teaches how something works or why it works
Organised logically, usually from problem to solution or cause to effect
Words like because, therefore, as a result tell you it is expository

content.heading: Go deeper: Answering explanation questions
paragraphs: Questions ask you to explain a process, identify a cause, name a consequence or describe how something is done. 'According to the passage, why did the crops fail?' is a pure explanation question. The answer is always in the passage and always direct.

Inference questions also appear: the passage may not state a cause, but it gives enough evidence that you must infer it. 'From the information provided, we can infer that —' These test your ability to read between lines.

Comparison questions are common: 'According to the passage, the difference between — and — is —' The passage will have explicitly compared them, usually with 'on one hand / on the other hand' or 'while / whereas / however'.
For step-by-step questions, mark each step in the order the passage gives it, then check which option mirrors that order. Process questions are pure sequence questions in disguise.

Remember that explanation questions never need you to look outside the passage. Everything you need is printed there. If the answer requires knowledge you do not have, the passage will have provided it.
bullets: The answer is in the passage; just find it
Inference questions need reading between lines
Step-by-step questions are order questions

content.heading: Go deeper: Vocabulary the examiner loves
paragraphs: Expository passages carry domain vocabulary — words tied to the topic. In health topics: fever, immunity, infection, treatment. In economics: inflation, deflation, market, capital. In science: evaporation, condensation, refracted. In geography: plateau, coastal, alluvial, erosion.
These dominant words are the examiner's favourite target. You will be asked their meaning, their opposite or their use in context. If your vocabulary is thin here, you will struggle.

Context clues always save you. Around the difficult word, the passage gives synonyms, examples, definitions and antonyms. 'Evaporation, the process by which water becomes vapour —' The dash tells you the definition is coming.

If you cannot find a clue, look at where the word sits in the sentence. Technical words usually sit next to other technical words — 'immunity boost' rather than 'boost immunity', 'inflation rate' rather than 'rate inflation'. The neighbours give you the neighbourhood.
Build a habit of collecting these words in a notebook. Five words a day, with their meanings and one example sentence each, will carry you far beyond any exam.
bullets: Domain words are always examinable
Context clues do the heavy lifting
Collect vocabulary in a notebook daily

content.question: A passage says, 'Unlike a mirror, a lens bends light as it passes through.' What is the passage contrasting?
hints: 'Unlike' marks a contrast.
One object reflects; the other bends light.
The answer is the difference between a mirror and a lens.

content.title: How a Solar Cooker Works
content.purpose: how the cooker traps heat, and why the design is shaped the way it is

options.text: a solar cooker works by trapping and directing solar heat
solar cooking is cheaper than cooking with gas
the glass lid is the most important part of a cooker
solar cookers cannot be used in hot countries

questions.question: The main idea of the passage is that
questions.explanation: The opening sentence states it — 'the whole device is an exercise in controlling where that heat goes' — and each paragraph then explains one way of controlling it: trapping, insulation and reflection.

options.text: the writer is moving to another stage of the explanation
a solar cooker is made of exactly two parts
the writer disagrees with the paragraph before it
the cooker described here is incomplete

questions.question: The phrase 'The second part of the design' tells the reader that
questions.explanation: It is a signpost. It tells you the writer is continuing the explanation and moving on to another aspect of it — trapping was the first part, insulation is the second. The cooker is not two parts; it is a frame, a lid, plates and lining.

options.text: it allows visible light in while holding back infrared heat
it reflects sunlight down onto the plates
it keeps rain off the food
it prevents the pot from being knocked

questions.question: The glass lid helps the cooker work because
questions.explanation: Stated directly: 'the glass lets the short, visible wavelengths in and holds back the longer, infrared ones'. Reflection is the job of the mirror or foil, which the passage gives separately.

options.text: dark surfaces absorb heat rather than reflecting it away
dark pots are cheaper to manufacture
it makes the food look more appetising
it prevents the heat from scorching the food

questions.question: The instruction that the pot must be 'dark on the outside' is best understood as
questions.explanation: The passage has already set up the principle in paragraph 1: sunlight lands on black-painted plates, which then get hot. The same principle explains the instruction, and the closing line confirms the purpose — 'the heat must go into the food, not into the kitchen'.

options.text: the cooker stores surplus heat during the day
people are free to cook at midday
the wind is usually calmer at midday
solar cookers cannot work at night

questions.question: Solar cooking is recommended for midday mainly because
questions.explanation: The passage says exactly this: 'For most of the day the cooker stores more heat than it uses. That surplus is why solar cooking is done at midday rather than at night.' D is wrong — the cooker works at night using stored heat, which is why the surplus matters.

paragraphs: A solar cooker does not burn fuel. It traps the heat of the sun and traps it well enough to boil water, and the whole device is an exercise in controlling where that heat goes. The simplest type, the box cooker, is built from a wooden or cardboard frame, a sheet of glass for a lid, and black-painted metal plates inside. Sunlight passes through the glass and lands on the dark plates; the glass lets the short, visible wavelengths in and holds back the longer, infrared ones, so the temperature inside climbs past what it would be in an open pan.

The second part of the design is insulation. The box is lined with a material that conducts heat poorly, so the heat the plates have collected is not lost quickly through the sides. Reflection plays its part too: a polished mirror or a sheet of aluminium foil on the lid bounces stray light back down onto the food instead of letting it escape through the glass.

For most of the day the cooker stores more heat than it uses. That surplus is why solar cooking is done at midday rather than at night, and why a pot in a solar cooker must be dark on the outside and have a tight-fitting lid: the heat must go into the food, not into the kitchen.

content.prompt: In How a Solar Cooker Works, the passage explains trapping, then insulation, then reflection — but the order of explanation is not the order of importance. Which of the three would you put first if you were explaining a solar cooker to a beginner, and which sentence in the passage tells you the writer's own priority? Write the one-sentence rule you will use to spot order questions in expository passages.
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names a rule that is a rule and not a preference — for example: 'in an exposition the signpost before a step tells you the writer's order, and the cause must come before the effect.' It should also acknowledge that trapping comes first because without trapping there is nothing to conserve, so the passage's order is defensible even if a teacher would start with the whole idea. If your answer says 'read carefully', that is not yet a rule — a rule has to tell you what to do with a specific word on the page.

lessons.title: Argumentation and Persuasion
lessons.objective: Separate an argument's claim from its reasons and evidence, and infer the writer's purpose and attitude from tone.

content.heading: Argumentation and persuasion
paragraphs: An argument passage wants you to accept a position. Its questions ask what the writer claims, why, and how the writer feels about the issue.

content.heading: A claim with reasons
paragraphs: Argumentation tries to persuade. It states a claim, supports it with reasons and evidence, and often answers an objection. Your job is to separate the claim from the support.

The claim is what the writer wants you to accept; the reasons explain why; the evidence makes the reasons credible. A counterargument shows the writer has considered the other side, not that the writer agrees with it.
