Tone is part of the argument. Words such as clearly, surely and no doubt signal confidence, while admittedly and although signal concession. An evaluative adjective such as reckless, sensible or overdue is often the quickest route to the writer's attitude.
bullets: The claim is the position.
Reasons and evidence support it.
Concession is not agreement.
content.takeaway: Find the conclusion first, then see which reasons serve it.

check.question: A writer says 'Admittedly, the charge is unpopular, but it is necessary.' What is the writer doing?
options: conceding a point before defending the charge
check.why: 'Admittedly' concedes an unpopular feature, while 'but it is necessary' returns to the writer's position.

content.heading: Recognise it
paragraphs: Look for evaluative language, a position on a disputed question, and connectives such as therefore, because and however. These mark the move from reason to conclusion. A passage that only reports what people said, without evaluating it, is closer to reportage than argument.
Distinguish argument from exposition. Exposition explains a mechanism; argumentation takes sides. A passage can explain a policy and still argue for it, so identify the conclusion first.
Beware of a balanced passage. A writer may present both sides and still commit to one in the last paragraph; the conclusion, not the balance, is the position.
bullets: Evaluative words signal a stance.
Connectives mark reason and conclusion.
A balanced passage can still take sides.
content.takeaway: The last paragraph often reveals which side the writer has chosen.

check.question: Which sentence is argument rather than exposition?
options: The engine converts heat into motion.
This policy is unfair and should be repealed.
check.why: It evaluates the policy and recommends an action, which is a claim; the others explain.

visual.caption: Both can discuss the same policy, but only one asks you to agree.

content.heading: Where the answers sit
paragraphs: Purpose questions ask what the writer wants to achieve, and the answer is the claim plus the action it recommends. Attitude questions ask how the writer feels, and the answer is carried by evaluative words and tone.
Inference questions ask what the writer assumes or implies. The answer must be a belief the argument needs, not a fact the passage merely mentions.
Detail questions ask what support is offered. Match the reason to the claim it supports, because an option can be true and still support a different point.
bullets: Purpose = claim plus recommended action.
Attitude = evaluative language.
Support must serve the stated claim.
content.takeaway: An argument answer must connect a reason to the writer's conclusion.

check.question: A writer argues for a charge and then says the money will fund buses. Why is the bus detail there?
options: to support the charge by answering a likely objection
check.why: The detail answers the objection that a charge alone would not help commuters, so it supports the claim.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: A concessive sentence is not the writer's conclusion. Read past 'although' and 'admittedly' to the clause after 'but'.

content.problem: A writer says there is no doubt the roads are overcrowded, that change must be affordable, and ends: 'Improve the alternative first. Then restrict.' A question asks for the writer's purpose.

steps.reason: The opening agrees the roads are overcrowded, which is common ground rather than the argument. Reach for the passage-type key with a claim-concession split because the stem tips you off to an argument. If stuck, ask what the writer accepts.
steps.result: The claim is about how to change, not whether to change.
steps.predictPrompt: What action does the writer recommend?

steps.reason: In persuasion, the purpose is usually the action urged on the reader. Reach for the purpose probe because persuasion asks the reader to act. If stuck, underline the final instruction and ask what it demands.
steps.result: Improve alternatives before restricting cars.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you choose between the possible routes?

steps.reason: The answer must include the recommendation, not just the problem. Reach for detail pairing because the answer must carry the recommendation, not just the problem. If stuck, cross off options that name only the overcrowded roads.
steps.result: The writer wants affordable alternatives before any restriction.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.heading: Go deeper: What an argumentative passage argues
paragraphs: An argumentative passage takes a position and defends it. The writer has a view, and every line of the passage either supports that view or attacks the opposite one. It is the passage that has a clear opinion, not just an explanation.

Every argument has four parts: the claim (what the writer believes), the reason (why the writer believes it), the evidence (the example, fact or case that proves the reason), and the counter (what the opposition would say). Good argumentative passages handle all four.

The tone is persuasive, never neutral. Words like should, must, ought, must be, cannot be allowed, always, never, definitely — these are the writer's colours. They are why argumentative passages generate strong exam questions.

The arrangement is usual: introduce the claim, give the reasons, give the evidence, handle the counter, conclude firmly. Occasionally the structure flips — counter first, then response — when the writer is anticipating objections.

As a reader, your task is to follow the chain: what does the writer want you to believe, and how hard does the writer push that belief? The answer is the position. The paragraphs around it are the push.
bullets: One clear position, defended through reasons and evidence
Words like should, must and ought mark it as argumentative
Find the chain: claim, reason, evidence, counter

content.heading: Go deeper: How to spot the writer's position
paragraphs: The topic sentence tells you the position, but the whole passage tells you its strength. A line like 'The government should ban plastic bags' is a position. A line like 'Some people believe plastic bags should be banned' is a report.

Look for the evidence pool. If the writer gives three strong examples, the position is deep. If the writer gives one weak example, the position is thin. Your job is to locate the strength, not just the claim.
Evidence comes as facts ('statistics show'), examples ('in Lagos last year'), or appeals to authority ('the World Health Organization says'). Each is used to convince; each weights the argument.

Counters are the writer's fairness. 'Critics say plastic bags are cheap, but they destroy crops.' The writer attacks the easy side and keeps the hard side. This balance is the examiners' best-friend anatomy.
Identify the position by finishing these sentences in your own words: 'The writer believes...' and 'The writer presents...' If both end clearly, you have the position.
bullets: The topic sentence names the claim; evidence shows its strength
Facts, examples and authorities weigh the argument
The counter shows the writer's balance

content.heading: Go deeper: Why argument questions are the hardest
paragraphs: Argument questions demand the most careful reading because the writer's position is not always shouted. 'Even so', 'nonetheless', 'in spite of' and 'while some argue' all carry hidden shifts. The writer may agree with opposition before pulling back to their own frame.

The commonest trap: an option that paraphrases the claim but stiffens or widens it — one word too strong is enough to kill the match. 'The government should ban plastic because pollution has gone too far' tracks the passage; 'all plastic must be banned forever' does not.
Another trap: taking an example as the evidence. An example proves a point, it does not prove the position by itself. A single case is one stone; a position is a wall.

The third trap: agreeing with the opposition. If the writer argues for one side, the other side's arguments are never the right answer — even when you agree with them personally. The exam does not test your opinion, it tests reading.

Use the 'two-minute rule'. If a passage splits three to one, the weight still sits with the writer's own paragraphs — but the conclusion decides the position. The writer's support always lands in the writer's paragraphs.
bullets: Hidden shifts live at even so, nonetheless, while some argue
An example proves a point, not a position
Count the paragraphs on each side

content.question: A writer says, 'Some claim the tax will hurt small shops. In fact, small shops will be exempt.' What is the writer doing?
hints: The first sentence reports an objection.
The second answers it with a fact.
The writer is defending the tax, not opposing it.

content.title: Banning Cars Is Not the Answer
content.purpose: what the writer thinks cities should do first, and who the policy is really aimed at

options.text: cities should improve the alternative before they restrict driving
cities should ban private cars entirely
congestion charging has never worked anywhere
air quality in large cities cannot be improved

questions.question: The writer's central argument is that
questions.explanation: The final paragraph is the verdict: 'not to ban the car but to price the journey and to make the alternative a real one. Build the bus lane first. Then charge.' The order of those two clauses is the argument.

options.text: granting a point in order to dispute it
criticising the cities that adopted it

questions.question: The sentence 'It is also a reasonable-looking answer' shows the writer is
questions.explanation: 'Also' adds to what came before, and 'reasonable-looking' carefully marks the answer as appearing reasonable rather than being reasonable. The next sentence — 'It is also the wrong answer' — turns the concession against it.

options.text: the people who set the policy do not understand the timings of the people it affects
the meeting at which the policy was made was badly organised
market traders are not permitted to attend public meetings
the policy ignores the volume of traffic

questions.question: The phrase 'the schedule is not in the room' suggests that
questions.explanation: 'Room' is doing the work of 'the room where decisions are made'. The point being made is that the timetable of the traders — the schedule — has no voice in the decision that rearranges their day.

options.text: reversing the expected order to make the writer's priority vivid
repeating a word purely for rhythm
offering the reader two equal options

questions.question: The closing 'Build the bus lane first. Then charge.' works by
questions.explanation: The expected order is 'charge first, then provide the alternative'. Putting the bus lane first makes the priority unmistakable — and the short, blunt sentences give it the force of an instruction.

questions.question: The overall tone of the passage is best described as
questions.explanation: The writer concedes properly, gives a concrete case, and ends with a recommendation. There is no exclamation, no insult and no apology — the force comes from the reasoning, not the temperature.

paragraphs: Every major city eventually reaches the same conclusion: the streets are full, the air is foul, and traffic has to be cut. The usual remedy is a ban or a charge — congestion charging, low-emission zones, odd-even restrictions. It is a reasonable-looking answer, and in several cities it has worked well.

It is also the wrong answer for most of the world. A ban assumes that the people who drive are the people who chose to drive, and that they can simply stop. In Lagos, a trader who drives between two markets at six in the morning, carrying goods that would cost more to move any other way, cannot be asked to take a bus that does not run at six. The policy is not aimed at the traffic; it is aimed at the schedule, and the schedule is not in the room.

That is not an argument against clean air. It is an argument against a single instrument. If the air in a city must improve, then the change has to reach the vehicles that cause the problem at the moment they cause it — and the cheapest way to do that in most cities is not to ban the car but to price the journey and to make the alternative a real one. Build the bus lane first. Then charge.

content.prompt: The writer concedes that bans have 'worked well' in several cities, then argues against them for most of the world. Write down one reason the concession might make the argument stronger rather than weaker. Then find the sentence in the passage that proves the writer is not writing about Lagos alone.
content.modelResponse: A strong answer identifies the risk of the concession — 'by admitting the policy works elsewhere, the writer makes it harder to dismiss the objection as ignorant' — and then quotes the scope phrase, 'It is also the wrong answer for most of the world'. A strong answer also notes that the concession makes the writer sound fair, which is why the closing instruction lands. If your reason was only 'it makes him look nice', push further: the concession is doing argumentative work, not just reputational work.

lessons.title: The Cloze Test
lessons.objective: Restore missing words by using the passage's meaning, grammar and collocation rather than guessing from the gap alone.

content.heading: The cloze test
paragraphs: A cloze passage removes words and asks you to restore them. The missing word must fit both the meaning of the sentence and its grammar.

content.heading: What a cloze test is
paragraphs: A cloze passage removes words at regular intervals and asks you to restore them. The missing word must fit both the meaning of the sentence and its grammar.

The passage is about two hundred words and usually comes from a science, history or everyday topic. Read the whole passage once before filling any gap, because the topic and tone constrain every choice.
Do not treat gaps as separate puzzles. A gap may depend on a word two sentences earlier, especially when the missing word is a pronoun, a conjunction or a repeated noun.
bullets: Meaning and grammar must both fit.
Read the whole passage first.
A gap can depend on earlier sentences.
content.takeaway: A gap is a hole in a passage, not a question on its own.

check.question: What should you do before filling the first gap?
check.why: The passage's topic, tone and grammar constrain every gap, so a first read prevents local guesses.

content.heading: Attack each gap
paragraphs: Read the sentence before and after the gap. Identify what the missing word must do: name, connect, modify, or carry the verb's tense and agreement. The sentence after the gap often supplies the consequence that confirms your choice.
Predict a word before you look at the options. Then test each option in the gap and re-read the sentence. The correct option fits the grammar and keeps the meaning.

If two options fit, check collocation (the words English habitually pairs, like 'make a decision') and register (the passage's level of formality). 'Make a decision' beats 'do a decision', and a formal passage rejects slang even when the meaning is close.
bullets: Read around the gap.
Predict before you look at the options.
Test grammar, meaning and collocation.
content.takeaway: Predict first, then let the options confirm or correct you.

check.question: Two options fit the meaning of a gap. What should you check next?
check.why: When meaning ties, fixed word partnerships and the passage's formality decide.

visual.caption: Work from the whole passage down to the single word.

content.heading: Gap types and traps
paragraphs: Most gaps test one of a few types: prepositions (depend on), conjunctions (although, because), pronouns (it, they), articles (a, an, the), verb forms (has gone, went), quantifiers (much, many) and vocabulary in context.
The trap is a word that fits the meaning but not the grammar, or the grammar but not the meaning. A singular subject still needs a singular verb, and a countable noun still needs many or fewer.
Watch the words around the gap for number, tense and polarity. A negative sentence may need 'anything' rather than 'something', and a past-time marker may rule out the present perfect.
bullets: Identify the grammatical job of the gap.
Meaning without grammar is a trap.
Check number, tense and polarity.
content.takeaway: The right option satisfies both the sentence's grammar and its sense.

check.question: The gap reads 'She ______ to school yesterday.' Which option is correct?
check.why: 'Yesterday' marks a definite past time, so the simple past 'went' is required.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Say the sentence aloud with your chosen word. Grammar errors and awkward partnerships are easier to hear than to see.

content.problem: A gap reads: 'The leaves were (1)____ blue-black when the iodine solution was applied.' Options: turned, grew, dried, fell.

steps.reason: The clause describes a change caused by the iodine. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, read the sentence before and after the gap for the clue.
steps.result: The leaves changed colour when the solution was applied.
steps.predictPrompt: Which verb describes a colour change?

steps.reason: Each option must fit the grammar and the scientific sense. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, check the grammar first, then the sense, and cut what fails either.
steps.result: 'Turned' fits the change; 'grew' and 'dried' do not describe colour, and 'fell' is unrelated.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the question tell you to find first?

steps.reason: The chosen word must sound natural in the whole clause. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, say the whole sentence aloud and listen for a wrong note.
steps.result: 'The leaves turned blue-black when the iodine solution was applied.'
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: What a cloze test is asking
paragraphs: A cloze test takes a passage of about 200 words and removes words — around every twentieth word for a ten-gap cloze — and asks you to fill the gaps. It is the only comprehension tool that asks you to produce the missing words, not just recognise them.
The passage is usually about a practical topic — a letter to a bank, a village notice, a government plan, a school newsletter. The tone is readable and slightly formal, never poetic, never legal.

Ten gaps is the typical shape of the cloze. Some gaps are easy (the, of, in), some need thinking (but, however, then, therefore). Every gap is a chance for the examiner to see whether you actually understand English as it is written.

The sentence around the gap always gives you a clue. Look at the signpost: if the previous words were about prices, the next blank is about money; if the gap needs a verb, look for time words like yesterday and will.
Do not panic if a gap looks strange on first view. Read the whole sentence aloud. Your ear usually hears the missing word that your eye cannot. This is a listening test disguised as a reading test.
bullets: Around ten gaps in the 200-word cloze
Each gap has a clue in the surrounding sentences
Say the sentence aloud to hear the gap

content.heading: Go deeper: Four classes of words that fill gaps
paragraphs: Type one: structural words. The, a, an, of, to, in, on, at, for, with, by, from. These are the glue of every English sentence. If you spend more than a second on one of these, you are thinking too hard.

Type two: connection words. But, and, however, therefore, because, so, consequently. These signal logic. A blank before an example is 'for example'. A blank after a contrast is 'however' or 'but'. If the previous sentence argued one side, expect 'however'.

Type three: content words. These carry meaning — spent, saved, won, lost, arrived. For guessing these, read the whole paragraph and match the missing word to the idea of its neighbourhood. The context is king.

Type four: vocabulary words. These test your knowledge directly. If you do not know the word, fall back on attack 1, attack 2 and attack 3. Most candidates fail here not because they missed vocabulary but because they missed the neighbourhood.
Attack everything with the whole paragraph, not just the sentence. Some gaps need three sentences of context, not one. Always read around a tricky gap before guessing.
bullets: Type one: structural glue words
Type two: logic connectives
Type three: content words matched to neighbourhood

content.heading: Go deeper: Why you can almost always fill the gaps
paragraphs: Examiners never set a gap that has no clue. If you are stuck, the clue is just farther away. Search one sentence back and one forward. The answer is sitting somewhere there, often in the exact word that follows the gap.

Every gap falls into one of four families. If the gap needs a verb, the neighbours will be tense-marks: yesterday, will, had. If the gap needs a noun, look for its number or article: this the is singular; those were is plural.
Type the answer into each gap and see which reads naturally. Often, only one option does. 'This was — difficult' is natural. 'This was however difficult' is not. Your ear knows.
If you are still stuck, look at the option letters. Sometimes the examiner groups four options where three sound wrong together with only one true. Elimination is a valid tool — use it.
Finally, check consistency. If you chose 'they' earlier, the next gap likely takes plural verbs; if you chose 'he', the verb is singular. Consistency across gaps is your final safety net.
bullets: If stuck, read one sentence back and one forward
Match each gap to its family: verb, noun, adjective, connector
Your ear is your best option eliminator

content.question: A gap reads: 'Neither the teacher nor the students ______ present.' Choose was or were, and explain why.
hints: Find the nearer subject.
'Students' is plural.
The verb agrees with the nearer subject after 'neither ... nor'.

content.title: The Light and the Starch Test
content.purpose: each gap is a grammar decision inside a working experiment

questions.question: Gap 1: 'This experiment was (1)____ out twice.'
questions.explanation: 'Was' takes a past participle: was carried out. 'Carry' needs 'has been carried'; 'carrying' cannot follow 'was'; 'carries' is a present-tense third person form.

questions.question: Gap 2: 'in the second, they were (2)____ in daylight for six hours each day.'
questions.explanation: 'Kept in daylight' is the exact parallel of 'kept in the dark' — the second run simply swapped the light. 'Left' loses the parallel construction; 'put' would need a destination; 'poured' needs a liquid. The answer is D.

questions.question: Gap 3: 'The amount of starch in each leaf was then (3)____ with iodine solution.'
questions.explanation: 'Was then' takes a past participle. And the meaning is passive: the starch was tested by someone else, with the solution applied to it.

questions.question: Gap 4: 'any leaf which (4)____ blue-black was recorded as positive.'
questions.explanation: This is a restrictive relative clause with 'which' as its subject, and 'turned' is the verb of the whole clause. It has to be past tense to match the reporting clause 'was recorded'.

questions.question: Gap 5: 'The results were (5)____.'
questions.explanation: 'Were' needs an adjective here, not an adverb or a verb. 'Consistently' would need a verb ('were consistently showing'). 'Consists' does not agree with the plural 'results' and is the wrong tense.

questions.question: Gap 6: 'those from the first run (6)____ negative throughout.'
questions.explanation: The subject 'those' is plural and the context is past — 'throughout' refers to the whole experimental period. So a plural past verb: remained.

questions.question: Gap 7: 'light is (7)____ for the formation of starch'
questions.explanation: The passage's conclusion is that light is required for starch to form — the leaves only went positive when they received light. 'Possible', 'visible' and 'rare' would each weaken or contradict that conclusion.

questions.question: Gap 8: 'although the experiment does (8)____ show that light is the only factor involved.'
questions.explanation: Insert 'not' and the sentence states its limit exactly: 'the experiment does not show that light is the only factor'. 'Never' is ungrammatical after 'does' in this pattern; 'hardly' and 'barely' would claim the experiment nearly proved the point, which is not what the passage says.

questions.question: Gap 9: 'The class discussed (9)____ the experiment could be improved.'
questions.explanation: The class was working out the way to improve it — and the next sentence shows the suggestions were about method: more plants, and so on. 'Why' would ask for a reason the experiment was poor; 'when' and 'where' make no sense.

questions.question: Gap 10: 'One suggestion was to use more (10)____ plants, so that an accident affecting one would not affect the whole result.'
questions.explanation: The reason given is that an accident affecting one plant should not affect the whole result. That only works if the plants are separate individuals. 'Identical' would make an accident more likely to affect them all.

paragraphs: This experiment was (1)____ out twice. In the first run, the samples were kept in the dark; in the second, they were (2)____ in daylight for six hours each day. The amount of starch in each leaf was then (3)____ with iodine solution, and any leaf which (4)____ blue-black was recorded as positive.

The results were (5)____. Leaves from the second run were positive in every case, while those from the first run (6)____ negative throughout. The conclusion was that light is (7)____ for the formation of starch, although the experiment does (8)____ show that light is the only factor involved.
The class discussed (9)____ the experiment could be improved. One suggestion was to use more (10)____ plants, so that an accident affecting one would not affect the whole result.

content.prompt: Go back to the ten gaps in The Light and the Starch Test and label each one with its gap type — verb form, agreement, article, preposition, relative, participle, conjunction, comparative, negative, or word choice. Then write the one rule you will run on every gap: what do you underline first, and what do you check second?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names a repeatable procedure rather than a tactic: 'I underline the subject and the verb of the sentence around the gap first; if the gap is where the verb goes, I check the subject for number and the sentence for tense; if the gap is where the noun goes, I check the verb for what it is doing.' It should also show that the labelling worked — that most of the ten gaps fell into two or three types, which is the point: the types repeat, so the practice compounds. If your ten labels are all different, you were probably labelling the individual words rather than the type.

lessons.title: Synonyms
lessons.objective: Choose the option nearest in meaning to a word as it is used in a sentence, allowing for shade, formality and collocation.

content.heading: Synonyms
paragraphs: A candidate replaces 'pleased' with 'delighted' and the sentence still stands, but replacing it with 'angry' breaks it. Synonym items ask for the nearest meaning, not any word from a thesaurus.

content.heading: Meaning is a shade, not an identity
paragraphs: A synonym shares a word's core meaning but rarely all of it. Big and large are close, yet 'a big brother' is not 'a large brother', because big also carries importance and age.

Synonyms differ in intensity, formality and connotation. Angry, furious and livid rise in intensity; begin and commence differ in formality; childlike and childish share a root but one praises and the other criticises.
JAMB tests this precision. The correct option must keep the sentence's meaning, tone and grammar, so a word that is merely related is a distractor rather than an answer.
bullets: Synonyms share a core meaning, not every shade.
Intensity and formality separate close pairs.
The option must fit the sentence's tone.
content.takeaway: Pick the word that preserves the sentence, not the word that merely looks related.

check.question: Which word is nearest in meaning to 'furious'?
check.why: Furious is stronger than annoyed, angry or irritated; enraged matches its intensity.

content.heading: Choose by context
paragraphs: Read the whole sentence before looking at the options. Identify the sense the target word carries there, because a word with several senses may need a different synonym in each.
'Bright' means clever in 'a bright student', cheerful in 'a bright smile', and luminous in 'a bright lamp'. Only the sentence tells you which sense is live at that point.
Predict a word of your own, then test the options by inserting each one. The option that fits without changing the meaning, tone or grammar is the answer.
bullets: Read the sentence before the options.
Decide which sense the word carries there.
Insert each option and re-read the whole sentence carefully.
content.takeaway: Context chooses the sense, and the sense chooses the synonym.

check.question: In 'She gave a bright smile', which word is nearest in meaning to 'bright'?
check.why: A smile is cheerful rather than clever or shiny; 'bright' describes the mood, not intelligence or light.

visual.caption: Work through the sentence before you commit to an option.

content.heading: Traps that cost marks
paragraphs: Near-synonyms are the commonest trap. Emigrate means leave a country and immigrate means enter one; they look alike but point in opposite directions. Affect is a verb and effect is a noun, so they cannot replace each other.
Watch part of speech. A noun cannot fill a slot that needs a verb, even when the meanings overlap: 'success' and 'succeed' are related, but only one fits 'she will ______'.

Watch collocation as well. We say 'heavy rain', not 'strong rain', and 'make a decision', not 'do a decision'. An option can be a true synonym and still sound wrong because English pairs words in fixed ways.
bullets: Near-synonyms may point in opposite directions.
Match the part of speech.
Respect fixed word partnerships.
content.takeaway: A synonym must fit the slot as well as the sense.

check.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to 'emigrate'.
check.why: Emigrate means to leave one's country to settle elsewhere; immigrate is the opposite direction.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If two options seem right, compare their intensity and formality with the original. The closer pair usually turns on one of those two features.

content.problem: Choose the word nearest in meaning to the capitalised word: 'The teacher was PLEASED with the students' performance.'

steps.reason: The adjective describes the teacher's reaction to good work. Reach for the collocation map because the words around the blank reveal the sense carried. If stuck, paraphrase the sentence in plain words first.
steps.result: Pleased means satisfied or glad.
steps.predictPrompt: Which options share that sense?

steps.reason: A synonym must fit the same slot without changing the meaning. Reach for the slot-substitution test because a true synonym drops into the same slot. If stuck, swap each option in and cross off the clashes.
steps.result: 'Delighted' fits; 'angry' and 'disappointed' reverse the meaning.
steps.predictPrompt: What information do you compare before deciding?

steps.reason: When several options fit, intensity decides. Reach for the intensity dial because close synonyms differ in strength. If stuck, rank the survivors from mild to strong and pick the nearest.
steps.result: 'Delighted' is stronger than 'pleased' but keeps the positive sense, so it is the nearest.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.heading: Go deeper: What a synonym really means
paragraphs: A synonym is a word that means the same thing as another word — or almost the same thing. English has few perfect synonyms; most synonyms agree in the centre of meaning and differ in the edges.

Near, beside, next to — near-synonyms, not perfect twins. Near and beside are close in space but not in use; "by the sea" travels to "near the sea", but "by accident" does not travel to "near accident". Synonyms agree in the valley of meaning and drift on the hills, so trust the sentence more than the dictionary.

Register also matters. Formal and informal synonyms pair up in almost every exam: rich/wealthy/affluent, cheap/inexpensive, important/significant/crucial. The register of the passage decides which word fits.

The examiner will never ask for a perfect twin. They ask for the closest cousin that belongs in the neighbourhood. Three attacks: nearest meaning, same register, same neighbourhood. Aim at all three, then check that the word is not too strong for its sentence. If it is, start again.
bullets: Few perfect synonyms in English
Register divides words
Collocation is the third test

content.heading: Go deeper: Why the right synonym fits the sentence
paragraphs: Sentences never stand alone. They have a flavour, a time, a voice and a cast of neighbours. The synonym you choose has to walk into the sentence, not stumble into it.

Consider: 'The footballer fell after a — tackle.' The word selected must go with footballer, fall, tackle. 'Tough' fits 'tackle' in sport language. 'Rugged' does not; 'brutal' does but is too strong for an ordinary match report. The passage overrules the dictionary.

Sentence position also matters. Verbs may take only one partner: 'The soldier — the order' accepts 'obeyed' — English pairs 'obey' with 'order'. Adjectives sit before nouns: 'a — decision' accepts 'wise' but would not feel 'obtuse'.
Tone is the final filter. A sentence about a child's lost pet cannot take 'expired'; the tone is wrong. A sentence about a company's closure cannot take 'passed away'; the collocation is wrong.

Sometimes the synonym differs only by strength: warm, tepid, hot, boiling, searing. The best answer is the one whose strength matches the adjective that the sentence already carries. Always ask: how hot does the sentence show?
bullets: A synonym must belong in its sentence, not just in its meaning
Sentence position filters verbs and adjectives
Match the strength of the word to the sentence

content.heading: Go deeper: The trick examiners use to catch you
paragraphs: The commonest trick: four options, all plausible, two too strong, two too weak or wrong register. Only one is balanced with its sentence. The examiner does the balancing for you, but you have to spot it.

Second trap: words that are spelled like synonyms but mean different things. 'Indifferent' is not a mild form of 'different'; 'sympathetic' is not 'sympathetic to your feelings' as much as it means 'showing pity'.

Third trap: words that only differ by a single letter. 'Imply' and 'infer' are not synonyms — imply means suggest, infer means conclude from evidence. 'Adverse' (unfavourable) and 'averse' (unwilling) look and sound alike but mean different things.
Fourth trap: words that come from a different story at all. 'Hostile' and 'hoarse' both start with 'ho' and fool in a hurry. The examiners love this trap for nervous candidates.
Read all four options aloud, phonetically. 'Imply' versus 'infer', 'adverse' versus 'averse', 'hostile' versus 'hoarse'. Your ear usually beats your eye on these quickfire traps.
bullets: Two too-strong options are usually on the table
Many letter-trap words catch candidates in a hurry
Say the options aloud and the traps fall away

content.question: Choose the word nearest in meaning to ENORMOUS: 'The crowd at the market was ENORMOUS.'
hints: Enormous describes size, not noise or mood.
Look for a word meaning very large.
Huge is the closest option.

content.title: The Village Market

questions.question: Which word is nearest in meaning to aroma as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Aroma means a pleasant smell. The context mentions the aroma of roasted maize and fresh bread.

questions.question: Which word is nearest in meaning to examining as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: Examining means looking at carefully to check quality or condition.

paragraphs: Every Saturday morning, the village market comes alive with activity. Traders spread their goods on mats: ripe mangoes, crisp vegetables, aromatic spices, and colourful fabrics. Buyers move from stall to stall, examining goods carefully and haggling over prices.

The air is filled with the aroma of roasted maize and fresh bread. Children weave through the crowd, while elders sit under trees discussing politics. By noon, the market is at its busiest, and by evening, it is quiet once more, waiting for the next market day.

content.prompt: Think about a word you often use. Can you think of three synonyms for it? Are they exactly the same, or do they have slightly different meanings? Write down your thoughts.
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names a word and lists at least two synonyms, noting whether they are exactly the same or have slightly different meanings. For example: happy = joyful, pleased, delighted. Each has a slightly different shade of meaning.

lessons.title: Antonyms
lessons.objective: Identify the option opposite in meaning to a word in context, distinguishing gradable, complementary and relational opposites.

content.heading: Antonyms
paragraphs: A sentence says the room was 'spacious', and the question asks for the opposite. 'Cramped' works, but 'small' is weaker and 'narrow' may describe only one dimension, so the kind of opposite matters.

content.heading: Three kinds of opposite
paragraphs: Gradable opposites sit on a scale with middle ground: hot and cold, rich and poor, tall and short. Something can be warm or neither rich nor poor, so the pair does not exhaust the possibilities.

Complementary opposites leave no middle: alive and dead, true and false, married and single. Relational opposites name two sides of one relationship: buy and sell, teacher and pupil, parent and child.

Many antonyms are built with prefixes: un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis- and mis-. Happy becomes unhappy, possible becomes impossible, legal becomes illegal, and approve becomes disapprove. The prefix does not always reverse meaning, as inflammable and flammable both mean combustible.
bullets: Gradable pairs allow a middle.
Complementary pairs allow none.
Relational pairs name two sides.
content.takeaway: Name the kind of opposite before you choose the word.

check.question: Which pair is complementary?
check.why: Alive and dead allow no middle state; the others are gradable or relational pairs.

visual.caption: The middle ground tells gradable and complementary opposites apart.

rows.right: Must it be one or the other?

content.heading: Find the opposite in context
paragraphs: Start with the sense the word carries in the sentence. 'Light' opposes heavy in 'a light bag', dark in 'a light room', and serious in 'a light remark'. The sentence, not the dictionary, decides.
Decide what kind of opposite the sentence sets up. If it contrasts two extremes on a scale, a gradable antonym fits; if it denies a state completely, a complementary one does.
Test each option by inserting it. The right antonym keeps the sentence logical and matches the word class. A noun needs a noun, and a verb needs a verb, even when the meanings are opposite.
bullets: Identify the sense in context.
Decide which kind of opposite fits.
Check word class and logic.
content.takeaway: The sentence fixes the sense, and the sense fixes the opposite.

check.question: In 'a light remark', which is the best antonym of 'light'?
check.why: A light remark is not serious; heavy and dark belong to the physical senses of the word.

content.heading: Traps that cost marks
paragraphs: A near-opposite is not an antonym. 'Cool' is not the opposite of 'hot' in a three-way scale if the question wants 'cold', and 'unhappy' is weaker than 'miserable'.

Beware of words that look like negatives but are not. 'Invaluable' means priceless, not worthless; 'inflammable' means combustible, not fireproof; and 'disinterested' means impartial, not uninterested.
Do not accept 'not' plus the word as an answer. An antonym is a word in its own right, and exam options rarely include a phrase such as 'not strong' when 'weak' is available.
bullets: A near-opposite may be too weak.
Prefixes do not always negate.
'Not + word' is not an antonym.
content.takeaway: Check the direction and strength of the opposite, not just its contrast.

check.question: Which word is the opposite of 'invaluable'?
check.why: Invaluable means priceless, so its opposite is worthless; the 'in-' prefix does not make it a negative.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Read the sentence with the original word, then with the option. If the two versions say opposite things, you have the antonym.

content.problem: Choose the word opposite in meaning to SPACIOUS: 'The room was spacious enough for a family of six.'

steps.reason: Spacious describes a room with plenty of space. Reach for the collocation map because the sentence shows how the word behaves in use. If stuck, paraphrase the sentence in plain words first.
steps.result: The word means large and roomy.
steps.predictPrompt: Which option describes too little space?

steps.reason: The antonym must reverse the sense, not merely differ from it. Reach for the morpheme breakdown because roots and endings expose a word's sense. If stuck, drop each option in and read the sentence aloud.
steps.result: 'Cramped' means too small for comfort; 'narrow' covers only width.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you verify this answer?

steps.reason: The replacement must keep the sentence logical. Reach for the sentence-logic check because the antonym must reverse the sense. If stuck, swap it in and ask whether the sentence still holds.
steps.result: 'The room was cramped enough for a family of six' is odd, so the option describes the opposite condition rather than fitting positively.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: What an antonym really is
paragraphs: An antonym is a word with the opposite meaning of another word. English antonymhood comes in three types: complementary (dead and alive), gradable (hot and cold), and relational (teacher and student).

Complementary pairs take no middle: something is either open or shut, on or off, yes or no, male or female. There is no in-between. Gradable pairs have in-betweens: hot, warm, tepid, cool, cold. Relational pairs mirror each other: a parent is a parent only because of a child; the roles face each other.

The exam loves complementary pairs most, because they are safest for distractors that look close but are not. One wrong option is usually the same side of the scale. 'Answering something and answering nothing' holds together; 'answering something and ignoring nothing' does not.

Relational pairs come out cleanest when used as verbs: 'he owns the car ... he uses the car'. 'He owns' is opposite to 'someone uses' only in role, not in fact. The examiner expects you to spot these relationships.
These three subtypes are the only antonym categories you need. Learn what each means in one sentence, then practise finding them in common words.
bullets: Complementary: no middle (open/shut)
Gradable: a spectrum (hot/cold)
Relational: role pairs (teacher/student)

content.heading: Go deeper: Why opposites turn up in pairs
paragraphs: Most antonym pairs are written about a single axis: the 'hot' axis, the 'open' axis, the 'tall' axis, the 'rich' axis. An antonym never travels across axes. Tall is not opposite to slow; rich is not opposite to tired.

That is why the exam asks for the opposite of a word given inside a specific sentence. 'A narrow lane' is opposite to 'a wide lane'. But 'a narrow victory' is often the opposite of 'a landslide'. The axis decides which meaning applies.
The same axis also limits the range. 'Not tall' can mean short, but 'not high' can mean low, that axis's other end. 'Not high' does not mean 'not short'. The axis and the range pair up.
Ask yourself: which axis does this word belong to? Height, width, speed, strength, honesty? Once the axis is named, the opposite follows almost automatically.
Build three antonym axes of your own — any three — and see how many words fall along each. Practice learning antonym pairs along their axis rather than as isolated pairs.
bullets: Antonyms live on one axis at a time
The same word can mean different things on different axes
Name the axis first, then find the opposite

content.heading: Go deeper: The trap examiners set on opposites
paragraphs: The most common antonym trap: four options, two of which are the same side of the axis and two of which are the other side. Your job is to separate the pair. 'Tall' has the pair 'short/small' and the trap 'long' is actually on the tall side of the height axis.

The second trap is the 'negation with a prefix'. 'Unhappy, impossible, antisocial' all use 'un-', 'im-', 'anti-' to mark the opposite. These look like antonyms but are not always — 'unfriendly' opposes 'friendliness', but 'unlock' does not oppose any kind of 'lock' in antonym sense.

The third trap is the 'same-axis but wrong direction'. 'Bought' and 'sold' oppose along the money axis. 'Sold' opposes 'given' only in generous sense, not as a true antonym. Watch for axis–direction mismatch.

The fourth trap is the 'all-or-nothing' answer. 'Not important' vs 'unimportant' vs 'insignificant' vs 'trivial'. Only one of these is the strict opposite of 'important'. The other three straddle the boundary.
Eliminate any option that straddles a boundary. Two or more options often mean the examiner expects the strictest sense of the word. Find it and take it.
bullets: Two options on one side of the axis, two on the other — sort them
Prefix-negations are not always antonyms
Boundary-straddling options are traps, not answers

content.question: Choose the word opposite in meaning to TRANSPARENT: 'The water in the stream was transparent.'
hints: Transparent means you can see through it.
Look for a word meaning you cannot see through it.
Opaque is the direct opposite.

content.title: The Night Train

questions.question: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to crowded as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage says the carriage was almost empty — nearly the opposite of crowded.

questions.question: Which word is most nearly opposite in meaning to dark as used in the passage?
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the almost dark carriage with the loud and bright platform at Kano — bright is the opposite of dark.

paragraphs: The night train rolled into Kaduna station just before dawn. The carriage was almost empty, lit by a single flickering bulb. A few passengers slept against their bags while the conductor walked past checking tickets, his lamp swinging from one seat to the next.

At every stop, the doors opened onto cold harmattan air. Farmers climbed on with baskets of tomatoes, and an elderly woman in a thick wrapper shuffled to the last row. When the train finally reached Kano, the platform was loud and bright, and the travellers stretched with relief after the long, dark journey.

content.prompt: Think of a word you use often. What is its opposite? Does the opposite change with context? Write down your thoughts.
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names a word and gives an opposite, noting any context dependence. For example: light = dark when talking about illumination, but light = heavy when talking about weight.

lessons.title: Common Grammar Errors
lessons.objective: Spot the tense, pronoun, preposition and modifier errors that recur in JAMB 'choose the correct sentence' items.

content.heading: Common grammar errors
paragraphs: A candidate writes 'I have gone to school yesterday' and the time marker alone proves it wrong. Most 'choose the correct sentence' items turn on one such rule.

content.heading: Tense and time markers
paragraphs: Tense must match the time marker. A finished action with a definite past time takes the simple past: 'I went to school yesterday', not 'I have gone to school yesterday'. The present perfect suits a past action with present relevance and no definite time: 'I have finished my revision'.
'Since' and 'for' with a present result take the perfect: 'I have lived here since 2019'. The past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions: 'By the time I arrived, the lesson had started'.
Reported speech shifts the tense back when the reporting verb is past: 'He said he was tired', not 'he is tired'. Time words shift too: 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day'.
bullets: Definite past time takes the simple past.
Present relevance takes the present perfect.
The earlier past action takes the past perfect.
content.takeaway: The time marker usually chooses the tense for you.

check.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have gone to school yesterday.
I had gone to school yesterday.
check.why: 'Yesterday' names a definite past time, so the simple past 'went' is required.

visual.caption: The time marker separates the simple past from the present perfect.

rows.right: have gone, have written, have seen

content.heading: Pronouns and agreement
paragraphs: Pronoun case depends on the job. Use the subject form for the doer and the object form after a preposition or verb: 'between you and me', not 'between you and I'. In formal English, complete the comparison: 'She is taller than I am'.
Reflexive pronouns need a subject to reflect: 'She dressed herself'. They cannot replace a plain subject, so 'Myself and Bola went' is wrong; say 'Bola and I went'.

Agreement follows the head noun, not the nearest noun: 'The list of items is on the desk'. With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject: 'Neither the teacher nor the students were present'.
bullets: Subject form for the doer, object form after a preposition.
A reflexive pronoun needs a subject to reflect.
Agreement follows the head noun.
content.takeaway: Find the word's job before you choose its form.

check.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Between you and I, the plan is risky.
Between you and me, the plan is risky.
Between yourself and me, the plan is risky.
Between you and myself, the plan is risky.
check.why: A preposition takes the object form, so 'between you and me' is correct; reflexives need a subject doing the action.

content.heading: Errors examiners repeat
paragraphs: Double negatives cancel in standard English: 'I did not see anything', not 'I did not see nothing'. Redundancy repeats an idea, so 'return back', 'repeat again' and 'advance forward' each need only one word.
Prepositions are fixed: good at, different from, prefer to, insist on, arrive at or in. Quantifiers split by countability: much water, many books, fewer books, less water.

Confusables change the sentence: its and it's, whose and who's, there, their and they're, affect and effect, borrow and lend, advice and advise. A dangling modifier must describe the subject that follows: 'Walking home, I was caught by rain', not 'Walking home, the rain started'.
bullets: No double negatives in standard English.
Learn each word's fixed preposition.
A modifier describes the subject that follows it.
content.takeaway: One wrong word is enough to disqualify an option.

check.question: Choose the correct sentence.
check.why: The fixed collocation is 'good at' a subject or skill.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Read each option word for word. Most 'best sentence' questions test one rule, so a single wrong word tells you the answer.

content.problem: Choose the correct form: 'By the time we arrived, the film ______ (start).'

steps.reason: One action happened before the other in the past. Reach for the parse ladder because naming each verb builds the clause map. If stuck, underline every finite verb and label its time.
steps.result: The film started before we arrived.
steps.predictPrompt: Which tense marks the earlier action?

steps.reason: The past perfect marks the action completed before another past action. Reach for the tense map because it orders past actions against their reference point. If stuck, find which action happened first and make it past perfect.
steps.result: The earlier action takes 'had started'.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the question tell you to find first?

steps.reason: The finished sentence must show the order clearly. Reach for the parse ladder because re-reading rebuilds the clause with its verb. If stuck, swap in had started and check the order still reads true.
steps.result: 'By the time we arrived, the film had started.'
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.heading: Go deeper: The errors that trip up every writer
paragraphs: Every average student makes the same handful of grammar errors. They are not exotic. They are not even hard to fix once named. The examiner asks about them because they reveal whether you can notice a wrong sentence without a teacher pointing it out.

The seven that return most often: the wrong past tense, the wrong auxiliary, subject–verb disagreement, dangling modifiers, the wrong preposition, the wrong comparative, and the confused article. Memorise these seven by name and example.
Each of these happens because the speaker's ear is faster than the writer's eye. Speaking accepts many things; writing rejects them. The gap between the two is the examiner's hunting ground.

Look at the three most common ear-speak: 'he go' for 'he goes', 'I haven't went' for 'I haven't gone', 'much people' for 'many people'. Every one of these is both easy to notice and easy to fix once it is seen.
Your ear may already tolerate these. Your eye must be trained to catch them. Read every sentence aloud in your head; if it sounds like a spoken slang, the examiner will mark it wrong.
bullets: Seven errors return every time: tense, auxiliary, agreement, dangling, preposition, comparative, article
Ear-speak passes; eye-write must stop it
Read every sentence aloud in your head

content.heading: Go deeper: Subject–verb agreement in detail
paragraphs: Subject–verb agreement means the verb matches in number: singular subject takes singular verb; plural takes plural. 'She goes' is correct; 'she go' is not. 'They go' is correct; 'they goes' is not.
The trap is the 'stuffed' subject. 'The boy in the blue shirt who ran the fastest in the race goes.' The head is 'boy', not 'race' or 'shirt'. Strip away the qualifiers and say 'the boy goes'.

The 'there is/are' inversion. 'There is a problem in the office.' Singular. 'There are problems in the office.' Plural. Use the true number of what is at the end of the sentence, not the word 'there'.

The collective noun trap. 'The team is winning.' Singular, acting as one unit. 'The team are wearing their own shirts.' Plural, acting as individuals. When the whole acts as one, the verb is singular; when its members act separately, the verb is plural.
Most items will not test the hard cases. They test three: stuffed subjects, there is/are, and team/club/family collectives. Master those three and the subject–verb mark is yours.
bullets: Strip the qualifiers; find the head
There is/are follows the final noun's number
Collectives: singular when one unit, plural when individuals

content.heading: Go deeper: The preposition puzzle
paragraphs: Prepositions are the smallest words in English and the ones that confuse most learners. 'In' and 'on' alone have a hundred uses each; English does not follow any one rule. You must learn them in pairings.
Three fix-it tricks help. The first: the word tells you. 'Arrive in Lagos' is right; 'arrive to Lagos' is wrong. 'Arrive' chooses 'in' for cities; 'leave' chooses 'for' for destinations.
The second: look at the neighbour. 'Ask for' is fixed. 'Ask about' is fixed. 'Ask to' takes an infinitive. 'Ask if' takes a clause. The preposition and its neighbour are married.

The third: fixed pairs. Some words allow only one preposition: 'accused of' (never 'accused for'), 'accompanied by' (never 'accompanied with'), 'capable of' (never 'capable for'). The word, not the prefix, decides the partner.
When you do not know, eliminate the ugly word. English has twelve ugly prepositions and their twelve beautiful partners. Most candidates lose marks by leaving the ugly ones in place.
bullets: It is 'arrive in', 'leave for', 'ask for', 'ask about'
Prepositions are married to their neighbours
Pair negatives only with their partners

content.question: Report this sentence correctly: 'He said, "I am tired."'
hints: The reporting verb 'said' is past.
Step the present tense back one stage.
'Am' becomes 'was'.

pair: The list of items are on the desk.
The list of items is on the desk.
content.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun (list), not with the noun nearest to it (items). Ignore prepositional phrases when finding the subject.
content.counterexample: The list of items is on the desk — but: The items on the desk are mine.

pair: Neither the teacher nor the students was present.
Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
content.rule: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it — students, so were.
content.counterexample: Neither the students nor the teacher was present. (Nearer subject: teacher → was.)

pair: He requested for permission to leave.
He requested permission to leave.
content.rule: Request is transitive here — it takes the object directly. “Request for” only appears in the noun phrase “a request for…”.
content.counterexample: She applied for the job (apply needs for), but: She requested an extension (request takes none).

pair: The reason he left is because he was tired.
The reason he left is that he was tired.
content.rule: “The reason is…” must be completed with a that-clause, not a because-clause — because already contains the reason, so the sentence repeats itself.
content.counterexample: The reason is that the road flooded — never “the reason is because…”.

content.rule: The relative pronoun already stands for the boy — adding “him” gives the clause two objects. One slot, one pronoun.
content.answer: The boy whom the teacher praised passed the examination. (Accept: The boy who was praised by the teacher passed.)
content.prompt: Rebuild this into one correct sentence: “The boy who the teacher praised him passed the examination.”

content.rule: Hardly/scarcely at the front forces inversion — auxiliary verb before the subject. No inversion, no mark.
content.answer: Hardly had the referee blown the whistle when the crowd rushed onto the pitch.
content.prompt: Rebuild this into one correct sentence: “Hardly the referee had blown the whistle when the crowd rushed onto the pitch.”
Which of the four pairs above would still catch you under time pressure — and what one-second check will you run on every underlining that looks like it?
content.modelResponse: A strong answer names the specific trap (“neither…nor distance agreement”), states the check as a physical habit (“cover the phrase between the subject and the verb, then re-read”), and gives the counterexample from memory. That check is your insurance policy on Saturday.

pair: She plays piano very well.
She plays the piano very well.
content.rule: Instruments take the definite article: play the piano, the guitar, the drums. Drop it only for the activity in general (“Piano is fun”).
content.counterexample: He plays the guitar — but: Guitar music filled the hall (general, no article).

pair: The meeting is on Monday morning at 10 o’clock.
The meeting is in Monday morning at 10 o’clock.
content.rule: Time ladder: at for clock times (at 10), on for days and dated mornings (on Monday, on Monday morning), in for months/years/periods (in June, in the morning).
content.counterexample: On Monday morning at 10 — never “in Monday”. But: in the morning (no day named).

pair: She said she will come tomorrow.
She said she would come the next day.
content.rule: Reported speech steps the tense back: will → would, and the time marker shifts (tomorrow → the next day). The reporting verb “said” is past, so the whole clause follows it.
content.counterexample: She says she will come tomorrow (present reporting verb — no shift). She said she would come.

pair: The principal suggested that he goes home.
The principal suggested that he go home.
content.rule: Suggest, insist, demand, recommend take the base form (subjunctive): no -s, no tense. “Suggested that he go”, never “goes” or “went”.
content.counterexample: They insisted that she stay — never “stays”. Test with: The rule demands it be so (not “is”).

pair: Walking home, the rain started suddenly.
Walking home, I was caught by sudden rain.
content.rule: An opening -ing phrase must describe the subject that follows. Rain cannot walk — attach the phrase to the walker (I), or the sentence dangles.
content.counterexample: Exhausted, the team slept (team can be exhausted ✓). Exhausted, the whistle blew (whistle cannot ✗).

pair: You are coming with us, isn’t it?
You are coming with us, aren’t you?
content.rule: Question tags echo the statement’s auxiliary and subject: are + you → aren’t you. “Isn’t it” answers nothing in this sentence — it is the tag of last resort, not a universal one.
content.counterexample: She can swim, can’t she? They left early, didn’t they? (Match auxiliary + pronoun every time.)

lessons.title: Parts of Speech
lessons.objective: Classify a word by the job it does in a sentence, and recognise when the same word changes class with position.

content.heading: Parts of speech
paragraphs: The same word can be a noun in one sentence and a verb in the next. Parts of speech are jobs, not permanent labels on words.

content.heading: Eight jobs, not eight lists
paragraphs: Every word in a sentence does one of eight jobs. A noun names a person, place, thing or idea; a pronoun stands in for a noun; a verb asserts an action or a state; an adjective modifies a noun; an adverb modifies a verb, adjective or another adverb.
A preposition shows relationship (in, on, under, between); a conjunction joins words or clauses (and, but, because, although); an interjection expresses sudden feeling (wow, ouch, oh).
Classify by the job, not by the word. 'Brilliant' is an adjective in 'a brilliant answer' and a noun in 'the brilliant' when it means brilliant people. Position tells you which job it is doing.
bullets: Nouns name, pronouns substitute, verbs assert.
Adjectives and adverbs modify.
Prepositions, conjunctions and interjections connect or exclaim.
content.takeaway: A part of speech is a job a word does in a sentence.

check.question: In 'She sings beautifully', what part of speech is 'beautifully'?
check.why: It modifies the verb 'sings', which is the job of an adverb.

visual.caption: Content words carry the message; function words hold the grammar together.

content.heading: The same word, a different job
paragraphs: Many words change class with position. 'Fast' is an adjective in 'a fast car' and an adverb in 'he drives fast'. 'Run' is a verb in 'I run daily' and a noun in 'a quick run'.
Test the job with a frame. A noun fits after 'the' or 'a'; an adjective fits between 'the' and a noun; an adverb answers how, when or where; a verb changes for tense.
Watch -ly. It usually marks an adverb (quickly, carefully), but friendly, lovely and lonely are adjectives, and 'hardly' means scarcely rather than 'in a hard way'.
bullets: Position decides the class.
Apply a frame to test the job.
-ly is a clue, not proof.
content.takeaway: Ask what the word is doing, not what it usually is.

check.question: In 'a quick run', what part of speech is 'run'?
check.why: It follows the adjective 'quick' and names an activity, so it is a noun here.

content.heading: Exam traps
paragraphs: Do not call 'the' an adjective; it is an article or determiner. Possessive adjectives (my, your, our) must be followed by a noun: 'my book', never 'I book'.
A full sentence needs a finite verb marked for tense, not just a participle: 'The man running' is a phrase, while 'The man is running' is a sentence.

'To' before a verb marks the infinitive, not a preposition: 'to swim' is a verb form, while 'to the pool' is a prepositional phrase. 'That' can be a pronoun, a conjunction or a determiner, so read its job.
bullets: 'The' is an article, not an adjective.
A sentence needs a finite verb.
'To' can mark an infinitive or a preposition.
content.takeaway: The commonest trap is a word that looks like one class and works as another.

check.question: What part of speech is 'to' in 'She went to the market'?
check.why: It introduces the place phrase 'the market', so it is a preposition; an infinitive marker would be followed by a verb.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Ask one question about the word: does it name, replace, assert, modify, relate, join or exclaim? The answer is the part of speech.

content.problem: Identify the part of speech of 'light' in: (a) 'The light failed.' (b) 'She carried a light bag.' (c) 'He likes to travel light.'

steps.reason: A word after 'the' and before a verb is usually the subject. Reach for the parse ladder because position reveals what a word does in the clause. If stuck, ask who or what the verb is about.
steps.result: 'Light' names a thing, so it is a noun in (a).
steps.predictPrompt: What does it modify in the second sentence?

steps.reason: A word between a determiner and a noun modifies that noun. Reach for the parse ladder because each rung tests one job. If stuck, check whether the word sits before a noun it describes.
steps.result: 'Light' describes the bag, so it is an adjective in (b).
steps.predictPrompt: In your own words, why does this step come before the next one?

steps.reason: A word modifying the verb 'travel' answers how. Reach for the parse ladder because the last rung tests how the verb is done. If stuck, ask whether the word answers how after the verb.
steps.result: 'Light' is an adverb in (c).
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.heading: Go deeper: What parts-of-speech questions really test
paragraphs: Parts-of-speech questions ask one thing: what job does this word do in the sentence? It is the only grammar question that has nothing to do with right or wrong; it is about seeing structure.

English has eight classes. You know most of them already: noun names, verb does, adjective describes, adverb modifies, pronoun stands in, preposition links, conjunction connects, interjection explodes. The examiner wants you to name them in order, not just recognise them.
Name the jobs, not the symbols. 'John' is a noun because it names. 'Slowly' is an adverb because it says how. 'Under' is a preposition because it places. 'But' is a conjunction because it joins.

The difficulty is the same word doing different jobs. 'School' is a noun in 'the school is old'. It is an adjective in 'school bell rings at seven'. It is a verb in 'the soldiers school themselves in discipline'. The only way to tell is the sentence around the word.
That is why examiners just love this question — it catches students who know the list but not the grammar.
bullets: Name the job, not the symbol
Same word does different jobs in different sentences
The sentence decides, not the word alone

content.heading: Go deeper: Verbs, nouns and adjectives in detail
paragraphs: A verb names an action or state. 'The boy runs.' (action). 'The boy is tired.' (state). The auxiliary 'is' merges with the main verb to make tense and number. 'Is running' tells time; 'runs' tells count and tense; 'was running' tells the past and duration.

A noun names a thing, a person, a place, an idea. 'The giraffe is tall' names an animal. 'Honesty wins' names an idea. 'Lagos is busy' names a place. Concrete nouns name what you can touch; abstract nouns name what you cannot.

An adjective describes a noun or pronoun. 'A beautiful singer' describes the noun 'singer'. 'The clouds are dark' describes the noun 'clouds'. Adjectives answer which one, what kind, how many — all three questions matter at the exam.

Three of the trickiest pairs are verb vs noun, adjective vs adverb, and determiner vs preposition. A verb can travel with its adverb; an adjective must anchor its noun; a determiner (the, a, this) points, a preposition connects.
Control by substitution: swap the word with a person's name. If the sentence still parses, the word is a noun. If swapping kills the meaning, the word is a verb or an adjective.
bullets: Verb: action or state, always with person or number marks
Adjective answers which one, what kind, how many
Substitute a person's name to confirm nounhood

content.heading: Go deeper: The connections and the sentences that fail without them
paragraphs: Prepositions link words and name positions: in, on, at, under, above, beside, by. Every preposition takes a complement. No complement no preposition. 'To the station', not 'to station'.

Conjunctions link clauses or phrases: and, but, or, so, because, although, since, unless, if. 'Although it was raining, we continued' — 'although' shows contrast. The clause it introduces is the subordinate clause; the other one is the main clause.

Interjections are noise: wow, oh, hey, um, uh, ouch. They never carry the grammar of a sentence, only its feeling. They sit at the start, tagged on with punctuation. Even in an exam they still only do that one thing.

Determiners are the little pointers: the, a, an, this, that, these, those, my, your, their, some, any. They never appear before verbs. A few can stand alone when the noun is understood: 'some left early', 'some of the bread is gone'.

The exam tests the linkages between these. 'In' links 'the' and 'station'; 'although' links 'it was raining' and 'we continued'; 'some' links 'water' and 'before meal'. Learn the links, and the sentence becomes a map you can walk through.
bullets: Prepositions always take a complement
Conjunctions link clauses at equal level or subordinate
Determiners point; they never carry grammar by themselves

content.question: In 'The rich should help the poor', what part of speech are 'rich' and 'poor'?
hints: The words normally describe nouns.
Here they follow 'the' and act as the subject and object.
Adjectives can become nouns in this pattern.

lessons.title: Mood, Tense and Aspect
lessons.objective: Distinguish tense, aspect and mood, and choose the correct verb form for time, completion and attitude.

content.heading: Mood, tense and aspect
paragraphs: A student writes 'I am living here since 2019' and loses the mark, because the sentence needs a tense and an aspect that agree with 'since'.

content.heading: Tense and aspect together
paragraphs: Tense locates the action in past, present or future. Aspect describes it: simple for a fact, continuous for progress, and perfect for completion with relevance to a later time.

The combinations give forms such as 'she writes' for a habit, 'she is writing' for now, 'she has written' for a finished action with present relevance, and 'she has been writing' for an action continuing up to now.
'Since' and 'for' with a present result take the present perfect: 'I have lived here since 2019', not 'I am living here since 2019'. 'For' names a length of time; 'since' names a starting point.
bullets: Tense tells you when.
Aspect tells you finished or continuing.
Since takes a point in time; for takes a length.
content.takeaway: Tense gives the time; aspect gives the shape of the action.

check.question: Choose the correct sentence.
check.why: A situation that began in the past and continues now takes the present perfect, and 'since' marks the starting point.

content.heading: Progressive and perfect
paragraphs: The progressive (be + -ing) presents an action in progress; the perfect (have + past participle) presents it as complete before a reference point. 'She was cooking when I arrived' sets one action inside another.
Stative verbs such as know, believe, own, belong and seem resist the progressive. Say 'I know the answer', not 'I am knowing the answer'.
The past perfect marks the earlier of two past actions: 'By the time we arrived, the bus had left.' The future perfect does the same for a future reference point: 'By June, she will have finished'.
bullets: Progressive: the action is in progress.
Perfect: the action is complete before a reference point.
Stative verbs avoid the progressive.
content.takeaway: Use the perfect when one action must be finished before another.

check.question: By the time we arrived, the bus ______.
check.why: The bus left before our arrival, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect.

visual.caption: Tense fixes the time; aspect fixes whether the action is finished or still unfolding.

content.heading: Mood
paragraphs: Mood shows the speaker's attitude to the action. The indicative states a fact, the imperative gives a command, and the subjunctive expresses a wish, a demand or a hypothetical.
The subjunctive keeps the base verb after expressions such as 'it is essential that', 'I recommend that' and 'if I were': 'It is essential that he go early' and 'If I were you, I would wait'.
The imperative has no subject and no tense: 'Sit down' and 'Do not enter'. Questions use the interrogative: 'Has she left?' The exam often tests 'If I were' against the incorrect 'If I was'.
bullets: Indicative: a fact.
Imperative: a command.
Subjunctive: a wish, demand or hypothesis.
content.takeaway: Mood tells you whether the speaker states, commands or imagines.

check.question: If I ______ you, I would apologise.
check.why: A hypothetical condition takes the subjunctive 'were', even with a singular subject.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Tense is not the same as aspect. 'She wrote' and 'She has written' are both past-related, but only the second links the action to now.

content.problem: By next June, Ada ______ here for five years. Choose the correct form: will live, will have lived, lives or lived.

steps.reason: 'By next June' points to a moment in the future. Reach for the tense map because it pins the sentence to a time point. If stuck, circle the time phrase and place it on the line.
steps.result: The sentence needs a future form.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the five-year period complete at that moment?

steps.reason: 'For five years' measures a period completed by the reference point. Reach for the tense map because aspect marks completion by the reference point. If stuck, ask whether the five years are finished at that moment.
steps.result: The action will be complete by next June, so the future perfect fits.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you choose between the possible routes?

steps.reason: The future perfect is will + have + past participle. Reach for the tense map because it builds the future perfect from its parts. If stuck, assemble will, have and the past participle aloud.
steps.result: Ada will have lived here for five years.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: What tense and aspect really mean
paragraphs: Tense is time. English has three tenses only: past, present, future. That is all. 'I went', 'I go', 'I shall go'. You may add adverbs like 'yesterday' and 'tomorrow' but the verb will not change its own time.

Aspect is the shape of the action inside the time. 'I am going' is in progress now. 'I have gone' is complete by now. 'I had gone' was complete before another past event. Three aspects frozen over the three tenses give you nine tense-aspect forms.

Mood is the writer's attitude to the action. Indicative: 'He runs'. Imperative: 'Run!' Subjunctive: 'I wish he were here' (not 'was'). Conditional: 'If he ran, I would walk'. Each mood opens a different door onto the same action.

Students confuse these two only because they are usually taught together. 'I have eaten' is present perfect — that is tense and aspect in one. 'If I had known' is past conditional — that is tense, aspect and mood.

Learn the nine tense-aspect forms by heart: simple, progressive and perfect past; simple, progressive and perfect present; simple, progressive and perfect future. When you hear one, name it in one second. Naming is the whole skill.
bullets: Tense: past, present, future — three only
Aspect: simple, progressive, perfect
Mood: indicative, imperative, subjunctive, conditional

content.heading: Go deeper: The perfect aspect as the single master key
paragraphs: The perfect aspect is the single most useful piece of English grammar to own. It links two times: now and then, or then and later. 'I have read that book' means sometime before now. 'I had read the book before she arrived' means an earlier past pointed at a later past.

The progressive aspect shows an event in the middle. 'I am reading' is an event ongoing as I speak. 'I was reading' is an event ongoing as something else happened. 'I will be reading' is an event ongoing at a future point. Progressive always means in the middle of a span.

The simple past places the whole event in the past. 'I ate'. The whole egg is in the past, not in the middle of it. 'I have eaten' places the egg in 'by now'. And 'I had eaten' places it in 'by before she ate'.

The exam usually tests the chain of past perfect. 'Before he left, he had finished the work.' Past (before), then past perfect (finished). Reverse the order and the meaning breaks. Know the links by heart.
Pair tense with time words: yesterday, now, by tomorrow, before, after, while, then, ago. Time words are the map; tense and aspect is the journey you describe on it.
bullets: Perfect links an earlier time to a later reference
Progressive shows the event in its middle
Simple past places the whole event in the past

content.heading: Go deeper: The examiner's two common tests
paragraphs: Test one: changing tenses inside a passage. The examiner will swap tenses mid-sentence and ask you to spot the error. 'He goes to the market yesterday' is wrong. 'He went to the market yesterday' is right. The time word 'yesterday' is a hard anchor.

Test two: conditionals. 'If he had worked harder, he would have passed' correct. 'If he will work hard' wrong. The past perfect and 'would' keep the tense sequence stable. Mixing tenses between the if-clause and the main clause is the exam's favourite error.

Test three: the 'if vs when' distinction. 'If he comes, he will see me' (maybe). 'When he comes, he sees me' (definite). Both are fine; the meaning differs. The exam often tests whether you can feel the difference.

For all three, read every sentence yourself and swap in the plain tense. 'He goes' can never pair with 'yesterday'. 'I will go' can never pair with 'was'. The time words tell you which tense must follow.
Learn the three commonest conditional frames: if + present, use will; if + past, use would; if + past perfect, use would have. Memorise the frames; the meanings follow.
bullets: Anchor tenses to time words; mismatches are the test
Match if-clause and main-clause tenses
Master the three conditional frames

content.question: I wish I ______ the answer yesterday. Choose: know, knew, had known or have known.
hints: The wish is about a past event that cannot be changed.
A past regret takes the past perfect after 'wish'.
The correct form is had known.

lessons.title: Concord Rules
lessons.objective: Match the verb to its true subject across interrupting phrases, paired conjunctions, quantities and fixed plurals.

content.heading: Concord rules
