paragraphs: A sentence says 'The list of items are on the desk', and the verb has agreed with the wrong noun. Concord questions reward the candidate who finds the real subject.

content.heading: The head noun rules
paragraphs: Concord means the verb agrees with its subject in number and person. A singular subject takes a singular verb and a plural subject a plural verb: 'The student studies', 'The students study'.

Words between the subject and the verb do not change the verb. In 'The box of matches is on the shelf', the head noun is 'box', so the verb is 'is'. Cross out the phrase 'of matches' before you choose.

Indefinite pronouns are singular: each, every, everyone, everybody, anybody, nobody and nothing take a singular verb: 'Everybody is here'. 'Neither' and 'either' are also singular when they stand alone: 'Neither of the answers is correct'.
bullets: The verb agrees with the subject.
Ignore phrases between subject and verb.
Indefinite pronouns are singular.
content.takeaway: Strip the sentence to its head noun before you choose the verb.

check.question: The list of items ______ on the desk.
check.why: The head noun is 'list', which is singular, so the verb is 'is'; 'of items' does not govern it.

content.heading: Proximity and special subjects
paragraphs: With 'either ... or', 'neither ... nor' and 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it. 'Neither the teacher nor the students were present' takes 'were' because 'students' is nearer.

'There is' and 'there are' agree with the noun that follows: 'There are many questions left'. With fractions and percentages, the verb matches the noun after 'of': 'Half of the cake has gone', 'Half of the students have gone'.
Collective nouns such as committee, team and family are usually singular when they act as one body: 'The committee has given its report'. 'The number of' is singular, while 'a number of' is plural.
bullets: Paired conjunctions follow the nearer subject.
'There is/are' follows the noun after it.
'The number of' is singular; 'a number of' is plural.
content.takeaway: When two subjects compete, the nearer one wins.

check.question: Neither the teacher nor the students ______ present.
check.why: The verb agrees with the nearer subject 'students', which is plural, so 'were' is correct.

visual.caption: One small word changes the number of the subject.

rows.left: The number of students has risen.
rows.right: A number of students are absent.

content.heading: Quantities, time and fixed plurals
paragraphs: An amount, distance or period treated as one unit is singular: 'Ten years is a long time', 'Five thousand naira is enough', 'Ten kilometres is a long walk'.

Some nouns look plural but take singular verbs: news, mathematics, physics, economics and measles: 'The news is good'. Others are plural despite looking singular: police, cattle and people: 'The police are investigating'.
Pair nouns such as scissors, trousers and glasses take plural verbs: 'The scissors are sharp'. 'One of the + plural noun' takes a singular verb: 'One of the students is absent'.
bullets: A unit of amount, time or distance is singular.
News and mathematics are singular.
Police, cattle and people are plural.
content.takeaway: Judge the noun by what it denotes, not by its final letter.

check.question: The news ______ better today.
check.why: 'News' ends in -s but is singular, so it takes 'is'.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Cross out every phrase between the head noun and the verb, then match the verb to what remains.

content.problem: Choose the correct verb: 'The quality of the students' projects ______ impressive.'

steps.reason: The verb agrees with the subject, not with the nearest noun. Reach for the agreement mirror because it reflects the true subject behind the phrases. If stuck, strip every prepositional phrase and see what remains.
steps.result: The subject is 'quality', which is singular.
steps.predictPrompt: What phrase sits between the subject and the verb?

steps.reason: Prepositional phrases do not change the number of the subject. Reach for the agreement mirror because stripping the phrase shows what the verb matches. If stuck, cross out everything after quality and read the bare sentence.
steps.result: The sentence reduces to 'The quality ... is impressive'.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you choose between the possible routes?

steps.reason: A singular subject takes a singular verb. Reach for the agreement mirror because singular subjects take singular verbs. If stuck, read it aloud with is and then with are and hear the match.
steps.result: 'The quality of the students' projects is impressive.'
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: What concord really is
paragraphs: Concord is the agreement between the subject and the verb — number against number, person against person. Singular subject with singular verb, plural subject with plural verb, first person with first person. That is the whole thing.

The interesting part is where the agreement breaks. 'None of the students is prepared' or 'none of the students are prepared'? 'Each is fine', 'each are fine'? These have answers, but they are picked by rule, not by ear.

The rule: if the subject is singular and the sense is singular, the verb is singular. If the subject is a collective noun — a team, a family, a government, a crowd — the verb follows the collective's action, not its size. 'The government is meeting today.' 'The team are wearing their shirts.'
The pronouns that follow: 'each is', 'either is', 'neither is', 'someone is', 'no one is'. 'Everyone is'. 'Everybody is'. Always singular, never plural, even if the noun seems to mean many.

The exam's favourite trap: a subject stuffed full of prepositional phrases. 'The boy in the blue shirt who came here late yesterday and missed the exam is singular — the subject is still 'the boy'.' The subject is still 'boy'. Singular verb.
bullets: Agreement is between the true subject and the verb
Collective nouns take singular verbs when acting as one
Either/each/no-one/everybody always singular

content.heading: Go deeper: The trickiest concord cases
paragraphs: The 'there is/are' swap. 'There is a table in the room.' Singular — the table is one. 'There are tables in the room.' Plural — tables are many. The number matches the noun after 'there', not the word 'there'.

The 'much/countable' mismatch. 'Much people are at the gate.' Wrong. 'Many people are at the gate.' Right. 'Much water.' Right. 'Many water.' Wrong. 'Much' pairs with mass nouns, 'many' with count nouns.
Pair nouns always take plural verbs — 'the scissors are on the table'. Only in the fixed phrase 'a pair of' does the verb turn singular: 'a pair of scissors is on the table'.

The 'neither ... nor / either ... or' mirror. 'Neither the boy nor the girl was there.' The verb follows the closer subject when names differ in number. 'Neither the boys nor the girl is.' Girl is singular.
The 'sum of money' singulars: 'Two thousand naira is too much.' 'Fifty years is a long time.' Time and money are often singular because the sum is one.
bullets: There is/are follows the noun after
Much with mass nouns, many with count nouns
Either/neither takes the number of the nearer subject

content.heading: Go deeper: The interplay of pronouns and agreement
paragraphs: A pronoun must agree with the noun it stands in for. 'The girl who arrived early ate her lunch.' Singular subject, singular pronoun. 'The girls who arrived early ate their lunch.' Plural subject, plural pronoun.

The trickiest is 'it' for non-people. 'Your book is on the table.' 'It is on the table.' Fine. But 'students who are diligent earn their degrees.' A modifier with plural antecedent takes a plural pronoun; the modifier agrees with its antecedent.

The possessive pronoun follows its noun, not the object of that noun: 'the boy's books are on the table' — singular boy, plural books. 'the boys books' — singular possession, singular books. 'the books of the boys' — same meaning, different syntax.
Reflexive pronouns follow agreement too: 'he drove himself', not 'he drove himselves'. 'They drove themselves', not 'they drove himself'. The suffix '-self' must agree with the subject.
One reliable test for concord questions: substitute 'he' or 'she' for the noun. If the sentence parses badly, the concord is wrong. If it parses well, you are done.
bullets: Pronoun takes number and gender of its antecedent
Reflexive agrees with subject: he drove himself
Test by swapping in he/she

content.question: Choose the correct verb: 'One of the boys ______ a bicycle.'
hints: The subject is 'one', not 'boys'.
'One of the' is followed by a plural noun but takes a singular verb.
The answer is 'has'.

lessons.title: Degrees of Comparison
lessons.objective: Form the positive, comparative and superlative degrees correctly, and choose the degree and marker that match the number of items compared.

content.heading: Degrees of comparison
paragraphs: A shopper says one phone is 'more cheaper' than another and the sentence collapses. Comparison runs on a small set of forms, and the exam checks whether you can pick the right one.

content.heading: Three degrees, three forms
paragraphs: The positive degree names a quality without comparing: 'This bag is heavy.' The comparative compares two things: 'This bag is heavier than that one.' The superlative sets one item above a group of three or more: 'This is the heaviest bag in the shop.'

Formation follows syllable count. One-syllable adjectives add -er and -est (cheap, cheaper, cheapest), while adjectives of three or more syllables use more and most (expensive, more expensive, most expensive).

Two-syllable adjectives vary: happy becomes happier, but careful becomes more careful. Spelling changes apply before the ending: y turns to i in heavier, the consonant doubles in bigger, and the silent e drops in larger. Learn the spelling alongside the form.
bullets: Positive: no comparison at all.
Comparative: exactly two items.
Superlative: three or more items.
content.takeaway: The degree tells you how many things are being compared.

check.question: Which is the superlative form of 'useful'?
check.why: 'Useful' has two syllables and takes 'most' for the superlative; 'usefullest' is not an English form.

content.heading: Comparing like with like
paragraphs: Use the comparative for two items and the superlative for three or more. 'She is taller than her sister' compares two people, while 'She is the tallest of the three sisters' compares three.

The markers differ. The comparative takes 'than'; the superlative takes 'the' and usually 'of' or 'in': 'the best of the three', 'the fastest in the class'. A comparative without 'than' is often incomplete, and a superlative without 'the' is often wrong.

Never double the marker. 'More better', 'most tallest' and 'more easier' are wrong because the form already carries the comparison. Compare like with like as well: say 'Lagos is bigger than Ibadan', not 'Lagos is bigger than Ibadan's population'.
bullets: Comparative: two items, followed by 'than'.
Superlative: three or more, preceded by 'the'.
Never combine 'more' with -er or 'most' with -est.
content.takeaway: Count the items first, then choose the form and its marker.

check.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She is more taller than her sister.
She is the tallest of the two sisters.
She is taller than her sister.
She is tallest than her sister.
check.why: Two people take the comparative 'taller' with 'than'; 'more taller' doubles the marker and 'tallest' is superlative.

visual.caption: The number of items decides both the form and the marker that follows it.

content.heading: Irregulars and fixed patterns
paragraphs: Some adjectives do not take -er or -est at all: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, further, furthest; little, less, least; many and much, more, most. There is no rule that generates these, so learn each set whole.
Several patterns are fixed. 'As tall as' states equality, 'not so tall as' states inequality, and 'the more you practise, the better you become' links two changes that rise together.

Watch the near misses. 'Elder' describes family order and never takes 'than', while 'older' is the general comparative; 'lesser' means smaller in importance, not size. 'Farther' is usual for physical distance, while 'further' covers distance or addition.
bullets: Good, better, best; bad, worse, worst.
'As ... as' states equality.
'Elder' takes no 'than'; 'older' does.
content.takeaway: Learn the irregulars as whole sets, because no rule will generate them.

check.question: The ______ of the two routes is the one through town.
check.why: Two routes take the comparative 'shorter'; 'shortest' would need three or more routes.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: 'More' and '-er' never work together. If the adjective already ends in -er, the comparison is complete.

content.problem: Choose the correct form: 'This is the (good) result of the three tests.'

steps.reason: The degree depends on how many things are compared. Reach for the degrees chart because the degree depends on how many are compared. If stuck, count the nouns that tell you what is being compared.
steps.result: Three tests are being compared.
steps.predictPrompt: Which degree handles three or more?

steps.operation: Check whether the adjective is regular
steps.reason: Irregular adjectives do not take -er or -est. Reach for the irregular-list check because some adjectives change shape entirely. If stuck, say good, better, best aloud and notice the shift.
steps.result: 'Good' is irregular: good, better, best.
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.reason: A superlative normally takes 'the'. Reach for the degrees chart because the superlative row carries the article. If stuck, place good, better, best on the chart and pick the last.
steps.result: This is the best result of the three tests.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you test this answer before writing it down?

content.heading: Go deeper: What the three degrees are
paragraphs: English compares adjectives in exactly three degrees. The positive (big, tall, happy), the comparative (bigger, taller, happier), and the superlative (biggest, tallest, happiest). Every adjective fits into one of the three slots.

Positive says nothing about comparison — it simply names the quality. Comparative is used when you compare two things. Superlative is used when you compare three or more, or when you single one out as above all others.
The grammar test is straightforward: comparative uses 'than' or 'of the two'. Superlative uses 'of the three' or 'in the whole country' or the article 'the'. Positive does not compare.
Long adjectives use 'more' and 'most' in place of '-er' and '-est': more beautiful, most beautiful. More than two syllables means 'more'; fewer syllables usually means '-er'.

And for adverbs, the same pattern runs: quickly, more quickly, most quickly. Slowly, more slowly, most slowly. Link them together in your head: positive, comparative, superlative, with no shortcuts in either adjectives or adverbs.

The exam almost always asks you to pick the right form from four options. Read all four, then ask: which compares two? which compares three or more? which gives no comparison at all? That one question solves most items in under a second each.

Irregular verbs keep the same shapes across adjective and adverb: quickly, more quickly, most quickly; badly, worse, worst. So whether the option says "more quickly" or "most quickly" only tells you whether the comparison is two or three. The verb asks the question before the noun does.
bullets: Three degrees: positive, comparative, superlative
Comparatives with two; superlatives with three or more
Two syllables vary: happier, but more useful

content.heading: Go deeper: The tricky irregular forms
paragraphs: Irregular adjectives break the pattern: good, better, best; bad, worse, worst; far, further/farther, furthest/farthest; little, less, least; many, more, most. Memorise these six groups by repeating them aloud once a day for a week. Nothing else anomalous is testing material at this level; after you own these six, every other adjective answers to its standard rule.

The exam also loves the adverb mirrored with the adjective. Well goes to better and best; badly goes to worse and worst. Both adjective and adverb share the same root, and English spells the transformation only once per pair of forms.
Adverbs: 'well, better, best; badly, worse, worst; little, less, least; much, more, most'. The sentence tells you which role each plays.
The double comparison trap: 'more bigger', 'most best' — wrong. No adjective takes both '-er' and 'more'. Pick one of them: bigger or more beautiful. Not both.
When in doubt, substitute a short, common adjective. 'Good' always passes, always. 'This is more good house' kills itself on first read.
bullets: Good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many-more-most, much-more-most, little-less-least, far-farther/further-farthest/furthest
Distance uses farther; figurative uses further
No double comparatives or superlatives

content.heading: Go deeper: The examiner's shortcut question types
paragraphs: The most common form: an adjective missing, replaced with four options. 'Of the two girls, she is — beautiful.' The answer is 'more', because the comparison is two, and the adjective is three syllables. Other options are designed wrong: 'the most', 'most', 'more most'.
The second form: 'the — of the three' with four options. The answer is the superlative. 'Of the three boys, he is the tallest.' Wrong choices: 'taller', 'more taller', 'the most tall'.
The third form: a sentence with 'as' in it. 'She is as — as he.' The answer is the positive: 'as tall as he', not 'as taller'. 'As' never takes the comparative form.

The fourth form: idiom. 'The more, the merrier.' 'The sooner, the better.' 'The graver, the worse.' These pairs are always matched comparative with comparative. Both are followed by the article 'the'.

When stuck, count the words being compared. Two: comparative. Three or more: superlative. Use '-er/-est' for one and two syllables, 'more/most' for three or more. That covers eighty per cent of the paper.
bullets: Two = comparative; three or more = superlative
'As' never takes comparative form
The more, the merrier: comparative paired with comparative

content.question: Complete each sentence: 'She is the ______ (intelligent) girl in the class' and 'My bag is ______ (heavy) than yours.'
hints: Count the items in each sentence.
The class has more than two girls.
Two bags take the comparative.

lessons.title: Question Tags
lessons.objective: Add the correct question tag by repeating the statement's auxiliary and tense, reversing polarity and replacing the subject with a pronoun.

content.heading: Question tags
paragraphs: A speaker says 'You are coming, aren't you?' and waits for a nod. The short tail turns a statement into a check, and its form follows rules rather than intonation.

content.heading: The tag mirrors the statement
paragraphs: A question tag is a short question added to a statement. It repeats the auxiliary and subject of that statement, and it reverses the polarity: a positive statement takes a negative tag, and a negative statement takes a positive tag.
'She is ready, isn't she?' is positive then negative. 'She isn't ready, is she?' is negative then positive. The subject becomes a pronoun: 'Musa is late, isn't he?' rather than 'isn't Musa?'.

The tag agrees in tense and person. 'They went home, didn't they?' keeps the past tense, and 'We can swim, can't we?' keeps the modal. A mismatch in auxiliary, tense or pronoun is the commonest error in this item type.
bullets: Reverse the polarity of the statement.
Repeat its auxiliary and tense.
Replace the subject with a pronoun.
content.takeaway: The tag repeats the statement and reverses its polarity.

check.question: Binta is coming, ______?
check.why: The statement is positive and uses 'is', so the tag is negative and keeps 'is' with the pronoun 'she'.

content.heading: Finding the auxiliary
paragraphs: When the statement already has an auxiliary, the tag uses it: is, are, was, were, have, has, had, will, would, can, could, may, might, must or should. 'They have finished, haven't they?' repeats 'have'.
When there is no auxiliary, the tag supplies do, does or did to match the tense: 'She sings well, doesn't she?', 'They left early, didn't they?' and 'You like tea, don't you?'.

Be careful with 'have'. As a main verb meaning possess, it can take do: 'You have a car, don't you?' As an auxiliary it repeats itself: 'You have seen it, haven't you?'. The same split applies to 'be' and 'do'.
bullets: Repeat an auxiliary if one is present.
Supply do, does or did if there is none.
'Have' as a main verb takes 'do'.
content.takeaway: If the statement has no auxiliary, build one with do, does or did.

check.question: They arrived late, ______?
check.why: The statement is positive and has no auxiliary, so the tag uses the past tense 'did' with 'n't' and the pronoun 'they'.

visual.caption: Build a tag by working through the statement in four moves.

content.heading: Special cases
paragraphs: Some tags do not follow the ordinary pattern. After 'let's' use 'shall we?', after an imperative use 'will you?' or 'won't you?', and after 'I am' standard British English uses 'aren't I?'.

Indefinite subjects take a plural pronoun: 'Everybody has arrived, haven't they?' and 'Nobody called, did they?'. 'Nothing' takes 'it': 'Nothing happened, did it?'. These pronouns follow meaning rather than grammatical number.

Negative adverbs change the polarity. Never, hardly, scarcely, barely and no one make the statement negative, so the tag is positive: 'He never smiles, does he?'. A statement with 'used to' takes 'didn't': 'She used to live here, didn't she?'.
bullets: 'Let's' takes 'shall we?'.
Imperatives take 'will you?'.
Negative adverbs force a positive tag.
content.takeaway: Special subjects and negative adverbs overturn the ordinary pattern.

check.question: Let's go now, ______?
check.why: 'Let's' is a fixed exception: it always takes 'shall we?' regardless of the ordinary polarity rule.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Say the statement and the tag aloud. If the two halves have the same polarity, the tag is wrong.

content.problem: Add the correct tag: 'The students had left before noon.'

steps.reason: The tag repeats the auxiliary of the statement. Reach for the tag chart because the tag repeats the sentence's own auxiliary. If stuck, underline the helping verb and copy it into the tag slot.
steps.result: The auxiliary is 'had'.
steps.predictPrompt: Is the statement positive or negative?

steps.reason: A positive statement takes a negative tag. Reach for the tag chart because the polarity column flips positive to negative. If stuck, check whether the statement is positive and take the negative twin.
steps.result: The tag begins 'hadn't'.
steps.predictPrompt: Which numbers or terms work with each other first?

steps.reason: The subject must become a pronoun that matches in person and number. Reach for the tag chart because the pronoun column matches the subject's person and number. If stuck, turn the subject into a pronoun.
steps.result: 'The students' becomes 'they', so the tag is 'hadn't they?'.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: What a question tag is
paragraphs: A question tag is a small question attached to the end of a statement, inviting the listener to confirm or deny it. 'You are coming, aren't you?' 'She can drive, can't she?' Tags are the most common spoken English constructions in the world.

The tag is formed from the auxiliary verb of the statement, flipped in polarity, and matched in person and number. The statement 'he has eaten' becomes 'hasn't he?' — has flips to hasn't. The statement 'it is raining' becomes 'isn't it?' — is flips to isn't.
English rules the answer is built from four ingredients. The auxiliary of the main sentence, the opposite polarity, the matching pronoun, and the matching number. Lose any one and the tag dies.
Substitute the auxiliary like a trick mirror: 'can you?' 'do you?' 'will you?' 'must you?' 'have you?' 'are you?' English learns these fast. Once you have 'can', every other auxiliary follows.

The exam tests your ability to see the auxiliary inside a sentence. English has no auxiliaries you haven't seen before; you just haven't noticed them all. This lesson is designed to make them visible.
bullets: Statement + auxiliary + flipped polarity + pronoun
Auxiliary comes from the main sentence
Mirror the subject pronoun, not the noun phrase

content.heading: Go deeper: Which auxiliary to use where
paragraphs: If the statement has an auxiliary, the tag copies it. 'He will come' → 'won't he?' 'He has arrived' → 'hasn't he?' 'They are coming' → 'aren't they?' 'They can wait' → 'can't they?' Always the auxiliary. Never a new auxiliary.

If the statement has no auxiliary — simple present or simple past — the tag is built with 'do', 'does' or 'did'. 'You like coffee' → 'don't you?' 'He works here' → 'doesn't he?' 'She went to Lagos' → 'didn't she?' The do-family is the neutral tag verb.
The 'let's' invitation takes 'shall we?' as its tag. 'Let's go' → 'shall we?' That is the one tag you must memorise separately; 'let's' never takes 'do we?' or 'don't we?'.
Grammatical people match exactly: he/she/it/they/we/you/I. The pronoun swaps the noun phrase: 'John is here' → 'isn't he?', not 'isn't John?' — pronouns only in tags, never names.

If the statement uses a word that looks like an adjective or noun, treat it as an adjective or noun: 'He is hungry, isn't he?' 'is' is the auxiliary. 'Hunger is real, isn't it?' Here again isn't is the auxiliary.
bullets: Statement with auxiliary: copy the auxiliary
Simple present/past: use do/does/did
'Let's' takes 'shall we'

content.heading: Go deeper: The exacting polarity test
paragraphs: Polarity flips: positive statement flips to negative tag; negative statement flips to positive tag. 'He is here, isn't he?' or 'He isn't here, is he?' 'They don't know, do they?' or 'They know, don't they?'

Watch for statements containing negatives with implied polarities: 'Never', 'hardly', 'scarcely', 'barely', 'seldom', 'rarely', 'nobody', 'no one' and 'nothing' make the sentence effectively negative, so the tag stays positive: 'He never came, did he?' 'Nothing is wrong, is it?'
The same holds for double negatives. 'He wasn't unhappy' means 'he was happy', so the tag is 'was he?' — positive. Memorise: an odd number of negatives flips polarity; an even number does not.

The stress trap is the strongest trap of all. Sometimes the speaker wants to tease, and the tag does not flip — the speaker is agreeing, not questioning. 'You're not serious, are you?' (surprise). 'You aren't listening, are you?' (irony). These read with stress on 'are'.

To master polarity, mark each sentence as positive or negative first. Then say the tag out loud. If it sounds like an honest question, the opposite polarity is right; if it sounds like a joke, the stress version is the intended one.
bullets: Polarity flips: positive → negative tag; negative → positive tag
Rarely, never, scarcely, seldom, no one — all count as negative
Double negatives count as positive

content.question: Add tags to these sentences: 'Nobody phoned, ______?' and 'You have eaten, ______?'
hints: 'Nobody' is negative, so the tag turns positive.
The subject 'nobody' takes 'they'.
'Have' here is an auxiliary, so it repeats.

lessons.title: Mechanics: Spelling and Punctuation
lessons.objective: Apply the spelling conventions and punctuation marks JAMB tests, including suffix rules, apostrophes, semicolons and confusable words.

content.heading: Mechanics
paragraphs: A candidate writes 'The dogs tail wagged' and loses a mark for a missing apostrophe. Mechanics is the set of small marks and spellings that carry meaning, and the exam tests them directly.

content.heading: Spelling rules that hold
paragraphs: Use i before e except after c, when the sound is long /iː/: believe, chief, receive and ceiling. The rule has exceptions such as seize, weird and either, so learn those words separately instead of trusting the rhyme everywhere.

Double the final consonant when a one-syllable word ending in one vowel plus one consonant takes a suffix beginning with a vowel: big becomes bigger, stop becomes stopped, run becomes running. Do not double when the stress is not on the last syllable: visit becomes visited, not 'visitted'.

Drop a silent e before a vowel suffix (make becomes making) but keep it before a consonant suffix (hope becomes hopeful). Change y to i after a consonant (carry becomes carried) but keep it after a vowel (play becomes played).
bullets: I before e except after c, with exceptions.
Double after a short stressed vowel.
Drop silent e before a vowel suffix.
content.takeaway: Spelling rules work by sound and stress, not by memorising each word alone.

check.question: Which spelling is correct?
check.why: After c the order reverses to ei, so the correct spelling is 'receive'.

content.heading: Punctuation that changes meaning
paragraphs: An apostrophe shows possession or marks a contraction. 'The boy's book' is one boy's book, 'the boys' books' is several boys' books, and 'it's' means 'it is' while 'its' shows possession.

A comma separates items and marks off extra information: 'After the meeting, we ate.' A semicolon joins two closely related clauses: 'The rain stopped; we continued.' A colon introduces a list or an explanation.

A hyphen joins the parts of a compound word (well-known, mother-in-law), while a dash marks a break in thought. Using one for the other is a common exam error, so check whether the mark is joining or interrupting.
bullets: Apostrophe: possession or contraction.
Semicolon joins related clauses.
Hyphen joins; dash interrupts.
content.takeaway: Each mark has one job, and swapping them changes the sentence.

check.question: Which is the correct plural possessive?
check.why: 'Children' is already plural and does not end in s, so the possessive adds 's: children's.

visual.caption: The same apostrophe does two different jobs, and the test tells them apart.

content.heading: Confusable words and capitals
paragraphs: Many errors come from words that sound alike. 'Its' is possessive and 'it's' is 'it is'; 'whose' is possessive and 'who's' is 'who is'; 'their' is possessive, 'there' is a place and 'they're' is 'they are'.

Other pairs differ in meaning: affect is a verb and effect is a noun; principal means head or main and principle means a rule; complement completes and compliment praises; stationary means still and stationery means paper.

Capitalise proper nouns, the first word of a sentence, days, months and nationalities, but not the seasons. Write 'Nigeria', 'Nigerian', 'Monday' and 'January', but 'summer'. Titles take capitals only when they precede a name.
bullets: Its is possessive; it's means 'it is'.
Affect is the verb; effect is the noun.
Capitalise proper nouns, not seasons.
content.takeaway: Test a confusable word by expanding the contraction or substituting a synonym.

check.question: The new rule will ______ everyone.
check.why: 'Affect' is the verb meaning to influence; after 'will' the base form is needed, and 'effect' is normally a noun.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: A missing apostrophe can reverse a meaning: 'the girls' bags' and 'the girl's bags' describe different owners.

content.problem: Correct the sentence: 'Its raining, so the childrens books are wet.'

steps.reason: 'Its' without an apostrophe is possessive, but the sentence needs 'it is'. Reach for the apostrophe chart because it splits it's into it is. If stuck, say it is aloud and see whether the sentence still works.
steps.result: 'Its' becomes 'It's'.
steps.predictPrompt: Which noun owns the books?

steps.reason: 'Children' is an irregular plural that does not end in s. Reach for the apostrophe chart because it shows where the mark goes in plurals without s. If stuck, write the plural first, then add the mark.
steps.result: The possessive is 'children's'.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the question tell you to find first?

steps.reason: Both marks must now carry the right meaning. Reach for the apostrophe chart because it re-checks both marks against their jobs. If stuck, circle each apostrophe and say what each one stands for.
steps.result: 'It's raining, so the children's books are wet.'
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.heading: Go deeper: What mechanics actually is
paragraphs: Mechanics is the set of rules that press words onto paper so a reader can read them. Punctuation splits the ideas. Spelling packs the right letters into the right order. Capitalisation folds in names. Paragraphing breaks the text into chunks that the eye can hold.

These are not decoration. Examiners test mechanics because wrong punctuation makes a sentence mean the opposite of what the writer meant. A misplaced apostrophe can change 'the dog's house' (house owned by one dog) to 'the dogs house' (many dogs in a house — not grammatical but close to wrong).

Three mechanical skills matter most: the apostrophe (possession and contraction), the comma (its jobs are listed next), and question and quotation marks (difference between asking and telling, difference between yours and theirs).

Spelling questions test common traps: 'their/they're/there', 'your/you're', 'its/it's', 'affect/effect', 'lose/loose', 'practice/practise'. Each word has one job and is sometimes two words squashed into one.
The exam will never test a lost word you have not seen before. It tests known words in suspicious disguises. Learn the disguises and the marks belong to you.
bullets: Punctuation splits ideas, spelling packs letters, caps name people
Three skills rule: apostrophe, comma, question and quote marks
Spelling tests common traps: their/there/they're, your/you're, its/it's

content.heading: Go deeper: The comma and its four jobs
paragraphs: The comma has five jobs. First: separate an opener. 'However, he was not surprised.' The opener is however, set aside by one comma. Without it, the sentence stumbles.
Second: mark a shift in subject. 'The boy went to school, but forgetting his bag, he came back.' The comma underlines the 'but' and the shift in actor. Removing it flattens the sentence.

Third: separate list items. 'She bought rice, beans, tomatoes, onions and yam' — every list bigger than two items needs those commas. The 'and' before the last item may take a comma or may not; both are acceptable.
Fourth: introduce a quote or a quotation. 'He said, "I see the problem."' Comma before the opening quote, not inside it. The comma marks the break between speech and attribution.

A fifth use — joining two independent clauses with a conjunction: 'I was late, but I made it to class.' The comma stops the two clauses from colliding. Never use a comma alone between two independent clauses — it must have 'but', 'so', 'yet', 'and' or 'or' to pair with it.
bullets: Comma: opener, shift, list, quote, conjunction
Every list of three or more needs commas
No comma alone between two independent clauses

content.heading: Go deeper: The apostrophe as the one crucial mark
paragraphs: The apostrophe does exactly two jobs, no more. Job one: show possession. 'John's book' — the book belongs to John. 'The boys' books' — the books belong to the boys. 'The boy's book' — singular boy, singular book. 'The boys book' with no apostrophe — many boys of some unspecified book.

The positioning rule: singular possessive takes the apostrophe before the s: boy's hat, dog's bowl, mother's advice. Plural possessive takes the apostrophe after the s: boys' hat, dogs' bowls, mothers' advice. The number of nouns decides where the apostrophe sits.

Job two: mark contraction. 'Do not' becomes 'don't'. 'It is' becomes 'it's'. 'He is' becomes 'he's'. 'They are' becomes 'they're'. The apostrophe replaces the missing letters. 'It's raining' asks 'what is raining?' 'Its raining' would be 'of raining' — no such word.

The trap: 'its' without apostrophe — possessive, like 'his'. 'it's' with apostrophe — contraction of 'it is'. 'Hers' always no apostrophe. 'Ours' always no apostrophe. 'Yours' always no apostrophe. 'Theirs' always no apostrophe.
To solve the trap, expand the word into 'it is' and see whether it sounds right. 'Hers is the last seat' expands to 'her is' — wrong. You know the word is 'hers', no apostrophe.
bullets: Apostrophe: possession (one means one book) or contraction (two means it is)
Singular possession: before s. Plural possession: after s
its is possessive; it's is 'it is'

content.question: Choose the correct word in each pair: 'The medicine had no (effect / affect)' and '(Whose / Who's) bag is this?'
hints: One word is a noun, the other a verb.
The second sentence means 'who owns'.
'Effect' is the noun; 'whose' is the possessive.

lessons.title: Vocabulary and Idioms
lessons.objective: Infer word meaning from context and interpret formal Standard British English idioms and phrasal verbs correctly.

content.heading: Vocabulary and idioms
paragraphs: A passage says the manager 'let the cat out of the bag', and a candidate looks for a cat. The phrase is an idiom, and its meaning has nothing to do with the animal.

content.heading: Context is the dictionary
paragraphs: When a word is unfamiliar, the sentence around it usually supplies the meaning. A definition may follow in apposition, an example may illustrate it, or a contrast may mark its opposite.

Look for these clues: 'that is', 'in other words' and dashes signal a definition; 'for example' and 'such as' signal an example; 'but', 'unlike' and 'whereas' signal a contrast; and 'because', 'so' and 'therefore' signal a cause or result.
Predict a meaning from the clues, then replace the word with your prediction and re-read. If the sentence still makes sense, the prediction is close enough to answer the question.
bullets: Definitions often sit beside the word.
Contrast and cause clues narrow the meaning.
Substitute your guess and re-read.
content.takeaway: The sentence usually defines the word it is testing.

check.question: In 'The arid land, unlike the fertile valley nearby, could grow nothing', what does 'arid' mean?
check.why: The contrast with 'fertile' and the result 'could grow nothing' point to dry land.

content.heading: Idioms are fixed
paragraphs: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be worked out from its separate words. 'Bite the bullet' means endure something painful, 'break the ice' means start a conversation, and 'once in a blue moon' means very rarely.
Phrasal verbs are idioms built from a verb and a particle: give up, put off, look into, run out of, carry out and bring about. The particle changes the meaning, so 'look after' is not 'look into'.

JAMB tests formal Standard British English, so learn the whole expression. 'Cost an arm and a leg' means be very expensive, and 'let the cat out of the bag' means reveal a secret, not release an animal.
bullets: An idiom's meaning is not literal.
The particle changes a phrasal verb's sense.
Learn the whole expression, not the parts.
content.takeaway: Treat an idiom as one word with one fixed meaning.

check.question: What does 'to break the ice' mean?
check.why: The idiom means to ease the initial awkwardness and begin talking; it is not literal.

visual.caption: The same words carry a literal sense and a fixed idiomatic one.

rows.feature: cost an arm and a leg

content.heading: Usage traps
paragraphs: Watch for idioms that differ by one word. 'Turn a blind eye' means ignore deliberately, while 'turn a deaf ear' means refuse to listen; mixing them changes the sentence.
Watch for Nigerian English coinages that are not standard. 'I am hearing you' should be 'I can hear you', 'senior brother' should be 'elder brother', and 'off head' should be 'from memory'.
Check the preposition that belongs to the word. We depend on, consist of, insist on, married to, and prefer something to something else. A correct meaning with the wrong particle is still wrong.
bullets: One changed word can change the idiom.
Use Standard British English, not coinages.
Learn each word's fixed preposition.
content.takeaway: Meaning alone is not enough; the whole expression must be standard.

check.question: Choose the standard expression.
check.why: Stative 'hear' does not normally take the progressive, and 'I am hearing you' is a Nigerian-English coinage.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If an idiom makes literal sense in the sentence, suspect it. Idioms usually make no literal sense at all.

content.problem: What does the idiom in this sentence mean? 'The new tax will cost the company an arm and a leg.'

steps.reason: The words form an idiom, so their literal meanings do not apply. Reach for the fixed-expression scan because idioms are memorised as whole units. If stuck, check whether the literal reading makes no sense.
steps.result: 'Cost an arm and a leg' is a set phrase.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the phrase usually mean?

content.heading: Go deeper: What an idiom really is
paragraphs: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning you cannot guess from its words. 'Kick the bucket' does not let you picture a bucket being pushed. 'Piece of cake' does not let you picture a portion of a dessert. You either know the phrase or you do not.

Every language has its own idioms, and they always make sense to its speakers. An English speaker never says 'kick the bucket' to mean 'die' while actually kicking any bucket. They simply choose the phrase.

The exam tests four groups of idioms. The first is animal idioms, like 'crying wolf', 'a dark horse', 'hold your horses'. The second is food idioms: 'a piece of cake', 'spilling the beans'. The third is body idioms: 'cold feet', 'a pain in the neck'. The fourth is time idioms: 'in the nick of time', 'better late than never'. Memorise a list of ten from each group and you will survive any idiom question.
Idioms also come in pairs with fixed meanings: 'break the ice', 'break new ground'. Each keeps its own link. English learners find them funny at first; the fun is fine, but the tests are serious.

To attack the questions, look for which word in the idiom set looks like its usual meaning and which makes no sense. The word that makes no sense is your anchor. 'Spilling the beans' — beans do not spill anything useful. So the phrase must mean 'reveal a secret'.
bullets: Idiom: fixed phrase, unpredictable meaning
Four groups: animal, food, body, time
The nonsense word is the anchor—the phrase's meaning doesn't sit there

content.heading: Go deeper: Why register divides vocabulary
paragraphs: Register is the level of formality in a word. 'Dad' is informal; 'father' is neutral; 'the senior male parent' is ultra-formal. English has the same three bands for every concept that matters.

The exam tests register in the answer choice. A passage about a university meeting will never accept 'kid' as the synonym for 'student'. A passage about a market will never accept 'progeny' as the synonym for 'children'. The register of the sentence pushes out the misfit.

Three registers you must command. Academic: 'illustrate', 'analyse', 'conclude', 'argue'. Neutral daily: 'show', 'look at', 'finish', 'say'. Colloquial: 'point out', 'check', 'wrap up', 'tell'. The first band is preferred in examiner's passages; the third band in most fictional passages.

The register trap is doubling. 'Very happy' is fine in speech; 'extremely happy' is expected in academic; 'overjoyed' is fine as the solution. 'Very' before a strong adjective is always weaker than a precise adjective alone.
Memorise a synonym list paired by register for thirty common pairs. 'Happy/Joyful/Elated', 'Sad/Sorrowful/Morose', 'Small/Petite/Minute'. Each step is one step up in formality.
bullets: Three bands: academic, neutral, colloquial
Passage register dictates which synonym fits
Memorise thirty common register pairs

content.heading: Go deeper: Words with tricky meanings
paragraphs: Contronyms: words that mean their opposite. 'Oversight' can mean a careful review or a careless mistake. 'Sanction' can mean approval or punishment. 'Left' can mean remaining or departed. The sentence, not the word, decides which one it is.

Homographs: same spelling, different meanings and sounds. 'Bow' is a decoration worn on a dress, a way to greet a person, or the front of a ship. The context selects one. No homograph is tested without context.
Homophones: same sound, different spelling and meaning. 'Their', 'there', 'they're'; 'your', 'you're'; 'its', 'it's'; 'affect', 'effect'. The exam uses these as trap pairs in almost every paper.

Pseudo-synonyms: pairs that look like synonyms and are not. 'Imply' means suggest; 'infer' means conclude. 'Adverse' means unfavourable; 'averse' means unwilling. 'Sensible' and 'sensitive' are not interchangeable. Every one of these is a trap you have to recognise by name.
The best guard is reading these pairs consciously, once a day for a week. Write them on a card and check them in the kitchen, in the classroom and in bed. By the end of the week, they will be yours.
bullets: Contronyms need context: oversight, sanction, left
Homographs owe their meaning to context
Homophones and pseudo-synonyms are the examiner's favourite traps

lessons.title: Vowels: Monophthongs, Diphthongs and Triphthongs
lessons.objective: Distinguish monophthongs, diphthongs and triphthongs by the number of vowel qualities a speaker glides through.

content.heading: Vowel sounds
paragraphs: A speaker saying 'sit' holds one vowel quality, but in 'sight' the tongue moves from one quality to another. That movement separates the vowel types JAMB asks about.

content.heading: One steady sound or a glide
paragraphs: A monophthong is one steady vowel sound. RP has twelve, including /iː/ in seat, /ɪ/ in sit, /æ/ in cat and /ɜː/ in bird. Five are long (/iː/, /ɑː/, /ɔː/, /uː/, /ɜː/) and the rest are short.

A diphthong glides from one vowel quality to another. It has eight members, such as /eɪ/ in bay, /aɪ/ in buy and /ɔɪ/ in boy. The schwa /ə/ is the weak vowel of unstressed syllables, as in the second syllable of 'sofa'.
A triphthong glides through three qualities, as in player /eɪə/ and fire /aɪə/. It is a diphthong followed by a schwa.
bullets: Monophthong: one steady quality.
Diphthong: a glide between two qualities.
Triphthong: a glide through three qualities.
content.takeaway: Count the vowel qualities you hear, not the vowel letters you see.

check.question: Which word contains a diphthong?
check.why: /aɪ/ moves from one quality towards another; the other three hold a single vowel throughout.

visual.caption: A monophthong stays put; a diphthong moves, whatever the spelling suggests.

rows.right: Often a, e, i, o or u plus y or w
The tongue moves during the sound

content.heading: Telling vowels apart in the exam
paragraphs: Two candidates may hear 'ship' and 'sheep' as the same word, yet the exam treats their vowels as different. Length and tongue position carry the distinction.

Minimal pairs expose it: ship /ɪ/ against sheep /iː/, bad /æ/ against bard /ɑː/, cot /ɒ/ against caught /ɔː/, and full /ʊ/ against fool /uː/. Length and tongue position separate each pair, not the spelling.

Spelling misleads. 'Bread' has one vowel sound /e/ despite two vowel letters, 'my' has the diphthong /aɪ/ despite one letter, and 'queue' is /kjuː/. Say the word aloud before you decide which sound it contains.
bullets: Use minimal pairs, not spelling.
Long and short vowels are different sounds.
Nigerian English may merge pairs the exam keeps apart.
content.takeaway: The exam tests sounds, and spelling is only a clue.

check.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'bird'?
check.why: Bird and burn both carry /ɜː/; bead has /iː/, bed has /e/ and bard has /ɑː/.

content.heading: Triphthongs and the traps
paragraphs: A triphthong appears where a diphthong is followed by /ə/: fire /faɪə/, our /aʊə/, player /pleɪə/, loyal /lɔɪə/ and lower /ləʊə/. Spelling gives no reliable signal, because the same letters can spell a monophthong in another word.

In fast connected speech the glide is often smoothed, so 'fire' may sound like one long syllable rather than three qualities. Exam items usually ask about the underlying sound, not the smoothed version.

The commonest error is counting letters. 'Beautiful' begins with /bjuː/, a consonant plus a vowel, while 'beauty' contains /juː/; neither is a triphthong just because it has many letters. Listen for the number of qualities, then label the sound.
bullets: Triphthong: a diphthong plus schwa.
Examples: fire, our, player.
Ignore spelling and letter count.
content.takeaway: A triphthong is three vowel qualities in one syllable, often smoothed in speech.

check.question: Which word contains a triphthong?
check.why: Buyer glides through /aɪə/; bay and boat are diphthongs and bit is a monophthong.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Vowel letters are not vowel sounds. 'Food' has two letters but one sound; 'my' has one letter but two qualities.

steps.result: Sight /saɪt/ is the answer.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.heading: Go deeper: What vowels are
paragraphs: A vowel is a speech sound produced with the mouth open and no block to the air. English has twenty vowels in its standard accent: twelve monophthongs (steady sounds, like /æ/ in cat) and eight diphthongs (glide sounds, like /eɪ/ in day) — twenty vowels in all, with the triphthong as a diphthong plus a schwa, like /aɪə/ in fire.

Every English word that you say aloud must have at least one vowel. A word like 'strength' has one vowel, 'length' — a consonant cluster, one vowel. The vowel is the engine of the word; the consonants hang off it.

The exam tests your ability to hear and name the vowel. 'Which word contains the same vowel sound as here?' The answer is 'hear' or 'near' — all three share /ɪə/. 'Bear' and 'chair' share /eə/, a different sound.

Monophthongs are the single sounds. Diphthongs are the joining sounds. 'Cat' has the first; 'day' has the second. The exam will not ask for the scientific IPA symbols; it will ask which sounds share the same vowel.

The key trick: name the vowel on your lips, not in your head. Move your jaw and feel the difference. /æ/ opens wide; /eɪ/ starts closed and opens slightly. Your mouth makes the difference, so your mouth can learn it.
bullets: Vowel: mouth open, no block to air
Monophthong: one sound; diphthong: glide sound
Feel the vowels on your lips, not in your head

content.heading: Go deeper: The three vowel families
paragraphs: Front vowels: /i/ (beat), /ɪ/ (bit), /e/ (bet), /æ/ (cat). These are produced at the front of the mouth. In many Nigerian-accented English learners, these four blur into two. Learn them by distinct opening of the jaws and tongue: /i/ closed spread, /ɪ/ closed relaxed, /e/ half open, /æ/ open.

Central vowels: /ʌ/ (cut), /ɜ/ (hurt), /ə/ (the, about). These sit in the middle of the mouth. The schwa /ə/ is the most common vowel in English — every unstressed syllable uses it. 'Sofa', 'banana', 'computer' — every 'a' and 'er' sound is a schwa.
Back vowels: /ɑ/ (hot), /ɔ/ (law), /ʊ/ (book), /u/ (boot). These sit at the back. 'Hot' and 'law' differ in one degree of rounding. 'Book' and 'boot' differ in length.
Most papers group the twenty vowels into these three families. If you can say the front, central and back vowels from a list you know by heart, you would pass any vowel identification question.
The exam rarely tests you on the names 'front/central/back'. It asks for same-sound matches. Train the three groups separately; once each group is fluent, the matching is a matter of hearing.
bullets: Front: /i/, /ɪ/, /e/, /æ/
Central: /ʌ/, /ɜ/, /ə/
Back: /ɑ/, /ɔ/, /ʊ/, /u/

content.heading: Go deeper: The examiner's vowel matching test
paragraphs: Typical paper item: 'Which of the following words contains the same vowel sound as in hat?' Options: mat, meet, out, seat. Your ear must hear /æ/ in 'hat', /e/ in 'mat'? No — same /æ/. /iː/ in 'meet'. /aʊ/ in 'out'. /iː/ in 'seat'.

The same method applies to diphthongs: 'Which of the following words contains the same vowel sound as in day?' Options: may, die, say, here. /eɪ/ in 'day'; /eɪ/ in 'may'; /aɪ/ in 'die'; /eɪ/ in 'say'; /ɪə/ in 'here'.
The fastest solve is to say the key word aloud, then say each option aloud. The ear catches the grouped sounds instantly; the eye misses them when the words are printed.

Beware of the spelling trap: English spelling lies. 'Granite' has the /æ/ sound (/ˈɡrænɪt/) even though the letters say 'a'. 'Comment' has the /ɒ/ sound. 'Record' has /i/ (verb) vs /ɒ/ (noun). Spelling teaches nothing; sound teaches everything.
Build a habit of saying each English word aloud for a week. Your ear will adjust in a few days. Then return to the paper and the matching questions will be obvious.
bullets: Say each word aloud; the ear catches what the eye cannot
English spelling lies; sound is the truth
Front, central, back — train the three families separately

content.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as 'caught': cot, coat, court or cut?
hints: Say 'caught' and hold the vowel.
It is the long open back vowel /ɔː/.
Cot has /ɒ/, coat has /əʊ/, cut has /ʌ/.

lessons.title: Consonants and Consonant Clusters
lessons.objective: Classify consonant sounds by voicing, place and manner, and count the sounds in clusters rather than the letters.

content.heading: Consonant sounds
paragraphs: Put two fingers on your throat and say 'pat', then 'bat'. The first leaves the throat still; the second buzzes.

content.heading: Voiced or voiceless
paragraphs: That buzz is voicing, the first division of English consonants. Pairs such as /p/–/b/, /t/–/d/, /k/–/g/, /f/–/v/, /s/–/z/ and /θ/–/ð/ differ only in voicing.

RP has twenty-four consonant sounds. Nine are voiceless: /p t k f θ s ʃ tʃ h/; the rest are voiced, including all nasals and /l r w j/. All vowels are voiced, so the question applies only to consonants.

Exam items ask which sound appears in a word, so say the word and isolate the sound. 'Think' begins with the voiceless /θ/, while 'this' begins with its voiced partner /ð/. Voicing can also change with a suffix: the -s in cats is /s/, but in dogs it is /z/.
bullets: Voicing is vibration of the vocal cords.
Voiceless and voiced sounds form pairs.
Isolate the sound, not the letter.
content.takeaway: If the throat buzzes, the consonant is voiced.

check.question: Which word begins with a voiceless sound?
check.why: Think begins with /θ/, which has no voicing; bat, this and judge all begin with voiced sounds.

visual.caption: Each pair uses the same mouth position; only voicing changes.

content.heading: Place and manner
paragraphs: Where the airflow is blocked gives the place: lips for /p b m/, lip and teeth for /f v/, teeth for /θ ð/, the ridge behind the teeth for /t d s z n l/, and the soft palate for /k g ŋ/.

How it is released gives the manner: plosives stop and release (/p t k/), fricatives force air through a narrow gap (/f s ʃ/), affricates stop then release slowly (/tʃ dʒ/), nasals pass through the nose (/m n ŋ/), and approximants barely obstruct (/r w j/).

The labels combine. /tʃ/ in church is a voiceless palato-alveolar affricate, and /ŋ/ at the end of sing is a voiced velar nasal. Every consonant has one place and one manner, so a full answer names both.
bullets: Place: lips, teeth, ridge, palate.
Manner: plosive, fricative, affricate, nasal.
Combine both labels for the full name.
content.takeaway: Name a consonant by voicing, place and manner together.

check.question: The first sound in 'judge' is ______.
check.why: /dʒ/ stops the airflow and releases it slowly, and the vocal cords vibrate, so it is a voiced affricate.

content.heading: Clusters
paragraphs: A cluster is two or more consonants with no vowel between them. English allows three at the start, as in street /str/, spring /spr/ and scream /skr/, and up to four at the end.

Nigerian English often breaks a cluster by inserting a vowel ('sitreet') or drops one of its sounds ('tes' for tests). Both change the syllable count and can cost marks, so practise the cluster without an inserted vowel.

Count sounds, not letters. 'Box' is /bɒks/, four sounds; 'thought' is /θɔːt/, three; 'strengths' is /streŋθs/, seven sounds, six of them consonants. Clusters can cross a syllable boundary in connected speech, but exam items usually test them inside one word.
bullets: No vowel sits inside a cluster.
Initial /str/, /spr/, /skr/; final /-sts/, /-sks/.
Count sounds, not letters.
content.takeaway: A cluster is consonants touching, with no vowel to separate them.

check.question: How many consonant sounds are in 'strengths'?
check.why: The sounds are /s t r e ŋ θ s/: six consonants around the single vowel /e/.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: The letter x usually spells two sounds: /ks/ in box and /gz/ in exam. Count the sounds, not the letters.

content.problem: How many consonant sounds are in the word 'strengths'?

steps.reason: The syllable must be heard before it can be counted. Reach for the consonant chart because it maps each sound to its symbol. If stuck, break the word into sounds, not letters.
steps.result: Strengths is one syllable: /streŋθs/.
steps.predictPrompt: Which sounds are vowels?

steps.reason: Each distinct sound counts once, even when several letters spell it. Reach for the phoneme inventory because every distinct sound earns one count. If stuck, write each sound down as you say it, letters ignored.

content.heading: Go deeper: Voiced and voiceless consonants
paragraphs: Every consonant is either voiced or voiceless. Voiced means the vocal cords in the throat are buzzing when you make the sound. Voiceless means the air just hisses through with no buzz at all.

Try it. Put two fingers on your throat and say B — you feel a buzz, so B is voiced. Now say P — no buzz, so P is voiceless. That throat trick works for every consonant, and it needs no book or teacher.

The voiced consonants are b, d, g, v, z, j and the sounds like l, m, n, r and w. The voiceless ones are p, t, k, f, s, sh, ch, th (as in think) and h. Most consonants come in pairs: p with b, t with d, k with g, f with v, s with z.

Why does the exam ask about this? Because the pair decides spelling. A noun ending in a voiceless sound takes the s you would expect, and so does a noun ending in a voiced one — but the sound tells you the consonant class, and knowing the class tells you how to pronounce the added s in plurals and the past tense.
Example: 'cats' ends with the voiceless /s/ sound, while 'dogs' ends with the voiced /z/ sound. Say both aloud and feel the throat. The exam loves to test exactly that difference.
bullets: Voiced = throat buzzes; voiceless = no buzz
The throat test needs no book
Pairs: p-b, t-d, k-g, f-v, s-z

content.heading: Go deeper: How the air is blocked or squeezed
paragraphs: Consonants are also grouped by how the mouth handles the air. Three groups matter for your exams: plosives, fricatives and nasals.

A plosive (also called a stop) traps the air completely, then releases it with a small burst. P, t, k, b, d and g are plosives. Say 'pin' and feel the p burst out. Say 'tin' and feel the t burst. That burst is the whole group.

A fricative never closes fully. It squeezes the air through a narrow gap so the air hisses. F, v, s, z, sh, th and h are fricatives. Put your hand in front of your mouth and say 'fan' — you feel a steady blow of air, not a burst.

A nasal closes the mouth but lets the air escape through the nose. M, n and ng are nasals. Pinch your nose and try to say 'man' — you cannot, because the air has nowhere to go. That is proof of a nasal.
Quick way to tell them apart in an exam: burst = plosive, hiss = fricative, nose = nasal. Three words, three groups, no textbook needed.
bullets: Plosives burst: p, t, k, b, d, g
Fricatives hiss: f, v, s, z, sh, th, h
Nasals go through the nose: m, n, ng

content.heading: Go deeper: Clusters at the start and end of words
paragraphs: A consonant cluster is two or three consonants touching each other with no vowel between them. 'Street' begins with str — s, t and r all touch. 'Text' ends with xt. Those are clusters.

English has rules about which clusters can start a word. 'Str' can open a word (street, strong). 'Tsr' cannot — no English word begins that way, even though it uses real letters. English keeps only the clusters people can say smoothly.

Starting clusters are tighter than ending clusters. At the start, English allows at most three consonants (spray, string, splash). At the end, four is rare (texts, twelfths) and most words end with one or two.

If a cluster cannot be said smoothly, English refuses to use it at the start. 'Spt' cannot open a word. That is why borrowing words from other languages sometimes forces English speakers to change the pronunciation.

The exam tests clusters by asking which word begins or ends with a particular cluster, or by asking you to spot the odd one out. Say the words aloud; your mouth knows the answer faster than your eyes do.
bullets: A cluster is consonants touching with no vowel between them
Street starts with str; text ends with xt
If you cannot say it smoothly, English will not open a word with it

content.question: Which word begins with /dʒ/: gin, game, gain or gone?
hints: Say each word and listen to the first sound.
Game, gain and gone begin with the voiced plosive /g/.
Gin begins with the voiced affricate /dʒ/.

lessons.title: Rhymes and Homophones
lessons.objective: Identify rhyme by the stressed vowel and following sounds, and distinguish homophones from near misses and homographs.

content.heading: Rhyme and homophones
paragraphs: A poet pairs 'moon' with 'June' and the ear accepts it, but 'moon' and 'book' do not rhyme. The difference is where the sound match begins.

content.heading: How rhyme works
paragraphs: A rhyme repeats the stressed vowel and every sound after it, while the sound before it changes. Cat and hat rhyme; cat and cap do not, because the final consonant differs.
The match starts at the stressed syllable, so nation and station rhyme on '-ation', and belief and relief rhyme on '-lief'. The sound before the stressed vowel is free to differ.

Words with the same ending letters do not always rhyme: love and move share no vowel sound, and food and good differ in vowel length. Rhyme is also not identity: a word does not rhyme with itself, and repeated sounds at the start of words are alliteration, not rhyme.
bullets: Rhyme starts at the stressed vowel.
Everything after it must match.
Spelling is not a guide.
content.takeaway: Rhyme is a sound match from the stressed vowel to the end.

check.question: Which word rhymes with 'though'?
check.why: Though and toe both end in /əʊ/; cow ends in /aʊ/, tough in /ʌf/ and through in /uː/.

visual.caption: Rhyme matches an ending; a homophone matches the whole word.

content.heading: Homophones
paragraphs: Homophones sound alike but are spelled differently and mean different things: sea and see, meat and meet, peace and piece, right and write, their and there. Some sets have three spellings, as in their, there and they're, where the apostrophe marks a contraction.
Homographs are the opposite trap: one spelling with different sounds or meanings, such as lead /liːd/ and lead /led/, or bow /bəʊ/ and bow /baʊ/.
The exam may ask which pair are homophones, or which word sounds like a given word. Test the pronunciation first, then check that the meanings differ.
bullets: Same sound, different spelling and meaning.
Homographs: same spelling, different sound or meaning.
Pronounce before choosing.
content.takeaway: Homophones agree in sound and disagree in spelling and sense.

check.question: Which pair are homophones?
check.why: Write and right are both /raɪt/; the other pairs differ in voicing or vowel sound.

content.heading: Near misses
paragraphs: Many pairs look like homophones but differ in one sound. Loose /luːs/ and lose /luːz/ differ in voicing; advice /ədˈvaɪs/ and advise /ədˈvaɪz/ do the same. Voicing is the commonest single-sound difference: /s/ against /z/, /f/ against /v/, and /θ/ against /ð/.
Rhyme traps work the same way: food /uː/ does not rhyme with good /ʊ/, and cloth /θ/ does not rhyme with clothe /ð/. Vowel length and final voicing decide most of these near misses.
Nigerian English sometimes merges hear and here, or keeps apart pairs that standard English joins. The exam follows the standard, so learn the contrast rather than your own habit.
bullets: Check voicing: /s/ against /z/, /θ/ against /ð/.
Vowel length can break a rhyme.
Exam answers follow standard pronunciation.
content.takeaway: A single sound can turn a homophone into a near miss.

check.question: Which pair differ only in voicing?
check.why: Loose ends in /s/ and lose in /z/; the other three pairs are true homophones.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Rhyme is about sound after the stressed vowel. 'Love' and 'move' share four letters but no vowel sound, so they do not rhyme.

content.problem: Which pair are homophones: lose and loose, write and right, food and foot, or advice and advise?

steps.reason: Homophones must sound identical in standard pronunciation. Reach for the minimal-pair list because homophones are identical sound with different spelling. If stuck, say each pair three times and listen for any stray sound.
steps.result: Write and right are both /raɪt/; the others differ.
steps.predictPrompt: Check the remaining pairs for a single differing sound.

steps.reason: One changed consonant can separate two similar words. Reach for the minimal-pair list because it isolates the one sound that separates lookalikes. If stuck, swap the suspect sound and hear whether the word changes.
steps.result: Loose /luːs/ and lose /luːz/ differ in voicing; food /uː/ and foot /ʊ/ differ in length; advice /s/ and advise /z/ differ in voicing.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you verify this answer?

steps.reason: A homophone pair must also differ in spelling and sense. Reach for the homophone card because it pairs identical sound with different spelling and sense. If stuck, write both words, then say what each one means.
steps.result: Write and right are spelled differently and mean different things.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: What a rhyme really is
paragraphs: A rhyme is a shared ending sound between two words. Cat and hat rhyme because both end with the same vowel plus the same final consonant: 'at'. The ends match, so the words rhyme.

A perfect rhyme shares the vowel and everything after it. Cat and hat are perfect. A near rhyme (also called slant rhyme) shares only part of the ending — cat and car share the vowel but not the final sound. Near rhymes are weaker, and for examination answers treat them as non-rhymes — perfect rhyme is the standard.

Rhyme is about sound, never about spelling. 'Though' and 'through' do not rhyme in sound even though their spellings look related. 'Eight' and 'late' rhyme perfectly even though they are spelt differently. Only the ear is the referee.

The exam will ask one of three things: which pair rhymes, which word rhymes with the given word, or which pair fails to rhyme. In all three cases you must say the words aloud in your head before choosing.
A quick trick: strip each word down to its last stressed vowel and everything after it. If those pieces match, the words rhyme. Cat → 'at', hat → 'at'. Match. Home → 'ome', dome → 'ome'. Match.
bullets: Rhyme = shared ending sound
Perfect rhyme shares vowel and all after it
Spelling is irrelevant; the ear decides

content.heading: Go deeper: Homophones and homographs
paragraphs: Homophones are words that sound exactly the same but are spelled differently and mean different things. There, their and they're. To, too and two. Their, there and they're — all three sound alike but each does its own job.

Homographs are the opposite case: words spelled the same but pronounced differently and meaning different things. 'Read' as in 'I read every day' is present; 'read' as in 'I read yesterday' is past. Same spelling, different sound, different time.

How to beat the questions. If the item asks you to pick the word that sounds alike, it is a homophone question — answer by ear. If the item asks about meaning in a sentence, it is a homograph question — answer by meaning and tense.
The classic pairs the exam loves: hear and here, sea and see, flower and flour, right and write, peace and piece, week and weak. Learn them as pairs, not as separate words.
In your own writing, the danger is choosing the wrong homophone — 'I no the answer' instead of 'I know the answer'. The exam will test whether you can spot that error inside a sentence.
bullets: Homophones: same sound, different spelling and meaning
Homographs: same spelling, different sound and meaning
Sound questions need the ear; meaning questions need the sentence

content.heading: Go deeper: Rhyme versus homophone — the key difference
paragraphs: Rhyme is a partial match at the end of two words. Homophone is a total match of the whole sound. Cat and hat rhyme, but they are not homophones — only their endings match, their starts differ.

Here is the flip side. Two homophones automatically rhyme, because identical sounds must share their endings too. 'There' and 'their' rhyme because they are the same sound from start to finish. Every homophone is a rhyme, but most rhymes are not homophones.

The exam sets the trap deliberately. It offers an option that is a rhyme where the question wants a homophone, or a homophone where the question wants a rhyme. The size of the match is the whole test.
Read the question word by word. 'Which word is a homophone of X?' — full match needed. 'Which pair rhymes?' — end match is enough. One word in the question decides which answer is correct.
Practise by sorting pairs into three boxes: rhymes only, homophones, and neither. Ten minutes of sorting makes the difference between a guessed answer and a known answer.
bullets: Rhyme = partial match at the end
Homophone = identical sound from start to finish
Every homophone is a rhyme; most rhymes are not homophones

content.question: Which word rhymes with 'great': greet, straight, grid or grade?
hints: Say 'great' and identify the vowel /eɪ/.
The rhyme must repeat everything from that vowel onward.
Straight ends in /eɪt/, exactly like great.

lessons.title: Word Stress
lessons.objective: Place stress on the correct syllable of polysyllabic words using word class, suffix and compound patterns.

content.heading: Word stress
paragraphs: A radio presenter says 'PREsent' for the gift and 'preSENT' for the verb, and listeners hear two different words. The difference is stress.

content.heading: Stress belongs to the word
paragraphs: Stress is the syllable a speaker makes louder, longer and higher. English does not mark it in spelling, so the same letters can carry different stress: a REcord is a file, but to reCORD is to store sound.

Monosyllabic words carry one stress by default, so the exam tests polysyllables most — but watch the two cases the exam actually tests: monosyllables stress their only vowel, and monosyllabic function words (to, and, it) often weaken to the schwa in sentences. Recognising a weak-form monosyllable is a connected-speech skill tested alongside word stress.
Nigerian English sometimes places stress differently, as in 'MAintain' for mainTAIN. The exam follows standard British pronunciation, so learn the pattern rather than your own habit.
bullets: Stress means louder, longer and higher.
Nouns often front-stress; verbs often end-stress.
Spelling does not show stress.
Polysyllables carry the examinable stress pattern; monosyllables stress their only vowel.
content.takeaway: Stress is a property of the spoken word, not of its spelling.

check.question: As a noun, 'record' is stressed on the ______ syllable.
check.why: The noun REcord stresses the first syllable; the verb reCORD stresses the second.

content.heading: Suffixes move the stress
paragraphs: Adding a suffix can pull the stress to a different syllable. Photograph stresses the first syllable, photography the second, and photographic the third, although the letters are nearly the same.

Words ending in -tion, -sion, -ic, -ical and -ity usually stress the syllable just before the suffix: educate becomes eduCAtion, politics becomes poLItical, and real becomes reALity. Words ending in -ify stress the syllable two places before -fy: JUS-ti-fy, SPEC-i-fy.
The rule explains why POlitics changes to poliTIcian and EConomy to ecoNOMic. Learn the word family together, because the exam often asks which word in a set is stressed differently.
bullets: -tion and -sion stress the syllable before.
-ic and -ical stress just before the suffix.
-ity pulls the stress to the syllable before it; -ify stresses two syllables before -fy.
content.takeaway: A suffix usually pulls the stress to the syllable before it.

check.question: Where is the stress in 'photography'?
check.why: Photography is pho-TOG-ra-phy: the -graphy ending attracts stress to the syllable before it.

visual.caption: The same spelling carries stress on the first syllable as a noun and the second as a verb.

content.heading: Compounds and contrasts
paragraphs: Compound nouns stress the first element: BLACKbird, FOOTball, TEApot and POST office. Compound adjectives and phrasal verbs often stress the second: well-KNOWN, old-FASHioned, underSTAND and turn OFF.

Stress can also distinguish meaning: a GREENhouse is a glass building, while a green HOUSE is a house painted green. The same contrast appears in 'English teacher' for a teacher of English and 'English TEACHER' for a teacher who is English.

In connected speech, stress falls on content words such as nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs, and weakens on articles, prepositions and auxiliaries. That sentence-level pattern is the subject of emphatic stress.
bullets: Compound nouns stress the first element.
Compound adjectives and phrasal verbs stress the second.
A stress shift can change the meaning.
content.takeaway: In a compound, the stressed element tells you which part is being named.

check.question: Which compound is stressed on its first element?
check.why: Blackbird is a compound noun, so it stresses BLACK; the others are an adjective and phrasal verbs that stress the second part.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Learn word families, not single words: photograph, photography and photographic together show the suffix rule at work.

content.problem: Mark the stress in 'political' and 'politician'.

steps.reason: The stress of the family is easier to see from the short form. Reach for the stress worksheet because it charts where the base word lands. If stuck, tap the stressed syllable and feel the beat.
steps.result: Politics stresses the first syllable: POL-i-tics.
steps.predictPrompt: Which suffix is added in each longer word?

steps.reason: Words ending in -ical stress the syllable before the suffix. Reach for the suffix stress table because -ical shifts stress to the syllable before it. If stuck, tap the syllable before -ical and feel the beat.
steps.result: Political becomes po-LIT-i-cal.
steps.predictPrompt: What could go wrong at this step, and how do you prevent it?

steps.reason: Words ending in -ian also stress the syllable before it. Reach for the suffix stress table because -ian likewise stresses the syllable before it. If stuck, tap the syllable before -ian and feel the beat.
steps.result: Politician becomes pol-i-TI-cian.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: What word stress is
paragraphs: Word stress is the one syllable in a word that carries the most force. English does not print the stress, so you must learn it by hearing. In 'photograph' the stress falls on the first syllable: PHO-to-graph. In 'photography' it moves to the second: pho-TO-gra-phy.

A stressed syllable is louder, longer and clearer. An unstressed syllable is shorter and its vowel often flattens to the weak 'schwa' sound (the 'a' in 'sofa'). Hear the difference: PHO-to-graph versus pho-TO-gra-phy — the unstressed vowels soften.

Why does the vowel change sound? English vowels are at full strength only in stressed syllables. In every other syllable they relax. That is why the same spelling can sound like a different vowel depending on where the stress lands.

The exam's favourite test: 'Which syllable is stressed in the word?' Say the word aloud three times, each time leaning on a different syllable, and pick the one that sounds like real English. Your ear knows the answer even when you cannot explain it.
Building the habit: every time you learn a new English word, mark its stress with a capital letter in your own notes. DOOR-way, not door-WAY. After a hundred words, the pattern becomes automatic.
bullets: One syllable per word carries the force
Stressed syllable: louder, longer, clearer
Unstressed vowels flatten to schwa

content.heading: Go deeper: Suffixes that pull the stress
paragraphs: Some endings grab the stress and drag it next to themselves. The commonest stress-grabbers are -tion, -sion, -ic and -ity. They place the stress on the syllable right before them: edu-CA-tion, re-vi-SION, scien-TI-fic, hu-MI-li-ty.

Other endings are neutral; they never move the stress. The commonest are -ness, -less, -ful, -ly, -er and -est. 'Happy' stresses the first syllable; 'happiness' also stresses the first. The root keeps its stress no matter what neutral ending you add.

Two words show the contrast perfectly: 'photograph' (root stress on PHO-) versus 'photography' (the -y ending lets the stress move to -TO-graphy). Actually, -graphy and -logy attract the stress to the syllable right before the ending: phoTOgraphy, biOlogy.

So the practical rule: if the word ends in -tion, -sion, -ic, -ity, -graphy or -logy, stress the syllable just before the ending. If it ends in -ness, -less, -ful, -ly, keep the stress where the root had it.
Learn the grabber-list as a song: tion, sion, ic, ity — stress the syllable before. Ten repetitions on Monday, five on Tuesday, and the list is yours forever.
bullets: -tion, -sion, -ic, -ity, -graphy: stress the syllable before
-ness, -less, -ful, -ly: keep the root's stress
Photograph → PHO-to-graph; photography → pho-TO-gra-phy

content.heading: Go deeper: The traps in stress questions
paragraphs: Trap one: the noun–verb pair. 'Record' the noun stresses the first syllable (RE-cord); 'record' the verb stresses the second (re-CORD). 'Present' the noun stresses the first (PRE-sent); 'present' the verb stresses the second (pre-SENT). Same spelling, two different stress patterns.

Trap two: the spelling trap. The spelling never tells you where the stress falls, so guessing from letters is a guaranteed mistake. Only the sound carries the answer. Say the word aloud and trust your ear over your eyes.

Trap three: the unknown word. Even if you have never seen the word, the suffix rules usually rescue you. Spot a -tion and stress the syllable before it. Spot a -ness and keep the root stress. You can answer a stress question on a word you have never heard.
