Trap four: mixing up word stress with sentence (emphatic) stress. Word stress lives inside one word; emphatic stress lives across the whole sentence. If the question asks for the loud syllable inside a word, word stress is what it wants.
Work fast but verify. Do the easy items first, mark the hard ones, then come back. A finished paper with two skipped items beats a perfect first half with an empty second half.
bullets: Noun RE-cord, verb re-CORD — same spelling, different stress
Suffix rules answer words you have never heard
Word stress lives inside the word; sentence stress spreads across it

content.question: Where does the stress fall in 'education', 'photographic' and 'ability'?
hints: Find the suffix in each word.
-tion, -ic and -ity all pull the stress to the syllable before.
Say each word aloud and mark the loudest syllable.

lessons.title: Emphatic Stress in Connected Speech
lessons.objective: Identify which word carries emphatic stress in a sentence and the question or correction that stress answers.

content.heading: Emphatic stress
paragraphs: A teacher says 'ADA wrote the letter', not 'Bola', and every student knows who wrote it. The emphasis does the work of a whole sentence.

content.heading: The stressed word is the correction
paragraphs: Emphatic stress is sentence-level stress placed on one word to contrast it with another. The stressed word answers the implied question or corrects a wrong assumption.
In 'ADA wrote the letter', the stress answers 'Who wrote the letter?'. In 'Ada WROTE the letter', it answers whether Ada wrote it rather than read or typed it.

The rest of the sentence is spoken more weakly, so the contrast is clear. In print, examiners often capitalise the stressed word or describe where the stress falls, and the capital letter is your cue.
bullets: Emphatic stress marks a contrast.
The stressed word answers the implied question.
Everything else in the sentence is weakened.
content.takeaway: Move the emphasis and you answer a different question.

check.question: 'Ada WROTE the letter' answers which question?
options: When did Ada write the letter?
check.why: The stress on WROTE corrects the doubt about the action, so it answers whether she wrote rather than read or typed it.

content.heading: Reading the question behind the stress
paragraphs: JAMB usually gives a sentence with one word capitalised and asks which question it answers, or gives a question and asks where the stress falls. Work from the contrast, not from loudness alone.
'Bola cooked RICE' answers 'What did Bola cook?', because rice is contrasted with other foods. 'BOLA cooked rice' answers 'Who cooked the rice?'.
A negative correction works the same way. 'He did not go to LAGOS' contradicts 'He went to Lagos', not 'He went to Abuja'; the stressed place is the one being denied.

Connected speech also links and reduces words: a final consonant joins a following vowel (AN apple, NOT it), and function words weaken into schwa (to /tə/, and /ənd/, for /fə/). Those weak forms are articulation, not spelling — they are how the words are actually said in a sentence.
bullets: Identify the word in contrast.
Match it to the question it answers.
A stressed negative denies that same item.
Linking joins a final consonant to a following vowel (AN apple).
Function words weaken to schwa: to /tə/, and /ənd/, for /fə/.
content.takeaway: Find the word in contrast, then read the question it answers.

check.question: 'Bola cooked RICE' answers which question?
check.why: The stress falls on the object, so it answers what was cooked rather than who cooked it.

content.heading: Word stress versus emphatic stress
paragraphs: Word stress lives inside a word and decides which syllable is strong; emphatic stress lives in a sentence and decides which word is strong. Confusing the two is the commonest oral-forms error.
The same sentence can shift emphasis without changing its words: 'I didn't say HE stole the book' denies that he was the thief, while 'I didn't say he STOLE the book' denies the theft.

Auxiliaries and prepositions can carry emphatic stress too. 'He IS coming' corrects doubt about the fact, and 'Put it ON the table' contrasts the place with another. The same words can therefore answer different questions as the emphasis moves.
bullets: Word stress chooses a syllable.
Emphatic stress chooses a word.
Any word can be emphasised, even a preposition.
content.takeaway: Word stress chooses a syllable; emphatic stress chooses a word.

check.question: Emphatic stress is best described as ______.
options: stress on one syllable of a word
stress on one word to show contrast
stress on the last word of every sentence
check.why: Emphatic stress highlights one word in an utterance so that it contrasts with another word or answers a specific question.

visual.caption: Word stress chooses a syllable; emphatic stress chooses a word.

content.title: Exam trap
content.body: Do not look for the longest word. The stressed word is the one that would change if the speaker were correcting a different mistake.

content.problem: The statement 'Mary sang at the PARTY' answers which question?

steps.reason: The capitalised word is the contrast. Reach for the stress worksheet because the capital marks the contrast beat. If stuck, cap a different word and hear how the meaning shifts.
steps.result: PARTY is stressed.
steps.predictPrompt: Which question asks about that item?

steps.operation: Match the item to a question
steps.reason: The stressed word must be the answer to the question. Reach for the question-match drill because each question type demands one stressed answer. If stuck, write the question whose answer is the capped word.
steps.result: The question asks where Mary sang.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you verify this answer?

steps.reason: A question about who or what would stress a different word. Reach for the stress worksheet because moving the capital moves the question. If stuck, cap each other word in turn and see which question it springs.
steps.result: 'Who sang at the party?' would stress MARY, and 'What did Mary do?' would stress SANG.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you explain why this beats the other options?

content.heading: Go deeper: Word stress versus emphatic stress
paragraphs: Word stress (last lesson) is locked inside a single word: PHO-to-graph. Emphatic stress is different — it is the extra push a speaker puts on one word inside a whole sentence to change or sharpen the meaning.

Take the sentence 'I didn't say he took it'. Stress HE and the sentence means someone else took it, not him. Stress TOOK and it means he did something else with it — maybe he borrowed it. Same words, four possible meanings, depending on which word carries the punch.

Word stress never moves: 'record' as a noun is always RE-cord. Emphatic stress moves wherever the speaker wants to point a finger. That is the core difference: fixed by the word versus chosen by the speaker.

The exam usually gives you the written sentence in full capitals on one word, or asks you to identify which word the writer emphasised by underlining or italics. Your job is to state what the emphasis excludes.
Learn the test shape: 'Which meaning is conveyed when 'he' is stressed?' — 'someone else did it'. The exam rewards the candidate who asks, 'what does the stressed word rule out?'
bullets: Word stress is fixed inside a word
Emphatic stress is placed on a word inside a sentence
The stressed word rules out every alternative meaning

content.heading: Go deeper: What happens to the rest of the sentence
paragraphs: When one word carries the emphasis, the words before and after it soften. They become shorter, quieter and less clear. This softening is the signal the listener uses to locate the stressed word.

Listen to a line like 'I NEVER said that'. The words around NEVER drop in volume, and NEVER stands up like a landmark. English speakers do this automatically, and English listeners hear it automatically — the technique is the message.

The softened words also lose their stressed syllable feel. Full, strong words around the emphatic word would drown it out, so the speaker clips them. That is why emphatic sentences sound different from ordinary ones — the edges are clipped so the centre can shine.

In the exam, you will sometimes be asked which word in a written sentence is likely to carry the emphasis. Choose the word whose meaning changes the sentence most, then check the written cues (capitals, italics) if they are given.
Training exercise: read any news headline aloud twice, stressing a different word each time, and notice how the meaning flips. Do this for five headlines a day; the reflex will be built in a week.
bullets: Words around the emphasis soften and shorten
The emphatic word stands up like a landmark
Capitals or italics in the question point to the stressed word

content.heading: Go deeper: The traps in emphatic-stress questions
paragraphs: Trap one: the word-stress confusion. A candidate hears the loud syllable inside 'record' and answers about sentence emphasis. Wrong tool. If the question shows a whole sentence, emphatic stress is what it wants, not syllable stress.

Trap two: the meaning trap. 'I didn't say HE took it' — the meaning excludes 'he' as the taker and includes every other possible taker. Exam options often phrase the answer as 'someone else took it'. Do not pick 'he did not take it' — that is the literal meaning, not the emphasis.

Trap three: the double-duty sentence. 'JOHN kicked the ball' excludes other kickers. 'John KICKED the ball' excludes other actions (he threw it, he caught it). 'John kicked the BALL' excludes other objects (the racket, the chair). Same words, three different expulsions, three different answers.

Trap four: the missing cue. In some items, no capitals or italics are given, and you must decide from meaning which word carries the emphasis. Pick the word whose emphasis produces the most sensible contrast with the rest of the sentence.

Work the options by elimination. Cross out any option whose explanation does not match a possible stress pattern. The remaining option is your answer; the exam is designed so the traps are internally inconsistent.
bullets: Whole sentence = emphatic stress; single word = word stress
Emphasis excludes the alternatives, it does not deny the action
Capitals, italics and 'rules out' phrasing are the keys

content.question: 'The students arrived LATE' answers which question?
hints: The stressed word answers the question directly.
LATE tells you when, not who or where.
Look for a question about time.

lessons.title: Section A Set and Synthesis
lessons.objective: Describe the three-passage Section A set (two passages + one cloze, about 200 words, various disciplines), explain passage coherence, and synthesise ideas from multiple passages into one summary.

content.heading: Section A set and synthesis
paragraphs: Section A sets one comprehension passage of about 200 words, one cloze of the same length, and ten questions on the approved novel. Good candidates read each text for its shape, then combine its central ideas into one faithful summary.

content.heading: What the three-passage set looks like
paragraphs: A candidate who has prepared for one long passage meets Section A and is startled. Instead of one text, she meets one comprehension passage of about 200 words, one cloze passage of the same length, and ten questions drawn from the prescribed novel — for 2026, The Lekki Headmaster by Kabir Alabi Garba.

The set is deliberately mixed. One passage may treat biology, another economics, history or health, and the cloze usually tests vocabulary and grammatical fit. The disciplines differ because the examination wants reading skill, not specialist knowledge.

Because each text is short, the skill lies in management rather than stamina. Candidates should move deliberately between texts, noting the main claim of each, since the final summary draws on more than one source.
bullets: Section A has two passages and one cloze, each about 200 words.
Passages span varied disciplines such as science, history, economics and health.
Roughly 200 words per text keeps the focus on quick, purposeful reading.
content.takeaway: One comprehension passage, one cloze and ten questions on the approved novel form Section A.

check.question: Which description matches the Section A set?
options: one comprehension passage, one cloze and ten questions on the approved novel
four short poems on one topic
a single legal document with questions
check.why: Section A sets one comprehension passage (5 questions), one cloze passage (10 questions), and ten questions on the approved novel.

content.heading: Coherence is how paragraphs link
paragraphs: A reader finishes without ever being lost, though she never looked up a hard word, because each paragraph announced its purpose and handed the reader to the next.

That linking is coherence: ideas are arranged so each paragraph earns its place. A topic sentence names the paragraph's claim, and later sentences develop only that claim. Unity therefore comes from one idea per paragraph, varied in wording but not in direction.

Signal words carry the reader between steps. However and but flag a turn, for example gives support, and therefore or consequently draws the conclusion. Reasoning follows when conclusions grow from those links, not outside knowledge.
bullets: Coherence means paragraphs link so the argument moves in one direction.
A topic sentence states what that paragraph alone must prove.
Signal words such as however, for example and therefore mark turns and conclusions.
content.takeaway: One claim per paragraph, linked by signal words, makes reasoning easy to follow.

check.question: A paragraph begins 'The diet improved; therefore...' What does 'therefore' signal?
check.why: 'Therefore' marks a conclusion that follows from the claims before it.

content.heading: Synthesis combines passages into one summary
paragraphs: Two passages describe a school garden project from opposite sides: one praises its harvest, the other warns about its cost. Asked for one summary, the candidate must hold both claims together instead of copying either passage alone.

Synthesis means combining distinct pieces into a complete whole. A Section A summary therefore merges main claims, reasons and conclusions from several texts, in fresh wording. It does not add opinions, and it leaves out minor detail.

The approved reading text is a complete novel — for 2026, The Lekki Headmaster by Kabir Alabi Garba; ten questions are drawn from it. Synthesis differs because it must balance two voices and show how they agree or differ.
bullets: Synthesis merges main claims from several passages into one coherent whole.
Keep the summary in your own words and drop examples and minor detail.
A single-passage summary uses one voice; synthesis must balance at least two.
content.takeaway: One summary, in fresh words, marries the main ideas of several passages.

check.question: Which summary shows synthesis of two passages?
options: quotes a long line from one passage
merges the main ideas of both passages in fresh words
adds an opinion absent from both passages
retells only the first passage in new words
check.why: Synthesis combines distinct pieces from several texts into one whole, in original wording.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: Plan Section A as one set. Read each passage for its main claim and note it down before moving on, because examiners reward the summary that can name the shared idea across texts, not the longest quotation from one.

content.problem: Passage A says a school garden boosts nutrition; Passage B says it strains budgets. Synthesise a one-sentence summary.

steps.operation: Extract the main claim of each passage
steps.reason: Synthesis starts from each text's actual claims, not its examples. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, underline the single claim in each passage and ignore the examples.
steps.result: A claims nutrition gains; B claims rising costs for schools
steps.predictPrompt: What information do you compare before deciding?

steps.operation: Compare the claims for agreement and tension
steps.reason: The summary must hold both voices and show their relationship clearly. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, write the two claims side by side and circle the shared word.
steps.result: Gains and costs are two sides of the same project
steps.predictPrompt: What would a weaker answer look like here?

steps.operation: Merge both claims into one sentence in fresh words
steps.reason: One sentence must cover both claims in new wording. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, join the two claims with but and drop everything outside them.
steps.result: The garden improves diets but demands careful budgeting from schools
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: Passage A praises free school meals; Passage B worries about their cost. What should your one-sentence summary do?
hints: Name the main claim of each passage first.
Keep both voices in the sentence, joined by a contrast link.
Use fresh wording and leave out figures and examples.

content.heading: Go deeper: What the Approved Reading Text means
paragraphs: Candidates sometimes hear the phrase 'Approved Reading Text' and imagine it names the passages printed in the paper. It does not. It names the complete novel JAMB prescribes for the year — for 2026, The Lekki Headmaster by Kabir Alabi Garba. You read it before the exam; JAMB then sets ten questions straight from it.

Why does the word 'approved' matter? Because JAMB chooses the novel once a year, and every serious practice must come from it. Random practice textbooks will not match its plot, its characters or its themes, and students who skip the novel lose ten marks they could have banked.

The catch is that examiners expect you to think with the passages, not just about them. A candidate who reads only for multiple-choice answers will freeze when asked to discuss one text at length in the summary task.
So read each passage twice: once for answers, once for arguments. Ask yourself after every paragraph — what is this text trying to make me believe? That habit is what Section A rewards.

One last fact. JAMB Section A passages change every year, but the questions do not: one cloze, one set of comprehension questions, and one summary. If you know those three shapes, every set you meet will feel familiar.
bullets: No special book — the exam passages are the reading text
Think with the passages, not just about them
Read twice: once for answers, once for arguments

content.heading: Go deeper: A harder summary, fully worked
paragraphs: Imagine two short texts. Text A says a mobile clinic visits twelve villages each month and gives vaccines free. Text B says fuel costs, bad roads and broken equipment force the clinic to miss one visit in every four.

A weak summary copies Text A alone and praises the free vaccines. That misses half the picture. Another copies Text B alone and complains about costs. That misses the other half. The exam set this exact trap on purpose.

The strong answer names both sides in one relationship: the clinic brings real free healthcare to villages that would otherwise have none, but the service still fails one visit in four because of fuel, roads and broken gear. Benefit and limit, one sentence.
Formula for a synthesis answer: 'Text A is right that X, but Text B shows that Y, so the full picture is Z.' Practise that frame on any two texts and Section A stops being scary.
bullets: Name the benefit and the limit in one breath
Benefit + limit = full picture
Use the 'A says X but B shows Y' frame

content.heading: Go deeper: The traps inside Section A
paragraphs: Trap one: treating Section A as three separate tasks. The cloze, the comprehension and the summary all belong to the same set of texts. Read the set as a set, or your summary will miss points sitting in the earlier passages.

Trap two: copying without connecting. A paragraph stuffed with 'therefore' and 'however' is not automatically logical. The examiner wants each linking word to do real work — turning an idea or closing a thought — not just decorating the page.

Trap three: the topic sentence that says nothing. If your paragraph opens with 'In conclusion,' followed by no actual claim, the examiner scores zero no matter how nice the next three lines are. Every paragraph must state one clear claim.
Beat the traps like this: read the set as one story, give every paragraph one job, and underline the linking words as you write to check they each earn their place.
bullets: Read the whole set as one connected task
Linking words must do real jobs, not decoration
Every paragraph needs one clear claim

lessons.title: Figures of Speech in Context
lessons.objective: Identify figurative and idiomatic expressions in passages and explain their functions — metaphor, simile, personification, hyperbole, irony and understatement — as comprehension items.

content.heading: Figures of speech in context
paragraphs: A reader in Surulere meets the line ‘His anger was a harmattan wind’ and may misread it literally. JAMB asks what it suggests, so figurative language must be read for meaning, not for form alone.

content.heading: Metaphor and simile
paragraphs: At a bus park, a reporter writes, ‘The queue moved like ants.’ A reader who pictures insects misses the point, which is steady, slow movement. The line is a simile because it compares the queue with ants using like.

The same reporter later calls the driver ‘a lion of the road.’ He is not an animal; he is brave, fierce and ready to fight through every jam. That is a metaphor because it declares that the man is a lion without like or as.
bullets: A simile uses like or as to compare two different things.
A metaphor says one thing is another without that signal.
JAMB asks what the comparison suggests, not which label fits.
content.takeaway: A simile compares with like or as; a metaphor declares that one thing is another.

check.question: In ‘The danfo driver is a lion of the road’, what is suggested about the driver?
options: He is brave and ready to confront any obstacle on the road.
He once transported a lion in his vehicle.
He resembles a lion in shape and size.
He drives only at night to avoid lions.
check.why: The metaphor transfers courage and ferocity, while the literal animal readings are absurd in context.

content.heading: Personification and hyperbole
paragraphs: During a heavy downpour at Oshodi Market, the rain ‘hammered angrily on the zinc roof’ and the chief’s generator ‘coughed and died’. The rain did not feel anger and the machine did not cough. Both lines give human life or action to non-human things, which is personification.

A trader who sold fifty orange crates in one morning told friends, ‘I have waited a thousand years for this rain.’ She had not lived that long. That is hyperbole, deliberate exaggeration for effect, and it suggests impatience so intense that waiting felt endless.
bullets: Personification gives human action or feeling to things that cannot act.
Hyperbole exaggerates beyond literal truth to stress a feeling.
JAMB asks what the figure suggests, not which term the examiner prefers.
content.takeaway: Personification acts human; hyperbole exaggerates to stress a feeling.

check.question: The line ‘The harmattan wind howled through the town’ suggests that the wind was
options: loud, wild and feeling alive with force
a person who shouted in the town
a sound record played through the town
a spirit that entered every house
check.why: The wind is given a human voice and movement, but the meaning is violent loudness, not a literal person.

content.heading: Irony and understatement
paragraphs: After six hours without light, a tenant told the landlord, ‘Beautiful planning,’ while staring at uncooked food. The praise was not sincere because the surrounding lines show familiar failure. That is irony: saying the opposite of what is meant, usually to expose folly with quiet humour.

A committee that calls a six-hour blackout ‘a little delay’ uses understatement, which makes a fact sound smaller than it is. Idioms work the same way in context, as in ‘He keeps an eye on the money,’ which means he watches it carefully. JAMB tests these items by asking for the meaning in the passage, so reject the literal opposite or the too-small reading.
bullets: Irony means the opposite of the literal words; the context proves it.
Understatement shrinks a fact; the correct meaning is larger than stated.
Always test an option against the surrounding lines before choosing.
content.takeaway: Read the lines around the figure; the context, not the literal words, decides.

check.question: A trader says ‘A small delay’ after a six-hour blackout. The phrase suggests that the delay was
options: serious, though the words dress it as small
pleasant because the stall stayed cool
check.why: Understatement calls a large fact small, so the passage means a major disruption despite the mild wording.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In meaning-in-context items, first ask what the words say literally, then ask what the surrounding lines show the writer means, and choose the option that matches the lines, not the dictionary or the label.

content.problem: Passage: ‘When the council opened the new library, the chairman called it a light in the dark room of illiteracy.’ What does the chairman most nearly mean?

steps.operation: Identify the figure and its source
steps.reason: The library is called light, which is a metaphor because it declares identity without like or as. Reach for the figure-to-meaning bridge because the metaphor declares an identity to unpack. If stuck, ask what the source and target are and underline both.
steps.result: Source is light; target is the library.
steps.predictPrompt: What plain meaning can replace the image?

steps.reason: A library cannot shine as a lamp does, so the literal reading fails in context. Reach for the figure-to-meaning bridge because the literal reading fails in context. If stuck, test the literal reading against the library and watch it break.
steps.result: Figuratively, light means knowledge and hope that remove ignorance.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you choose between the possible routes?

steps.operation: Choose the meaning the passage supports
steps.reason: The surrounding idea is that the library ends illiteracy, not that it replaces electricity. Reach for the answer-control discipline because it keeps you inside the text. If stuck, cross off every option that reaches beyond the passage.
steps.result: The answer is that the library brings knowledge and hope.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you sanity-check this answer against the evidence?

content.question: A passage says, ‘The crowd after the match was a river flowing towards the gates.’ What does the image suggest about the crowd?
hints: A river flows steadily, in one direction and without pause.
The gates tell you where the movement is heading.
Choose steady, directed movement, not water or boats.

content.heading: Go deeper: How context fixes a figure's meaning
paragraphs: A figure of speech never means anything on its own. The words around it pin down the meaning. A writer cannot drop an image into a passage and leave you guessing — the context always whispers the answer, usually within the same sentence or the one before it.

Watch the signal words. 'But', 'however' and 'yet' mark a turn; the figure after them usually flips the earlier meaning. 'For example' after a metaphor supports it. The turns are where the writer hides the point, so find the figure after the turn first.

Try this one: 'The committee worked like a beehive during the flood relief.' The flood tells you the scene is urgent and busy, so 'like a beehive' means tight, organised cooperation — not danger, not noise. The flood fixed the meaning.
The exam usually asks such questions as 'What does the writer mean by ...?' The answer is never the literal image (bees); it is the sense the context forces on it (organised teamwork under pressure).

One last habit. When you meet a strange image in a passage, pause and ask: what is happening in the sentence before this figure? That one question turns a confusing image into a clear answer faster than any memorised list of definitions ever will.
bullets: The figure never stands alone; context pins it down
But, however and yet mark the turn where the meaning lives
Answer with the sense, never the literal image

content.heading: Go deeper: Metaphor, simile and personification
paragraphs: Metaphor and simile do the same job — they let one idea borrow strength from another. The difference is packaging. A simile announces the borrowing with 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor does it silently. 'He is like a lion' borrows like a simile; 'he is a lion' borrows without warning.

Personification is the special case where the borrowed strength is human. Wind 'howls', roads 'invite', markets 'smile', death 'knocks'. The thing given human behaviour must be non-human for the figure to count.

Not every 'like' is a simile. 'Men like the chairman worked late' uses 'like' to mean 'such as', comparing equals. A true simile compares two unlike domains — a queue with ants, a voice with harmattan wind. Ask yourself: are two unrelated things being set side by side?

The exam will hand you a line and ask you to name the figure. First check for 'like' or 'as' (simile). Then check for silent substitution (metaphor). Then check whether something non-human is doing human things (personification). That order catches almost every item.
bullets: Simile announces with like/as; metaphor borrows silently
Personification gives human behaviour to non-human things
Like meaning 'such as' is not a simile

content.heading: Go deeper: Hyperbole, irony and understatement
paragraphs: Hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration. 'The price jumped to the moon' does not carry a real number — it carries the writer's anger about the rise. In argumentative writing, hyperbole is a signal, never a statistic. The exam wants you to hear the feeling, not trust the math.

Irony means the opposite of what is said — usually praise said to attack, as in 'Beautiful planning' said about a failed project. Understatement does the opposite: 'a little delay' about a three-month failure confesses the true problem by shrinking it. The two figures point in opposite directions.

Both rely on a gap between words and truth. Irony's gap is a glow — it inflates praise. Understatement's gap is a small door — it shrinks the problem. Spot which direction the gap faces and you have named the figure.

In an exam, if the option mentions 'criticism masked as praise', that is irony. If the option mentions 'criticism shrunk to nothing', that is understatement. If it mentions 'feeling inflated beyond fact', that is hyperbole. Three labels, three directions — learn the directions and the labels follow.
bullets: Hyperbole inflates a feeling beyond fact
Irony masks criticism as praise
Understatement shrinks a problem to nothing

lessons.title: Clause and Sentence Patterns
lessons.objective: Identify simple, compound and complex sentence patterns, identify noun, adjective and adverbial clauses and their functions, identify various grammatical patterns in use, and interpret information conveyed in sentences.

content.heading: Clause and sentence patterns
paragraphs: Sentences classify by clause number and clause function, and JAMB asks you to label patterns and interpret what each clause contributes to meaning in examination questions.

content.heading: Simple, compound or complex
paragraphs: A candidate faces three sentences and must label one simple, one compound and one complex. Count clauses rather than length, because longer does not always mean more complex.

A simple sentence has one independent clause with one subject and one finite verb, as in 'The traders closed early'. A compound sentence joins two independent clauses with and, but or so, as in 'The traders closed early, but the driver waited'.

A complex sentence keeps one main clause and adds a dependent clause with because, when, although or if. 'The traders closed early although the market was busy' is complex because the although part cannot stand alone.
bullets: Simple: one independent clause, for example Ada sold pepper.
Compound: two independent clauses joined by and, but, or, so.
Complex: one main clause plus a dependent clause with because, when, although, if.
content.takeaway: Count clauses: one is simple, two equal is compound, unequal is complex.

check.question: Which sentence is complex?
options: The traders closed early, but the driver waited.
The traders closed early although the market was busy.
The traders closed early and the driver waited.
check.why: It has one main clause plus a dependent although clause; the others are simple or compound.

content.heading: Three kinds of dependent clause
paragraphs: A student writes 'I know that he passed' and cannot label 'that he passed'. It is the object of 'know', so it is a noun clause, which does the job of a noun.

A noun clause can be subject or object and often begins with that, what, whether or who. What he said was true shows a noun clause as subject, while She asked what happened shows one as object. It answers what.

An adjective clause describes a noun through who, which or that, as in 'The school that stands near the market is old'. An adverbial clause tells time, cause or purpose through when, because or so that, as in 'Students left when the bell rang'.
bullets: Noun clause: subject or object, introduced by that, what, whether, who.
Adjective clause: describes a noun with who, which, that, where.
Adverbial clause: tells when, why or for what purpose with when, because, so that.
content.takeaway: Ask what the clause does: noun, adjective or adverbial decides its name.

check.question: In 'The boy who sang won the prize', what is 'who sang'?
check.why: Who sang describes the noun boy, so it is an adjective clause.

content.heading: Patterns, meaning and number
paragraphs: A candidate reads 'The boy who passed received a book' and must tell what the sentence means. The who clause limits which boy, and the singular noun book tells that one book was given.

Use patterns to rebuild broken sentences. A correct pattern keeps main and dependent clauses in order, joins equal ideas with and, but or so, and places adverbial clauses where they explain time, cause or purpose without breaking the main idea.

Form plurals with regular endings. Add s to book, books, es after s, sh, ch or x, as in boxes, and ies for consonant plus y, as in stories. Uncountables such as information and furniture take no plural s.
bullets: Pattern in use: main clause plus dependent clause in logical order.
Meaning: ask who, what, when, why or for what purpose the clause answers.
Number: countable nouns take s and es, uncountables take no s.
content.takeaway: Read the pattern for structure and the number for meaning and agreement.

check.question: Which noun is uncountable and takes no plural s?
check.why: Information is uncountable, so it takes no plural s and a singular verb.

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: In an item that asks for the pattern, count clauses first, then ask what each clause does. Two equal ideas joined by and, but or so is compound; a clause that describes a noun is adjective; one that cannot stand alone is dependent.

content.problem: Classify this sentence and state its clause pattern: Students who worked hard succeeded because they prepared early.

steps.reason: Each finite verb marks one clause in the sentence. Reach for the parse ladder because each finite verb marks one clause boundary. If stuck, hunt the sentence for every verb and mark its subject.
steps.result: Three verbs show three clauses: worked, succeeded, prepared.
steps.predictPrompt: What does the who part do if it is not the main clause?

steps.reason: Students who worked hard succeeded is main; who and because parts are dependent. Reach for the parse ladder because splitting clauses shows which depend on which. If stuck, bracket each clause and ask what each one is doing.
steps.result: Who part describes students; because part gives the cause.
steps.predictPrompt: What exactly does the question want you to write down first?

steps.reason: A main clause with dependent clauses is complex. Reach for the parse ladder because naming the pattern locks in the structure. If stuck, count main clauses and match to simple, compound or complex.
steps.result: Complex sentence with adjective and adverbial clauses.
steps.predictPrompt: How would you prove this claim to a sceptic?

content.heading: Go deeper: When coordination looks like subordination
paragraphs: A linker (and, but, so, because, when) does not fix the pattern by itself. The real test is counting finite verbs — verbs that can stand alone with a subject. Two finite verbs means two clauses; one finite verb means one clause.
'The cat and the dog slept' — one finite verb (slept), so it is simple, even though it contains 'and'. The 'and' joined two nouns, not two sentences.
'The cat slept and the dog barked' — two finite verbs (slept, barked), each with its own subject. Two independent clauses joined by 'and' makes it compound. Same linker, different structure.

So ignore the linkers at first. Count the verbs and match each to a subject. Clauses that can stand alone are independent (main); clauses that cannot stand alone are dependent (subordinate). That count never lies.
bullets: Count finite verbs, not linkers
And joining two nouns keeps the sentence simple
Two independent clauses joined = compound

content.heading: Go deeper: Noun clauses and the missing that
paragraphs: English often drops the word 'that' at the head of a noun clause. 'I know he passed' really means 'I know THAT he passed' — but whether 'that' is written or not, 'he passed' is the object of 'know', not a separate sentence standing on its own.

The same drop happens with adjective clauses. 'The book I bought is heavy' means 'The book THAT I bought'. The noun 'book' is the head; the clause 'I bought' describes it. The missing pronoun fools candidates into calling the whole thing a fragment.

The safe method: find the head noun or verb first. 'I know' wants an object — the whole remaining string is that object. 'The book' is a noun — the clause next to it describes the book. Heads first, clauses second.
Spot the head and the structure becomes obvious. Without it, every missing 'that' looks like broken English; with it, every missing 'that' is a dropped twin doing its job silently.

Interestingly, English also drops the relative pronoun at the start of adjective clauses. 'The man I saw' means 'The man whom I saw'. The drop is silent, but the clause is still working as an adjective on 'man'. Spotting the dropped word is the same skill, applied in a second place.
bullets: Missing 'that' is normal, not broken English
Find the head noun or verb first
The clause around a head describes or completes it

content.heading: Go deeper: Irregular plurals and uncountables
paragraphs: Most plurals take a simple s. A small set breaks the rule, and JAMB loves them. Child becomes children, not childs. Person becomes people in general use (persons in formal reports). Analysis becomes analyses, crisis becomes crises, thesis becomes theses.

Then come the uncountables — nouns that can never take a number: information, advice, research, furniture, luggage, homework, news, progress. You can never say 'informations' or 'advices'. They pair with 'much' (much information), never 'many'.
The exam also tests the verb that follows. 'Much information was available' — singular verb. 'Many reports were filed' — plural verb. 'News is good' — news is uncountable, so singular verb.

Memorise this pocket list: children, people, analyses, crises, theses, information, advice, research, furniture, luggage, news. Every one of them has appeared on a real JAMB paper. When you see them in a sentence, check the verb and the quantifier first.

Practice makes these lists stick. Write five sentences of your own using children, analyses, information and news with the right verb each time. The exam rewards the ear, and the ear is trained by your own voice, not by reading silently.
bullets: children, people, analyses, crises, theses — never regular s
Information, advice, research, news — never plural
Much + uncountable takes a singular verb

content.question: Classify this sentence and state its pattern: The students who arrived late left when the hall was full.
hints: Count the finite verbs to find how many clauses are present.
Ask what each dependent part does: one describes students, the other tells time.
A main clause with dependent clauses gives the complex pattern.

lessons.title: The Lekki Headmaster — the Book in One Sitting
lessons.objective: Describe the shape of Kabir Alabi Garba’s The Lekki Headmaster (the Dusk → Dawn circle), why JAMB prescribes it, and how to use the chapter lessons to sit the ten Section A novel questions.

content.heading: The Lekki Headmaster — the book in one sitting
paragraphs: Kabir Alabi Garba published The Lekki Headmaster in 2023. It is JAMB’s approved reading text for 2026, and ten questions in Section A come straight from it. This lesson is the map; the chapter lessons are the territory.

content.heading: What the novel is about
paragraphs: Adebepo Adewale — “Bepo” — is principal of Stardom Schools in Lekki. He is six foot two, strong-voiced, quick to spot cheating, and beloved by his learners. His wife Seri, a nurse in London, and their children Nike and Kike press him to move too.

The story turns on one question — will Bepo choose home or money? Stardom depends on him. The UK offers about £3,600 a month. The novel ends where it must, with Bepo choosing Stardom, the most dramatic way a man can refuse a flight.
The twelve chapters run Dusk to Dawn. An assembly collapse opens the book; a passport battle, a farewell and a plane ride follow; a dream and a return close it.
bullets: Bepo is the Lekki principal torn between Stardom and London
The twelve chapters run Dusk to Dawn — through breakdown, passport, farewell and flight
Ten Section A questions come from this one book every sitting
content.takeaway: The whole novel boils down to one question — will Bepo choose home or money?

check.question: What is The Lekki Headmaster, for JAMB purposes?
options: A poetry collection prescribed for Section B
JAMB's approved reading text for Section A
A Shakespeare play listed for literature
A grammar handbook for the cloze test
check.why: This book is the set text — the ten Section A questions come straight from it

content.heading: The circle: Dusk to Dawn
paragraphs: Chapter 1 is “Dusk” — Bepo breaks down at morning assembly, and nobody, not even the MD, can get him to say why. The pressure he has been carrying for years cracks open in front of everyone.

Chapters 2 to 10 are the slow build: the japa arithmetic, the diaspora tales, the passport, the lies at the embassy. Chapter 11 is the farewell. Chapter 12 is “Dawn” — the plane, the dream, and the shout every candidate should remember: “I didn’t go!”
bullets: Dusk opens the book — Bepo breaks down at the podium
The middle chapters build the japa case and the passport battle
Dawn closes it — the flight never taken and the return
content.takeaway: Read the shape first — Dusk, the build, then Dawn

check.question: Which two chapters frame the novel’s circle?
check.why: Chapter 1 is Dusk and Chapter 12 is Dawn — one day-night circle for the whole story

content.heading: How to use these chapter lessons
paragraphs: Study one chapter lesson a day. Read the summary, then the three teaching sections, then drill the recall cards at the bottom. Say the names and the numbers out loud — ₦95 million, ₦165,000, forty students, seat 56.

Then attempt the worked example and the guided question in each lesson. Do not look at the answer first. JAMB rewards candidates who can find the line that proves an answer — practise that muscle on every chapter.
When all twelve are done, attempt the full Set A practice questions under timed conditions. You should pass them with room to spare.
bullets: Study one chapter a day, in order, from Dusk to Dawn
Drill the recall cards cold — names, figures, dates, chapter order
Leave timed practice for last, never first
content.takeaway: Learn the circle first, then the chapters, then the clock

check.question: What should you do before looking at a worked-example answer?
options: Skip it — worked examples are for reading only
Attempt it yourself and compare after
Copy the steps into your notebook first
check.why: The habit that scores marks is finding the proving line yourself before the answer is shown

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If you have one free hour, spend it on the chapter map — the ten Section A questions pay that back to you

content.problem: JAMB-style item: “How did Stardom Schools’ lateness problem transform after the boarding fees were cut from ₦250,000 to ₦165,000?”

steps.operation: Find the fact the question asks about
steps.reason: This question wants one exact fact, so go to the Chapter 1 details, not your feelings — when stuck, recall the boarding numbers
steps.result: Boarding fee cut: ₦250,000 → ₦165,000

steps.operation: Anchor it to the consequence in the same breath
steps.reason: The stem asks “how”, so your answer must connect the cut to what it changed — a lone fact can’t carry a “how” question; when stuck, ask what the school gained
steps.result: Over 80% of parents moved their children into boarding; nearly everyone reached assembly by 7:45 a.m.

steps.operation: Pick the option that pairs cause with effect
steps.reason: The trap is true facts from the wrong moment — take the full pair the question wants; when stuck, read the verb “transform” and give it a before and an after
steps.result: The fee cut moved families into boarding and assembly became punctual

content.question: From memory, say what “Dusk” opens the novel with — and why that opening matters for the whole book.
hints: Name the scene, the place and who is at the podium.
Say what Bepo was doing before the breakdown.
Say why a book about a man who never breaks down opens this way.

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB sets the ten novel questions
paragraphs: JAMB sets the ten novel questions in a fixed shape. Roughly two test plot recall — what happens in a chapter. Two test characters — what a person is like or why. Two test themes — decision versus loyalty, home versus money. Two test language and technique — proverbs, irony, symbols. Two test inference and sub-plot — what a scene implies or which side-story carries an idea.

Notice what none of the ten test: your opinion of the book. Every question has one proved answer inside the text. The correct option is always the one the summary can line up with a chapter, a scene or a number.

JAMB also recycles its favourite facts. Expect: the ₦165,000 boarding fee, the ₦95 million cooperative purse, the ₦100,000 Tai passport fee, the $10,000 farewell envelope, seat 56 at the airport, and the anthem. If you know those cold, you have already passed a third of the section.

The trap option is usually true somewhere else in the book. An answer that describes another chapter accurately but not this one is the most dangerous wrong option on the paper. Read the chapter tag inside every question stem carefully.
bullets: JAMB asks about plot, character, theme, language and inference
Every answer is provable inside the text
The traps are true facts pulled from the wrong chapter

content.heading: Go deeper: The whole plot on one staircase
paragraphs: Climb the twelve chapters like a staircase. Dusk: Bepo breaks down at assembly and cannot say why. The Enticement: he admits he plans to leave for the UK. Migration Tales: the diaspora stories — money, dignity, dust. A Case of Visa Denied: the Ignatius family collapses over a DNA result.

Snake in the Roof: the MD finds staff cars behind the school and the cooperative is capped at ₦250,000 per loan. Ade as Well as Jide: Fafore nearly loses his job over one perfect sentence. Ritualists: at Beesway, Bepo discovers the director burying a live cow at 2:30 a.m. Missions Unaccomplished: the prefect election splits the school between Banky and Tosh.

Laughing Waterfalls: the Badagry excursion, and the Point of No Return that changes Bepo forever. Passport Pains: two years lapsed, COVID, and the Ibadan agent Tai. Point of No Return: the three-day farewell — the banner, the cheque, the canoe dance. Dawn: the flight, the dream, and “I didn’t go!”
bullets: Four chapters of quiet pressure, then the farewell year
Two chapter titles echo each other — Passport Pains and Point of No Return
Every chapter pushes the same question: will he stay?

content.heading: Go deeper: How to revise the novel in one evening
paragraphs: Evening one: read this whole set again — the circle map first, then the twelve chapters in order. Dusk to Dawn. Do not skip the chapter you find dull; JAMB does not care which chapter bores you, only which facts you retained.

Evening two: cover the titles and rehearse the sequence aloud: Dusk, the Enticement, Migration Tales, Visa Denied, Snake in the Roof, Ade as Well as Jide, Ritualists, Missions Unaccomplished, Laughing Waterfalls, Passport Pains, Point of No Return, Dawn. If you can say all twelve in order without peeking, the shape of the book is yours.

Evening three: drill the recall cards chapter by chapter. Speak names, figures and places out loud — ₦165,000, ₦95 million, forty students, seat 56. The exam does not forgive numbers guessed silently.

Last: attempt the fifty most recent novel questions you can find, timed. Mark them harshly. Every miss goes to a chapter — reread only that chapter. That loop, repeated, is worth more than any number of whole rereads of the novel.
bullets: Evening one is the circle map, evening two is the sequence aloud
Evening three is the figures, spoken out loud
Then a timed fifty — and every miss loops back to that one chapter

lessons.title: Chapter 1 — Dusk
lessons.objective: Describe how the novel opens — the assembly collapse — name the people in the room, and explain what the breakdown reveals about Bepo.

content.heading: Chapter 1 — Dusk
paragraphs: One assembly morning at Stardom, Bepo delays, freezes at the podium, and breaks down in tears — and nobody can get him to say why. Recall Chapter 1 as the morning the school’s strongest man failed in public.

content.heading: The morning that broke the school open
paragraphs: It is assembly. A pep talk launched seven years earlier has everyone excited. Ikenna Egbu, an SSS science poet, has just returned from Jos and is praising Nigeria over Canada and the UK. His mother is a broadcaster and award-winning poet.

Chapel Prefect Angel passes the microphone. Bepo walks in from the back, slow, smiling little. He takes the mic — and nothing comes. His head drops. His eyes find the floor tiles. He cries in trickles, then in full — and the microphone slips and clatters on the twin speakers.

Vice-Principal Grace Apeh and four staff rush to him. Nurse Titi brings a handkerchief. Apeh orders Justus Anabel, the chemistry teacher, to close the assembly. Oyelana the CRK teacher and Apeh steer him to the office. Guidance counsellor Beke Egbin joins. More teachers gather by 8:05.
bullets: The assembly starts after Ikenna’s Jos excursion speech
Bepo freezes at the podium; the mic clatters
Apeh, nurse Titi and Anabel manage the evacuation
content.takeaway: The novel opens at the exact moment Bepo breaks

check.question: What is Bepo doing when the novel opens?
options: Reading the morning announcements as usual
About to speak at assembly when he freezes and breaks down
Arguing with the MD about the boarding fees
check.why: Chapter 1 drops you straight into the collapse — a normal assembly thrown off course at the podium

content.heading: What inside him broke
paragraphs: Bepo has carried everything for twenty-four years — the sacks he delivers, the results he celebrates, the fees he holds, the faces he wears. This morning, at the moment of maximum attention, the weight cracks open.

The MD, Mrs Ibidun Gloss — “popularly called MD” — drives back from morning business, takes off her glasses, and receives him in the second-floor Admin Building. She asks why. He cannot say. She calls in Oye Wande, the physics teacher and pastor. He still cannot say.

Bepo writes his wife’s international number on a card from his grey suit pocket. Two calls do not ring. The MD sends him home — the school is for learning and earning, not rehabilitation — and thinks about the parents who will press her next.
bullets: Twenty-four years of holding everything in burst out in one collapse
The MD and Oye Wande both fail to get a word from him
Two calls to Seri do not ring; he is sent home
content.takeaway: Bepo cannot name his pain — he can only fall apart

check.question: Why do the MD and Oye Wande fail to get a word from Bepo?
options: He refuses to speak to anyone junior to him
The breakdown is real — he cannot name what is inside him
He is only performing for attention
The card he writes has the wrong number
check.why: It shows a man broken open, not a game — even the MD and a pastor can’t get a word out of him

content.heading: The numbers behind the pressure
paragraphs: Stardom is an elite Lekki school with an obsessive results culture. The previous day it had celebrated above 90% WASSCE success — snacks, wine, ₦20,000 to every SSS 3 teacher, ₦30,000 to distinction-scoring teachers. No candidate scored F9, so nobody was sacked.

Boarding fees were cut from ₦250,000 to ₦165,000 to force punctuality — above 80% of parents moved their children in, and assembly attendance jumped: nearly everyone by 7:45 a.m. The school quietly raised Excursion and Other Items by ₦93,000 to balance the books. Audu called the MD “a witch and a wizard rolled into one.”
bullets: Above 90% passed — SSS 3 teachers got ₦20,000, distinction subjects got ₦30,000
The boarding fee dropped to ₦165,000 and over 80% moved to board
Excursion and Other Items rose ₦93,000 — and everyone was at assembly by 7:45
content.takeaway: Stardom runs on pressure — money, results and reputation

check.question: What happened after the boarding fee was cut to ₦165,000?
options: Fewer pupils paid, and the school nearly closed
Over 80% of parents boarded their children; punctuality jumped
The MD resigned over the shortfall
Audu quit to start a rival school
check.why: The fee cut was an attendance strategy that worked — the school made its money back through the ₦93,000 excursion levy

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If the question mentions assembly or the podium, it’s Chapter 1 — the collapse is all of that chapter’s exam weight

content.problem: JAMB-style item: “How did Stardom Schools’ lateness problem transform after the boarding fees were cut from ₦250,000 to ₦165,000?”

steps.operation: Locate the chapter and the fact asked
steps.reason: This item wants one exact Chapter 1 fact, so go straight to the boarding-fee numbers — when stuck, recall the fee cut and the punctuality jump
steps.result: The fee cut was the lever; punctuality was the result

steps.operation: Name the actual result in the same breath as the cause
steps.reason: The stem asks “how”, so your answer has to tie the cut to what it changed — a lone fact can’t answer a “how” question; when stuck, recall the 7:45 a.m. assembly
steps.result: Over 80% of parents boarded their children; nearly everyone reached assembly by 7:45 a.m.

steps.operation: Choose the option that holds both halves
steps.reason: The wrong options use true numbers from the wrong moment, so take the full pair — the cut and the 7:45 assembly; when stuck, rule out options naming the cut without the assembly
steps.result: The fee cut filled the boarding houses and made the school punctual

content.question: From memory, narrate the assembly collapse in six steps — who speaks, what fails, who rushes in, where he is taken, and what the MD does.
hints: Start with Ikenna and the Just-Jos speech.
Name who takes the mic, and what falls.
Name the office he is carried to, and the driver of the decision.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recall cards — Chapter 1
paragraphs: Adebepo Adewale, “Bepo” — tall, fair, six foot two, strong voice, playful strict teacher; University of Benin, English and History; about twenty-four years at Stardom; four years as Kiddies head, the rest as secondary principal; left-pocket-hand habit; quick to spot cheating; the headmaster everyone nicknamed “The Lekki Headmaster”, after King Oloja of Village Headmaster.

Ikenna Egbu — SSS science poet from a broadcaster family; his mother an award-winning poet; back from the Jos excursion praising Lamingo Dam, the University of Jos, Shere Hills, Wase Rocks and Solomon Lar Amusement Park; declares he would rather settle in Jos than japa to Canada or the UK.

Assembly prayer order — Monday, Wednesday, Friday: Christian/Muslim prayers plus the first anthem stanza; Tuesday and Thursday: the second anthem stanza (“Oh God of creation, direct our noble cause”); then the school anthem. Stardom’s F9 rule: one F9 and the teacher is sacked — even the MD’s cousin Funso Daniels was not spared.

The punctuality gambit — boarding ₦250,000 → ₦165,000; above 80% boarded; assembly attendance jumped; school recouped through Excursion and Other Items, up ₦93,000. Previous evening: above 90% WASSCE, ₦20,000 cash to SSS 3 teachers, ₦30,000 to distinction scorers. Obong Ukaku (Chemistry) and Taye Kareem (Geography) had two-candidate D-lines.
bullets: Bepo is a Benin graduate, 24 years in — Kiddies first, then secondary
Ikenna’s Jos speech opens the book; Bepo breaks after it
An F9 gets a teacher sacked — and the ₦165,000 boarding fee fixed lateness

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 1
paragraphs: JAMB almost never asks “what happened”. It asks “what does the opening reveal”, “what does the mic clatter symbolise”, “why does the breakdown come at the pep talk”. Technique questions live here: the breakdown at the very peak of the seven-year pep talk is deliberate — the school’s biggest celebration is its strongest man’s smallest hour.

Symbol questions: the falling microphone is the fallen voice — the instrument of his authority on the floor. The tiles Bepo stares at, the palm-covering, the office on the second floor — each keeps the reader low, close, and inside a man’s private emergency.

Character questions probe the gap between public role and private person. Bepo fixes everything for everyone; he cannot fix the one thing pressing on him. The MD and Oye Wande cannot pull a sentence from him — so the reader learns the pressure is real, not strategic.

Watch the wrong options: anything that names the farewell, the flight or the passport is Chapter 10–12 material dressed in Chapter 1 clothes. The correct Chapter 1 option always stays inside the assembly scene.
bullets: Notice the trick — the collapse lands at the very peak of the celebration
The fallen mic is the fallen voice
Watch for later-chapter facts offered as Chapter 1 answers

content.heading: Go deeper: The Chapter 1 cast — who is who
paragraphs: Angel — the chapel prefect who passes the microphone at the morning assembly; her calm hands are the last ordinary thing before the collapse.

Ikenna Egbu — SSS science poet, broadcaster’s son; his Jos-excursion praise-song about Lamingo Dam, Shere Hills, Wase Rocks and Solomon Lar Amusement Park is what Bepo hears before the mic lands in his hand.

Vice-Principal Grace Apeh — the school’s steady spine; she alone moves as fast as the crisis needs, sends Anabel to dissolve the assembly, walks Bepo to the office, and keeps the school alive on an ordinary Tuesday.

Mrs Titi — the nurse; a handkerchief; the smallest mercy of the scene. Mr Justus Anabel — chemistry teacher, the man who clears the hall. Mr Oyelana — CRK teacher, first at the office, first to laugh, first to clock that pounds — not naira — is Bepo’s real arithmetic.

Mrs Beke Egbin — guidance counsellor; joins the small group by mid-morning. Mrs Ibidun Gloss, “the MD” — proprietor; her own glasses off, on the tea stool; her one conclusion: the school is for learning, not rehabilitation. Mr Oye Wande — physics teacher and pastor; the man the MD trusts with Bepo’s silence.
bullets: Angel and Ikenna fill the last ordinary minutes before it happens
Apeh, nurse Titi and Anabel run the first response
Gloss and Oye Wande get nothing out of him

lessons.title: Chapter 2 — The Enticement
lessons.objective: State the case for japa in Bepo’s numbers — salary, entitlement and remittance — and explain what still holds him at Stardom.

content.heading: Chapter 2 — The Enticement
paragraphs: After five days of quiet interrogation, Bepo admits it: he plans to leave for the United Kingdom. Recall Chapter 2 as the chapter that opens the japa file — every number on the table.

content.heading: The five days that cracked him open
paragraphs: The MD calls Bepo in again and again. For about five days it feels like interrogation. At last he says it: he plans to emigrate to the UK. His marriage was at the brink because he dragged his feet — Seri is in London with Nike and Kike, and the teaching post there is secured.
He loves Stardom and his learners. He feels it is wrong to abandon a developing nation for an already-developed one. But family pressure is stronger — and the pounds are persuasive.
bullets: Five days of interrogation lead him to the truth
Seri and the children are already in London; the post is secured
Duty says stay; love and money say go
content.takeaway: The UK offer is secured before the chapter begins

check.question: What does Bepo finally admit after five days?
options: He plans to resign and start a school in Ifo
He plans to leave Nigeria for the United Kingdom
He plans to divorce and stay in Lagos
He plans to extend his contract by ten years
check.why: The Enticement is exactly this: the MD’s quiet interrogation ends in the confession — the UK post is secured

content.heading: The arithmetic that haunts him
paragraphs: Stardom pays Bepo about ₦400,000 a month. The UK post promises about £3,600 a month in entitlements. At about ₦1,700 to the pound, that reads as about ₦6 million — fifteen times his present salary.

Oyelana the CRK teacher notes the flaw: Bepo will spend in pounds, not naira, so the naira comparison deceives. Audu brushes that aside — if Bepo sends £1,000 home each month, that is above ₦1.7 million, more than nobody earning ₦400,000 can match. Then he mocks Bepo as “bewitched”, shoves books under his armpit and announces he is “heading to the airport” — and is late for class, as usual. His jokes save him.
bullets: It’s ₦400,000 here against about £3,600 — near ₦6 million — there
Oyelana says pounds are spent in pounds, not sent home
Audu says £1,000 sent home every month beats any naira salary
content.takeaway: Follow the money: fifteen times the salary, one remittance

check.question: What is Mr Oyelana’s objection to the japa arithmetic?
options: The pound will crash within a year
Bepo will spend in pounds, so the naira comparison is false
Teachers are not paid in the UK
The exchange rate is illegally fixed
check.why: Oyelana argues that money goes around in pounds in London — not as naira sent home

content.heading: The dream he had before London
paragraphs: Bepo had been planning to retire at fifty-five — four years away. He attended entrepreneurship seminars, picturing a school of his own after Stardom, or failing that, transport leasing, a small farm, food ventures, sachet pure water. The masala of experience plus endless ambition.

His own cautionary tale was always in his mouth: Fruitful Future School, the small neighbourhood school he and a colleague started just after National Youth Service. It collapsed — socio-economic challenges in the location defeated it. Seri would never finance any project that tied him to Nigeria.
bullets: Retirement at 55 was the plan — four years away
He dreamed of entrepreneurship — his own school, leasing, sachet water
Fruitful Future died young, and Seri won’t fund any Nigeria-linked dream
content.takeaway: His old dream of a school of his own died at Fruitful Future

check.question: What became of Fruitful Future School?
options: It thrived and was sold to Stardom Group
It collapsed — the location could not sustain it
It is now his holiday home in Ifo
It merged with Beesway Group of Schools
check.why: The novel’s favourite cautionary tale is this — the young Bepo’s school failed on socio-economic ground

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If your options argue salary against pounds, bring both — ₦400,000 here versus about ₦6 million there — that’s the chapter’s one decision

content.problem: JAMB-style item: “What argument does Mr Audu use to persuade Bepo over his wife’s salary objection?”

steps.operation: Find the exact speech attributed to Audu
steps.reason: The stem wants Audu’s own line, so find his exact words — several adults weigh in and JAMB tests who said what; when stuck, recall the “bewitched” scene
steps.result: Audu: if Bepo sends £1,000 home a month, that is above ₦1.7 million

steps.operation: Match the figure to the direction of the money
steps.reason: The persuasion turns on money sent home, not on entitlement — Oyelana argues the opposite direction, so tell which way the money travels; when stuck, ask whether the money leaves or enters Nigeria
steps.result: A monthly £1,000 remittance beats any naira salary at home

steps.reason: Oyelana is the cautious voice and Audu is the persuader — the stem asks you to be persuaded, so give Audu’s position; when stuck, reread the stem for the word “persuade”
steps.result: Audu’s remittance argument — not Oyelana’s pounds-are-spent-in-pounds caution

content.question: From memory, reconstruct the japa case from both sides: Bepo’s pull to London, and what still pins him to Stardom.
hints: Name the secured post, the £3,600 and the ≈₦6 million reading.
Name Seri, Nike and Kike — where they are, what Kike is doing.
Name the cost he keeps naming: leaving a developing nation.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recall cards — Chapter 2
paragraphs: Bepo’s Nigerian life — Stardom salary about ₦400,000 a month; planning to retire at fifty-five, four years away; entrepreneurship seminars attended; dreams: his own school, transport leasing, a farm, food ventures, sachet pure water.

The London offer — UK post secured; about £3,600 a month in entitlements; at about ₦1,700 to the pound, ≈₦6 million; separation from Seri already the norm; Seri in London as a nurse; Nike at university; Kike still at secondary school; the marriage nearly broke over his feet-dragging.

The cautionary past — Tyana Ipaja, Iyana Ipaja, Lagos: a crowded face-me-I-face-you house in Agbeni-style; at the height of unemployment Bepo “ate” ₦2,500 collected as tenants’ electricity tariff; NEPA cut the cable; Iya Mathew, wife of co-tenant Mr Adio, dumped a bowl of elubo over his head singing “Oga Tisa, ole! O na owo ina!” — Mr Teacher, thief!

The Fruitful Future School — started with a colleague just after National Youth Service; grew enrolment but later crumbled from socio-economic challenges in the location; Bepo’s standard warning to anyone who dreams of a quick school venture in a poor neighbourhood.
bullets: ₦400,000 here; ≈₦6 million there; Seri is in London
The ₦2,500 tariff at Tyana Ipaja that he “ate” — and the elubo
Fruitful Future died of its own location

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 2
paragraphs: Chapter 2 questions split cleanly into money items and shame items. Money items: the ₦400,000 salary, the £3,600 entitlement, the ₦1,700-per-pound conversion, the £1,000-home remittance comparison. JAMB expects exact figures, not impressions — write them with the naira and pound signs, not words.

Shame items: “Oga Tisa”, the elubo bowl, Iya Mathew, NEPA, the tariff. The novel’s deepest shame is also its most quoted. The exam-safe framing: not “Bepo is a thief” but “Bepo stole from tenants in desperation and the community marked him for life.”
The Oyelana–Audu swap distractor: options that mix up Oyelana (pound-caution) and Audu (remittance-persuasion). Fix it by asking of every option — who said this, and which way does the money flow?
Character trap: options claiming Seri emigrated with Bepo, or that he was pushed against his will. The text keeps him torn, choosing with his eyes open. The correct option preserves the ambivalence.
bullets: Money items want exact figures, never impressions
Keep the speakers apart and you never swap Oyelana for Audu
He’s torn on purpose — he chooses with his eyes open

content.heading: Go deeper: The money ladder — conversion in one line
paragraphs: Write the ladder once and never guess again. Step 1: Stardom pays ₦400,000 a month. Step 2: the UK post promises about £3,600 a month in entitlements. Step 3: at about ₦1,700 to the pound, £3,600 × ₦1,700 ≈ ₦6.1 million — fifteen times his Nigerian salary.

Step 4 is Audu’s twist: even a modest remittance changes everything. If Bepo sends £1,000 home a month, that is about ₦1.7 million transferred to Nigeria by post — above ₦400,000 in one sweep, for one month of one salary, earned alone in London.

Oyelana’s caution — pounds are spent in pounds, not remitted home — does not destroy the arithmetic; it only means the two salaries cannot be compared as if they were the same currency. JAMB loves this ambiguity and writes options that blur the distinction.

The ladder’s real use is exam-ready discipline: whenever a question hands you a figure, ask what step of the ladder it sits on, and react accordingly — detail if it is a step number, inference if it is a comparison between steps.
bullets: ₦400,000 versus £3,600 — about ₦6.1 million, fifteen times the salary
£1,000 home every month is about ₦1.7 million
Oyelana says spend-in-pounds is not send-home — keep the two apart

lessons.title: Chapter 3 — Migration Tales
lessons.objective: Narrate the diaspora stories Bepo collects — the pragmatic wage, Sola’s Manchester life, Jare, Hope, Riike and Akindele — and state what the japa case actually weighs.

content.heading: Chapter 3 — Migration Tales
paragraphs: Once Bepo is leaning toward London, he floods himself with stories from the diaspora — money, work, dignity, dust. Recall Chapter 3 as the chapter where every argument for japa is spoken and every crack in it shows.

content.heading: The money stories
paragraphs: A friend in the US tells him one can earn between $150 and $250 a day, up to four days a week — about $2,400 a month. The Yoruba proverb at issue: “oga ta, oga o ta, owo alaaru a pe” — whether the boss gains or loses, the worker takes home full pay. That is the pragmatic wage system, one of the ideals powering developed countries.

Nobody mentions the down-side. Rent, taxes and maintenance are paid in hard currencies; what remains still transfers. A Nigerian who switched from driving to a maintenance job earning $500 a day works out to about ₦800,000 daily. Even toilet-cleaners are out-earned by cabbies abroad.
bullets: He earns $150–$250 a day, up to four days a week — about $2,400 a month
The wage pays you whether the boss gains or not
A $500 maintenance job is about ₦800,000 a day — even for humble work
content.takeaway: Abroad, even ordinary work is paid in hard currency

check.question: What does the “pragmatic wage” system mean?
options: Workers take home fixed full pay regardless of the boss’s profit or loss
Workers are paid only when the employer declares profit
Workers negotiate pay per task each morning
Employers may cut pay whenever debts rise
check.why: “Oga ta, oga o ta, owo alaaru a pe” — the worker’s pay is fixed no matter what the owner sells or loses

content.heading: The system stories
paragraphs: The government admits about 3,000 doctors emigrate yearly, plus many Master’s seekers. Study visas cover holder, spouse and children — whole families sell everything. Stardom’s own registers the casualties: Mr Nku took a ₦2 million cooperative loan and vanished in two days; a driver tried a school bus theft.

Sola — nearly sacked over a crèche, saved to three months’ suspension — phones from Manchester. They sold everything and still borrowed about ₦4 million. She earns up to £200 a day; they rent an unfurnished two-room flat at £650 a month, paid month by month; the rail to London runs thirty minutes. A seizure got two ambulances and a car in under five minutes — a birthday in hospital.
bullets: 3,000 doctors leave every year, and study visas carry the whole family
Mr Nku vanished in two days with a ₦2 million cooperative loan
Sola lives in Manchester on £200 a day, £650 a month, paid month by month, and the rail to London takes 30 minutes
content.takeaway: The State itself admits the system loses it doctors and nurses

check.question: What did Sola and her husband need to sell to emigrate?
options: Only their car and their fridge
Everything they owned, plus about ₦4 million more in loans
Just the crèche business at Stardom
Nothing — the visa covered all costs
check.why: They sold all their assets and still borrowed about ₦4 million — the true weight of the japa ticket

content.heading: The dignity stories
paragraphs: Jare, a young banker, wept to find caring for an old couple in London docked his dignity — the pound could not restore it. Hope, an accountant, had his UK Master’s wife-financed until she stopped after four months — “the demands of her job are too heavy,” she said; her parents in Nigeria agreed.

Riike, in the US under three years, bought two Ibadan houses, brought two sisters over, and hopes for her youngest brother Wemimo once the visa clears. Akindele migrated at fifty-five after an eighteen-year marriage ended; his first jobs were freight loading and then correctional service. “There is no easy job in America” — even seventy-year-old permanent secretaries end up moving mail.
bullets: Jare wept — lawful care work far from home still cost him his dignity
Hope’s wife stopped paying for his Master’s after four months
Riike bought two Ibadan houses in three years; Akindele learnt there’s no easy work at 55
content.takeaway: The japa stories are not a loose bunch — each of them has a dignity price

check.question: Why did Jare weep?
options: Caring for an old couple in London docked his dignity
He was deported for an expired visa
The old couple underpaid him for six months
check.why: He left a banking job and found that lawful work in London still stripped his dignity — the point of the story

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If your options pair a name with the wrong detail, strike it out — Riike is Ibadan houses, Sola is Manchester, Akindele is freight at 55, Jare is the old couple

content.problem: JAMB-style item: “Which example best illustrates that age grants no exemption from manual labour abroad?”

steps.operation: Scan the chapter for a migrant whose age is named
steps.reason: The stem says age gets you no exemption, so pick the older migrant, not the young banker — list everyone’s ages in your head; when stuck, recall Akindele’s job in the freight dock
steps.result: Akindele — migrated to the US at fifty-five

steps.operation: Check what work he ended up doing
steps.reason: The claim is manual labour, so check the job itself, not just the pay — a task shows it, not a feeling; when stuck, recall the freight and correctional-service jobs
steps.result: His first jobs were freight loading, then correctional service

steps.operation: Rule out younger migrants with softer jobs
steps.reason: Jare and Hope fit dignity but not the age rule — every adjective in a JAMB stem is a filter; when stuck, reread “age grants no exemption” — only a man with a stated age fits
steps.result: Akindele — the fifty-five-year-old in manual labour

content.question: From memory, reconstruct Sola’s call with Bepo — Manchester rent, the rail to London, the children’s schooling, and the five-minute ambulance story.
hints: Give the monthly rent, the furniture status, and the month-by-month arrangement.
Give the London rail time and the fee-free schooling detail.
Give the three-year-old’s seizure and what happened in under five minutes.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recall cards — Chapter 3
paragraphs: Pragmatic wage — “oga ta, oga o ta, owo alaaru a pe”: boss sells or boss doesn’t, the worker’s pay is full and fixed; presented as an ideal of developed countries; paired with hard-currency maintenance costs that still leave good remittances.

Sola — former Home Economics teacher at Stardom; opened a crèche near the school; investigated and saved from sack to a three-month no-pay suspension, then monitored; emigrated six months before the call; mentor of Bepo’s japa thinking; husband currently on a Master’s supported by her earnings; sells everything, borrows ≈₦4 million; £200/day; Manchester unfurnished two-room £650/month, month-by-month, rail to London ≈30 minutes; NHS seizure response: two ambulances + car in under five minutes.

Other migrants — Jare (banker → carer, dignity docked); Hope (wife stopped funding his UK Master’s after four months); Riike (two Ibadan houses in under three years; fee-free children till 2027; brought two sisters; Wemimo still pending); Akindele (migrated at 55; eighteen-year marriage, three children aged 16–10; freight then correctional service; “no easy job in America”; seventy-year-old permanent secretaries do mail work).

Stardom gossip — Mr Nku, ₦2 million cooperative loan, vanished in two days; a school driver tried to steal a school bus to fund his son’s college abroad and confessed to police; the government admits ≈3,000 doctors emigrate yearly; study visas carry holder + spouse + children.
bullets: The wage works without the boss’s gain — about $2,400 a month, and some earn ₦800,000 a day
Sola is in Manchester on £200 a day, ₦4 million in debt, with that five-minute NHS ambulance story
Mr Nku and the bus driver are japa’s local casualties

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 3
paragraphs: Chapter 3 is where JAMB gets fact densest. Practise the figures until they are reflexes: $150–$250 a day, $2,400 a month, $500 a day ≈ ₦800,000, £200 a day, £650 rent, ₦4 million borrowed, 3,000 doctors a year, ₦2 million Nku loan. If you can chant them, half the chapter’s questions are already answered.

Character-swap traps: Riike’s Ibadan houses are not Sola’s Manchester flat; Akindele’s correctional-service job is not Hope’s wife-financed Master’s. The correct option always pairs the right person with the right detail — on both counts.

The exam favours purpose questions over fact questions here: “why does the novel include Sola’s five-minute ambulance story?” — because it shows, through one child’s birthday in hospital, what the Nigerian system cannot yet guarantee. Technique: miniature portrait over argument.

One more trap: “pragmatic wage” is not “minimum wage”. Minimum wage is a floor; pragmatic wage is the wage that does not move with the boss’s profit or loss. They are neighbours, not twins — and JAMB writes options that blur them.
bullets: This chapter is dense with facts, so chant the numbers
Know who is Riike, who is Hope, who is Akindele, and you never mix them up
The wage is full and fixed; the minimum is just the floor — different things
