content.heading: Go deeper: Who said what — Chapter 3’s cast
paragraphs: Assign every tale a mouth, and Chapter 3 stops being a blur. The unnamed US friend — the $150–$250-a-day line; the $2,400 monthly cap; the proverb “oga ta, oga o ta”. Sola — the Manchester £200-a-day, £650 unfurnished flat, month-by-month, thirty-minute rail; the five-minute ambulance story; her own near-sack over the crèche.

Jare — “I left a banking job and wept to find caring for an old couple docked my dignity.” Hope — the accountant whose UK Master’s his wife financed, then abandoned after four months. Riike — three years, two Ibadan houses, two sisters over, Wemimo pending.

Akindele — fifty-five; at the Lagos media company he was invited to the US after an eighteen-year marriage ended; three children aged 16–10; freight loading, then correctional service; “no easy job in America”; even seventy-year-old permanent secretaries move mail.

And the cautionary Stardom gossip — Mr Nku vanished with a ₦2 million cooperative loan in two days; the school driver stole a school bus. Every mouth in the chapter teaches one lesson; misassign them and the theme questions fail.
bullets: The wage is the US friend’s line; Manchester is Sola’s life
Riike built Ibadan houses; Akindele broke his back at 55
Mr Nku and the bus driver are japa’s cautionary local stories

lessons.title: Chapter 4 — A Case of Visa Denied
lessons.objective: Narrate the Ignatius visa denial — the oil-firm husband, the DNA result, Lyi’s suspicion — and the parallel Ladele/Ayesoro thread, and say what both episodes show about plans at home.

content.heading: Chapter 4 — A Case of Visa Denied
paragraphs: One 11:55 p.m. phone call collapses a Lagos marriage — an embassy says no to the London dream, and the DNA result behind it splits a family. Recall Chapter 4 as the night the visa died.

content.heading: The 11:55 p.m. phone call
paragraphs: Mrs Ignatius phones Bepo at his room in Adeniyi Jones, Ikeja, sobbing that her son Ibe is not home. Ibe, an oil-firm manager, had bought into japa — sick of the system, vowing no child would be left behind. The maths drew them: $1,000 remittance a month at ₦1,600 black-market rate ≈ ₦1.6 million.

Mrs Ignatius had prepared her own trade — tailoring, hairdressing, irun didi (bridal art), and Yoruba braids such as suku, kojusoko and onilegogoro, promised at $100 per head in the UK, about ₦160,000. Ibe had wound down his clearing-and-forwarding side business in preparation.
bullets: Mrs Ignatius rings Bepo at 11:55 p.m. — her son Ibe is not home
Her husband is an oil-firm manager bent on London — $1,000 a month, about ₦1.6 million
Her trade is bridal art and Yoruba braids — about ₦160,000 a head
content.takeaway: The call sounds like a missing-son case — it is really a visa case

check.question: Why had the Ignatius family been preparing to relocate to London?
options: Ibe secured a transfer within the same company
Together they calculated a $1,000 monthly remittance case
They had already bought a house in Manchester
Mrs Ignatius won a visa lottery
check.why: The $1,000 a month at the black-market rate came to about ₦1.6 million — that number was the whole plan

content.heading: The DNA that broke the family
paragraphs: At the advanced visa stage, a DNA test showed Ibe is not the father of their eldest daughter, Favour — fifteen, an SS2 girl at Stardom. The visa was refused. The family never survived the fallout.

Ibe refuses to believe it. “Favour and I have to go,” he says. Favour does not know the saga. Her brother Lyi suspects why the visas were refused — visa rules require paternity evidence for applicants below eighteen. Ibe left home two hours before Bepo finished the call. Bepo thinks immediately of a memo on school events as a possible book — a recurring motif.
bullets: The DNA says Favour, the 15-year-old SS2 girl, is not Ibe’s daughter — and the visa is refused
Lyi suspects the real reason — the below-18 paternity evidence rule
Favour never learns what happened, and Ibe walks out mid-call
content.takeaway: One DNA result killed the whole relocation

check.question: Why was the visa refused?
options: Expired passports and unpaid school fees
A DNA result showing Favour is not Ibe’s daughter
Mrs Ignatius failed the English test
The embassy flagged the oil company for fraud
check.why: The paternity test at the advanced stage is what killed the visa — everything else followed

content.heading: The other thread — Ayesoro and Bibi
paragraphs: A parallel thread runs inside the same chapter. Mrs Mary Ladele watches a Nollywood film at one in the afternoon, children asleep, in GRA — her husband Dele is a senior civil servant in Abuja with a ten p.m. bed rule.

She is terrified of Mr Ayesoro, a government teacher with deep tribal marks, whom pupils nickname Mr Wala or Mr Owata. Three-month-old Bibi sees him at a Saturday basketball court visit and screams for months in nightmares. Bibi’s relations force a move to Green House. Stardom, anxious to keep the family, transfers Ayesoro to Stardom Hub, the property arm of the Stardom Group.
bullets: Mary Ladele watches one-o’clock Nollywood at home in GRA — and her husband Dele is in Abuja
Bibi is three months old, and after seeing Ayesoro’s marks she lives in nightmares
The family moves to Green House, and Stardom moves Ayesoro to Hub, its property arm
content.takeaway: Two families, two terrors — the embassy and the playground

check.question: What force moved Bibi Ladele to Green House?
options: Her nightmares about Ayesoro after the basketball court visit
Ayesoro lodged a complaint against her parents
A transfer of her father to Abuja
check.why: A three-month-old’s screaming nightmares — begun in a Stardom-linked setting — forced the family out of the school

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If the stem says visa or DNA, stay with the Ignatius thread — Favour, Lyi, the below-18 rule; if it says Green House, stay with the Ladele thread — Ayesoro and Bibi

content.problem: JAMB-style item: “What is the reason the embassy denied Mr Ibe’s family’s London visa?”

steps.operation: Locate the visa episode in the chapter
steps.reason: Both threads are Chapter 4, but the visa belongs to the Ignatius side — don’t cross them; when stuck, recall 11:55 p.m. — the missing son and the tears
steps.result: The visa stage fails at the advanced DNA step

steps.operation: Name the document and the person it fails
steps.reason: The question wants the specific reason, not the fallout — the document is the DNA test; when stuck, recall Favour, SS2, fifteen years old
steps.result: The DNA test showed Ibe is not Favour’s father

steps.operation: State the consequence in one clause
steps.reason: JAMB wants a full answer, not a fragment — both DNA and refusal together; when stuck, recall that the embassy said “refused”
steps.result: The visa was refused; the family never survived the fallout

content.question: From memory, reconstruct Lyi’s reasoning — why he suspects the visa refusal turned on the below-18 paternity-evidence rule.
hints: Name Favour’s age and class at Stardom.
Name the rule Lyi knows: paternity evidence for applicants below eighteen.
Name the fact he cannot unknow: the DNA result.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recall cards — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Mrs Ignatius — parent at Stardom; oil-firm-manager husband, Ibe; the room in Adeniyi Jones, Ikeja; the call at 11:55 p.m.; the japa case ($1,000/month × ₦1,600 ≈ ₦1.6 million); her own trade: tailoring, hairdressing, irun didi (bridal art), and Yoruba braids — suku, kojusoko, onilegogoro — at $100 per head ≈ ₦160,000; the husband winding down his clearing-and-forwarding side business.

Favour — fifteen, SS2 at Stardom, eldest daughter; DNA shows Ibe is not her father; visa refused at the advanced stage; Favour does not know the saga; Lyi — the perceptive brother — suspects the below-18 paternity-evidence rule; Ibe “Favour and I have to go”; he leaves home two hours before the call ends; Bepo, listening, thinks of a memo on school events as a possible book — a recurring motif.

Mary Ladele — watching Nollywood romances at 1 p.m., children asleep, in GRA; her husband Dele is a senior civil servant in Abuja; a ten p.m. bed rule; the terror: Mr Ayesoro, government teacher, deep tribal marks, nicknamed by pupils Mr Wala or Mr Owata.

Bibi’s ordeal — meets Ayesoro at a Saturday basketball court visit; three months old; screams and nightmares recur; her relations force a move to Green House; Stardom, anxious about losing the Ladele children to a rival school, transfers Ayesoro to Stardom Hub, the property arm of Stardom Group of Companies.
bullets: The Ignatius thread — 11:55 p.m., the oil manager, the DNA, the refusal
Lyi reads the below-18 paternity rule from the sidelines
Bibi’s nightmares move her — Ayesoro ends up at Hub

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 4
paragraphs: JAMB’s favourite Chapter 4 question is one sentence long: “What is the reason the embassy denied the family’s visa?” The correct option always contains both halves — DNA and refusal. Options that name only the passport, the oil company or the braiding trade are all false friends.

Lyi is the examiner’s quiet favourite. Questions from him test reading between lines: a child who never saw the DNA result still reasons from the below-18 paternity-evidence rule and from his sister’s silence. The correct option always pairs the rule with the fact he cannot unknow.

The Ayesoro thread is JAMB’s second favourite. Watch for options that move Ayesoro to Stardom Primary, dismiss him, or keep him in the classroom — all wrong. Stardom Hub, the property arm, is the only destination the text gives — and transferring a frightening teacher out of teaching entirely is the quietly damning detail.

One motif question could surface: the “memo” Bepo keeps imagining. It signals the novel’s self-awareness — books about schools contemplating themselves. If JAMB asks what the memo foreshadows, the answer is Bepo’s own story, not a school rulebook.
bullets: Always DNA and refusal together — never just one
Ayesoro lands at Stardom Hub — the property arm, not a sack
Bepo’s memo idea is the book imagining itself

content.heading: Go deeper: The two threads — side by side
paragraphs: Thread one, the Ignatius marriage: a late-night call, an oil-firm husband, a London dream, $1,000 a month at black-market rates, a braiding trade — suku, kojusoko, onilegogoro — worth $100 (≈₦160,000) per head, a DNA result that strips Favour’s paternity, a visa refused, an ex-husband who walks out shouting “Favour and I have to go,” and a school principal quietly remembering every such call ever made.

Thread two, the Ladele panic: a Nollywood film at one in the afternoon; an Abuja husband with a ten p.m. bed rule; a frightened government teacher with tribal marks nicknamed Mr Wala or Mr Owata; a three-month-old’s nightmares after one Saturday basketball visit; a family that simply moves to Green House — and a school that quietly diverts the teacher to its property wing, Stardom Hub.

Both threads teach the same lesson from opposite directions: the dream dies not only at embassies but in nursery fears, and institutions — schools included — will always save their reputation before their teachers. JAMB scrambles these two threads; hold them in separate columns.

The motif that links them is Bepo’s notebook. He keeps thinking of writing “a memo on school events” — the novel imagining itself as a book about a school, anthologising every crisis, hers and his own.
bullets: The Ignatius story — call, plan, DNA, refusal
The Ladele story — Nollywood, Ayesoro, nightmares, Stardom Hub
Bepo’s meme-memo idea is the book imagining itself

lessons.title: Chapter 5 — Snake in the Roof
lessons.objective: Describe the parked-cars inspection, the cooperative’s true position, and the family board’s verdict — and explain the MD’s hidden illness.

content.heading: Chapter 5 — Snake in the Roof
paragraphs: The MD walks to the back gate on impulse, sees half the land packed with staff cars — and suspects embezzlement. Recall Chapter 5 as the day the cooperative’s quiet books went public.

content.heading: The cars behind the school
paragraphs: Lunch at Stardom — about 1,500 students and staff. Mrs Ibidun Gloss privately suffers chronic sitting pain tied to her back — soothed in a private room in her office, ten minutes at a time, unknown to most. Doctors from here and abroad, even spiritual and traditional treatments, have all failed.

One afternoon she walks to the land behind the school on impulse — bought two years earlier, five minutes from the back gate. Jombo at the gate tells her the cars belong to staff. Half of three plots are packed — Toyota (the “Muscle” included), Hyundai, Venza, Mazda; two buses far back, one white, one Lagos-yellow — she summons the principal and the accountant, Jeremi Amos.
bullets: The MD’s illness is sitting pain — and neither doctors nor tradition can fix it
She inspects the land on impulse, and Jombo names the cars staff cars
Half the plots are packed — Toyota, Hyundai, Venza, Mazda, and two buses
content.takeaway: Her eyes became the audit — and her fear was embezzlement

check.question: What did the MD see at the back gate, and what did she suspect?
options: A new sports stadium; she suspected overspending
Half the plots packed with staff cars; she suspected embezzlement
The Governor’s convoy; she suspected protocol breaches
Nothing — she was inspecting new buildings
check.why: Half of the three plots were packed with staff vehicles — so she smells theft

content.heading: ₦95 million and not a kobo missing
paragraphs: On arrival, Jeremi Amos begins his soft soothing talk. The MD cuts in: “Accountant, I didn’t call you for a motivational speech.” He explains the real position.

Most of the cars are funded through the school cooperative. The cooperative’s purse holds about ₦95 million, of which over ₦50 million had already been loaned out. Deductions are taken straight from source — from salary — so repayment is automatic. Nobody is stealing. The visible wealth is a cooperative’s honest work, parked in the open.
bullets: She tells him straight — “I didn’t call you for a motivational speech”
The cooperative holds about ₦95 million, and over ₦50 million is out on loan
They take the money straight from source pay
content.takeaway: The audit closed in one meeting — the purse was clean

check.question: How did the cooperative fund the staff cars?
options: Each teacher paid cash up front
The ₦95m purse, with ₦50m+ already loaned, repaid at source
The bank gave Stardom a corporate loan
Parents funded the fleet as a goodwill gift
check.why: The accountant’s whole case rests on the ₦95 million purse and salary-source deductions

content.heading: The snake in the roof
paragraphs: Her mother — Chief Mrs Solape Bayo — chairs a family board that includes Martins Bayo (non-executive director) and Oye Bayo (last-born, the board secretary). They convene after the inspection.

Their verdict: no staff member may borrow more than ₦250,000; every loan requires the MD’s sign-off; the management must be duly informed of cooperative elections. Her remark: “It’s like hanging a snake in the roof and going to bed.” The cooperative without oversight is the snake — a hidden danger resting above everyone’s heads.
bullets: The family board meets — Solape Bayo chairs, with Martins and Oye Bayo
No loans above ₦250,000, every loan needs the MD’s sign-off, and the board must hear of cooperative elections
“Snake in the roof” is danger sleeping above everyone they never see
content.takeaway: The snake is money with no oversight hanging over everyone’s head

check.question: What did the family board impose on the cooperative?
options: A ₦250,000 loan cap, MD sign-off, and election reporting
A ban on all staff owning cars
A yearly audit by an external firm
check.why: The ₦250,000 cap, the MD’s sign-off and the election reporting are the three things that take the snake off the roof

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If the stem walks from cars to the cap, it is the cooperative chain — Jombo at the gate, Jeremi Amos’s ₦95 million purse, Solape Bayo’s ₦250,000 rule

content.problem: JAMB-style item: “What was the official answer to how teachers afforded those cars?”

steps.operation: Name what the MD suspected before the audit
steps.reason: The question asks how the mystery was solved, so build from the suspicion — the answer overturns it; when stuck, recall she “suspected embezzlement”
steps.result: Suspicion: the school’s money had leaked into staff cars

steps.reason: The official answer lives in Jeremi Amos’s figures — the purse and the loans — vague answers never score; when stuck, recall ₦95 million and ₦50 million
steps.result: ₦95m purse; over ₦50m loaned out; repaid from salary at source

steps.operation: Close with the conclusion the accountant gave the MD
steps.reason: JAMB’s answer key rewards the whole arc — suspicion, evidence, verdict — the verdict is the mark; when stuck, recall nobody was stealing
steps.result: The cars were honest cooperative purchases — no embezzlement

content.question: From memory, reconstruct the family board’s verdict in three clauses — who convenes it, what it imposes, and the remark that names the danger.
hints: Name the chair and the two other members.
Give the ₦250,000 cap and the MD sign-off rule.
Quote — approximately — the “snake in the roof” remark.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recall cards — Chapter 5
paragraphs: The MD’s hidden illness — chronic sitting pain tied to a back condition; rested about ten minutes several times daily in a private room inside her spacious office; doctors within and outside the country failed; spiritual and traditional treatments also failed; unknown to most of the community.

The back-gate land — acquired two years earlier; about five minutes from the back gate; an impulse inspection one afternoon; Jombo the guard; about half of the three plots packed with staff vehicles — Toyotas (“Muscle” included), Hyundai, Venza, Mazda; two buses far at the back, one white, one Lagos-yellow; embezzlement suspicion; summons to principal and accountant Jeremi Amos.

The cooperative — Stardom Staff Cooperative Society; self-managed; the ₦95 million purse; over ₦50 million loaned; deductions straight from salary source; the MD interrupted the accountant’s soothing: “Accountant, I didn’t call you for a motivational speech.” Verdict: no theft; honest cooperative work in the open.

The family board — Chief Mrs Solape Bayo (the MD’s mother) chairs; Martins Bayo (non-executive director); Oye Bayo (last-born, board secretary); verdict: ₦250,000 loan cap per member; every loan needs the MD’s sign-off; the management must be duly informed of cooperative elections; the remark: “It’s like hanging a snake in the roof and going to bed.”
bullets: Her pain sits in her back — ten minutes in a private room several times a day
The ₦95 million purse is intact — ₦50 million out, repayments from source
The cap is ₦250,000, the MD signs everything, and elections must be reported — the snake sleeps no more

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 5
paragraphs: Chapter 5 rewards sequence. JAMB asks “what did the MD discover, what did she suspect, who explained, what was the verdict, what was imposed.” Answer in that order and the marks follow. Options that skip the suspicion stage and jump to “the MD praised the staff” are false — she never did; she was furious, then relieved, then legislative.

Figures carry this chapter — ₦95 million, ₦50 million, ₦250,000. If you write “₦95 million lent out” or “₦50 million cap”, you lose both marks. Money figures in this chapter are never interchangeable.

Symbol question alert: “snake in the roof”. The correct option always keeps two parts — hidden danger, and resting above everyone. Options that make the snake the MD’s greed, the buses, or embezzlement all fail the second half of the image.

Character question alert: the MD’s private illness is the mother’s decision engine. The family board does not convene because cars appeared; it convenes because her body is failing and the cooperative is uncontrolled — both are the roof she sleeps under.
bullets: The sequence is find, suspect, explain, verdict, impose
The ₦95 million purse, the ₦50 million loaned, the ₦250,000 cap — never swap them
The snake is a hidden danger above everyone — both halves, always

content.heading: Go deeper: How the cooperative actually works
paragraphs: Follow the money in slow steps, because JAMB will ask them in random order. Step 1: a staff member wants a car; Step 2: the cooperative — Stardom’s own fund, self-managed, no juju-boss, no outside intervention — lends from its purse; Step 3: the purse held about ₦95 million, of which over ₦50 million had already gone out as loans; Step 4: repayment is automatic — deductions straight from salary, at source, every month.

Step 5 is why the cars were honest: nobody stole because nobody could — the money returns before it can wander. Step 6 is why the family board then piled on new controls anyway: the cooperative ran without the school’s elected oversight; a sign-off misplaced anywhere is a snake living in the roof.

The three controls: no staff member borrows more than ₦250,000; every loan needs the MD’s sign-off; the management must be duly informed of cooperative elections. That is belt, braces and a locked door — the family trusts no single control after meeting the ₦95 million open question.
Notice what the board does not do: it does not audit the cars, does not summon witnesses, does not demand repayment. It restructures the future — the surest sign that the school believes itself.
bullets: Follow the money — ₦95 million in, ₦50 million out, straight-from-salary repayments
Nobody could steal — that’s the whole trick of it
The cap is ₦250,000, the MD signs, and elections are reported

lessons.title: Chapter 6 — “Ade as Well as Jide Comes”
lessons.objective: Explain why Fafore’s sentence was grammatically correct, who nearly paid for it, and how Audu defused the room — and why Stardom stopped copying notes.

content.heading: Chapter 6 — “Ade as Well as Jide Comes”
paragraphs: At Open Day, a parent finds a “mistake” in an English teacher’s notebook — and nearly costs the hardest-working man in the school his job for a sentence that is perfectly right. Recall Chapter 6 as the day grammar saved a teacher.

content.heading: Open Day and the Guta bomb
paragraphs: Open Day is one of the biggest deals at Stardom — parents attend; staff must be at their best; the best-dressed teacher is identified and prized at session’s end. Parents bring gifts: the Gbayi family sends packets of beverages — Mrs Nike Gbayi’s husband works for a leading beverage company. Parents also come loaded with complaints.

Into this walks Mr Guta — father of Dorah (SS2) and Nicholas (JSS2). He spots what seems an error in Mr Fafore’s marked exercise books: “Ade as well as Jide comes early.” In the heat of an emergency meeting, the MD threatens to dismiss Fafore publicly, in front of the whole staff.
bullets: Open Day has its best-dressed prize — and the Gbayi family’s beverage gifts
Mr Guta spots Fafore’s line — “Ade as well as Jide comes early”
The MD threatens a public sack in front of the whole staff
content.takeaway: One sentence nearly cost Fafore his job on Open Day

check.question: What did Mr Guta find in Fafore’s notebook?
options: A deliberate insult aimed at parents
The sentence “Ade as well as Jide comes early”
check.why: The whole chapter turns on that one sentence — it looked like an error, it’s actually correct

content.heading: The sentence that was actually right
paragraphs: Fafore — twenty-two years of service, a single parent of two — commutes from his unplastered house in Ifo, Ogun State, because his salary has stood at ₦175,000 while Lekki two-bedroom rents pass ₦2 million a year. He wakes at 4 a.m., leaves at 4:30, reaches Stardom by 6, and naps at his desk an hour. Twice he has won the Most Punctual Teacher Award. His family: two children, a third on the way, school fees owed.

Bepo intervenes: in standard English, verbs in phrases such as “as well as”, “together with” and “alongside” are singular governed — the verb agrees with “Ade”, not with the plural “Jide”. The MD orders everyone to check online; every one confirms Fafore is right. She stumbles, humiliated.
bullets: He earns ₦175,000, wakes at 4 a.m., and twice won Most Punctual Teacher
“As well as” takes the singular — the verb agrees with Ade
Every staff member checks online — Fafore is right, Bepo is right
content.takeaway: The verb agrees with Ade — “comes”, not “come”

check.question: Why is “Ade as well as Jide comes early” correct?
options: It is a compound subject joined by “as well as” and takes the plural
“As well as” constructions keep a singular verb agreeing with the first noun
Jide is the true subject and takes the verb “come”
Both forms are acceptable Nigerian English
check.why: “As well as” does not make a plural subject — the verb stays singular and agrees with “Ade”

content.heading: Audu acquits everybody
paragraphs: Audu defuses the room with mock courtroom English: “Fafore as well as the Principal is hereby pardoned, discharged and acquitted. And the MD is also pardoned.” The room roars. The storm passes.

Also embedded here: years back, a phrase from a teacher’s copying practice triggered a lawsuit — a photogenic girl’s father, an oil-firm accountant, sued over his daughter being made to write to the board; the school paid out of court, the girl received one tuition-free term, the teacher a three-month no-pay suspension. That is why Stardom stopped note-copying.
bullets: Audu’s mock-court laughter cushions the MD’s humiliation
A copying lawsuit cost the school an out-of-court pay-day
Stardom stopped note-copying because of that case
content.takeaway: Humour acquits what grammar had already settled

check.question: How does Audu end the emergency meeting?
options: He files a motion of no confidence in the MD
He holds a mock court and acquits both Fafore and the MD
check.why: His mock verdict — “Fafore as well as the Principal is hereby pardoned…” — turns fear into laughter

content.title: Exam tip
content.body: If you see “as well as”, pick the singular verb and move on — Fafore was right and the exam bets you know why

content.problem: JAMB-style item: “Which English rule does Bepo invoke to defend Fafore?”

steps.operation: Recall the sentence and what was challenged
steps.reason: The stem points at one grammar rule, so find the exact phrase in dispute — “as well as” is the whole question; when stuck, recall his sentence word for word
steps.result: The disputed phrase is “as well as”

steps.operation: State the rule Bepo named at the meeting
steps.reason: JAMB wants the rule, not the verdict — name it exactly; when stuck, recall the novel’s phrase “singular governed”
steps.result: Singular-governed constructions: the verb agrees with the first noun

steps.operation: Apply it to the sentence to confirm the answer
steps.reason: Proof beats memory — test the rule on the sentence; JAMB designs distractors around “comes/come”; when stuck, ask yourself who leads — Ade, and it’s “comes”
steps.result: “Comes” agrees with Ade — Fafore was right all along

content.question: From memory, reconstruct Fafore’s life in five figures — salary, rent he can’t afford, wake time, arrival time, and the award he won twice.
hints: Give the salary and what Lekki two-bedroom rents demand.
Give 4 a.m., 4:30 a.m., 6 a.m. and the lunchtime desk-nap.
Give the award and his years of service.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recall cards — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Mr Fafore — English teacher, twenty-two years of service, a single parent of two (with a third child on the way); self-built, unplastered house in Ifo, Ogun State; salary ₦175,000; Lekki two-bedroom rents over ₦2 million per annum; wakes 4 a.m., leaves 4:30 a.m., reaches Stardom 6 a.m., naps at his desk about an hour; twice Most Punctual Teacher Award; school fees owed.

Mr Guta — father of Dorah (SS2) and Nicholas (JSS2); opens the Open Day crisis by flagging Fafore’s notebook sentence; the MD — in an emergency meeting — threatens public dismissal before the whole staff.

The rule — “as well as”, “together with” and “alongside” constructions keep a singular verb, governed by the first noun: “Ade as well as Jide comes early.” The MD orders all staff to check online; every one confirms Fafore and Bepo. Audu’s verdict: “Fafore as well as the Principal is hereby pardoned, discharged and acquitted. And the MD is also pardoned.”

The copying lawsuit — years back, a photogenic girl’s father (an oil-firm accountant) sued Stardom over note-copying; settled out of court; the girl received one tuition-free term; the teacher a three-month no-pay suspension; the school stopped the practice; the lesson-ghost haunts teachers to this day.

Open Day texture — best-dressed teacher prized at session’s end; dress-code firing; Gbayi family gift: packets of beverages (Mrs Nike Gbayi, wife of an employee of a leading beverage company); parents arrive loaded with complaints for any teacher who steps on a pupil’s toes.
bullets: The figures are ₦175,000, wake 4 a.m., reach 6 a.m. — twice Most Punctual
“As well as” takes a singular verb — Fafore is correct
Audu’s mock-verdict laughter — and the lawsuit that banned note-copying

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 6
paragraphs: Two JAMB flavours live here. First, the grammar item: “which rule does Bepo invoke”. Options will offer “compound subject”, “subject–verb agreement”, “singular governed”, “commutative property”. Only the third is the text’s own phrase — JAMB sets answers in the novel’s wording, not in generic grammar labels.

Second, the man item: “what does Fafore’s schedule reveal”. Options will offer laziness, a night job, crime — all false — and the truth: a long-commuting teacher whose salary has not moved in years, whom the school barely knew until this episode. The correct option always preserves the tragedy, never the slander.

Discourse-mark question: “as well as” vs “and” — JAMB may test which coordinating word would have made the verb plural. Answer: “and” — “Ade and Jide come early.” The distinction is the whole chapter.

The MD humiliation beat: JAMB could ask why the room roared. The honest answer has two halves — grammar had already vindicated Fafore, and Audu’s comic acquittal let the MD keep her dignity. The correct option holds both halves together.
bullets: Learn the novel’s exact phrase — “singular governed”
Fafore’s story is tragedy, not slander
“And” would make it plural; “as well as” won’t

content.heading: Go deeper: The rule tested, with four sentences
paragraphs: Apply singular governed to four sentences. One: “Ade as well as Jide comes early” — singular, agrees with Ade, correct. Two: “Ade together with Jide comes early” — same rule, same answer. Three: “Ade alongside Jide comes early” — same rule again. Four: “Ade and Jide come early” — “and” makes a plural subject, “come”. The difference is the coordinating conjunction, not the meaning.

Now train the eye for JAMB’s traps. “One of the boys, together with his friends, were late” — wrong; “was late”. “The principal as well as the staff were present” — wrong; “was present”. “Either the MD or the teachers were wrong” — hmm, different rule (proximity), not this one. Keep the traps in labelled boxes.

Why does Standard English obey the first noun? Because “as well as” is an additive — the thing added is incidental; the subject is Ade, Jide merely attends him. The verb belongs to the subject it agrees with, not to the nearer noun its feet stand on.

Nigerian English, and spoken British English too, often accept the plural after “as well as”. The exam is not asking what feels natural — it asks what is standard. Fafore wrote standard; the parent who flagged it did not listen to the sentence.
bullets: “As well as”, “together with”, “alongside” — all singular, the first noun leads
“And” makes it plural; “as well as” just tags something extra
Standard English, not habits — the exam punishes feeling

lessons.title: Chapter 7 — Ritualists
lessons.objective: Describe the Beesway episode — the “Group of School” fight, the 2:30 a.m. live-cow burial, and what Bepo learns about shortcuts.

content.heading: Chapter 7 — Ritualists
paragraphs: Before Stardom made Bepo, Beesway made him — and nearly broke him. Recall Chapter 7 as the chapter where the honest teacher stood alone against the ritual and walked away.

content.heading: The name that was wrong — “Group of School”
paragraphs: Beesway Group of School stands in Ojikutu, on the outskirts of Lagos. Bepo serves there as senior English teacher under its director, Mr Egi Meko — a man of divine confidence.

Bepo keeps correcting the school’s grammatical name: a group must contain more than one school — “Group of Schools”. Meko refuses: the name was divinely inspired, CAC-registered, backed by the Ministry of Education — “it has a spiritual undertone; you are not a kid.”

PTA meetings become battlefields. One parent raises the point and is backed by others. Meko forces Bepo to eat his tongue in front of the meeting, calling him “too-know” — and invokes the vegetable-seller proverb, as if Bepo protesting too much makes him the guilty one.
bullets: Beesway Group of School sits in Ojikutu — its director is Mr Egi Meko
Bepo asks for “Group of Schools” — and Meko calls it divinely inspired
The PTA becomes a battleground — and Meko forces Bepo to eat his words
content.takeaway: Grammar lost to “spiritual undertone” in a single meeting

check.question: What correction did Bepo want at Beesway?
options: “Group of School” should read “Group of Schools”
check.why: The extra word is just an —s — a group holds more than one school, so the school needs the plural “Schools”

content.heading: The 2:30 a.m. discovery
paragraphs: Two nights later, at about 2:30 a.m., the floodlights fail while Bepo lies awake in the staff quarters. Two hundred metres away, the houses are still lit. He slips out — and finds shadows moving behind the school. Five men. A cow. A pit.

The director is there directing the burial of a cow alive in a pit — an occult rite to increase enrolment. Bepo strides in shouting; a man clubs his wrist with a log; two others beat him to the ground. The director orders “handle him gently” — and his men comply. Bepo recovers and says nothing.
Later, Mr Ogo, a parent, offers to sprinkle corn grains round the school for ₦35,000 to “multiply” enrolment. Bepo refuses.
bullets: The floodlights die at 2:30 a.m. — the shadows move 200 metres from the houses
Five men, a cow alive on the way in, a pit below
Mr Ogo offers ₦35,000 to sprinkle corn and “multiply” enrolment — Bepo refuses
content.takeaway: In the dark Bepo finds five men, a live cow and an open grave

check.question: What does Bepo find at 2:30 a.m.?
options: The pump room leaking into the pit
The director and men burying a live cow — an occult enrolment ritual
Students hunting treasure behind the school
The security guard slaughtering cattle for a naming ceremony
check.why: Five men and the director bury a live cow — all for more pupils crossing the gate

content.heading: What the shortcut costs
paragraphs: Ten years later a news broadcast reports Ogo murdered a client — ₦29 million for a fertility ritual; the spiritualist sat atop a chair over a grave-sized pit; accomplices clubbed the client to death. Bepo wakes to find what he always suspected: shortcuts kill.
So one morning, quietly, Bepo packs his belongings and leaves Beesway. Meko apologises that night was a “special prayer for his late father, who gave the land.” Bepo says not a word.

Woven in here also: Bepo’s own Fruitful Future — founded after Youth Service, built on the pupil-teaches-parent tactic he picked up at Waari, Delta State, and grown past seventy pupils by its third session — later crumbled from road failure and a burst water main.
bullets: Ogo murdered a ₦29 million ritual client — on a chair over a pit the size of a grave
Bepo packs and goes without a word
Fruitful Future grew from a pick-up in Waari — and died of bad roads
content.takeaway: Every shortcut in this novel ends in a grave

check.question: What does the news broadcast reveal ten years later?
options: The Ministry finally corrected the school’s name
check.why: Ogo — the corn-grains man — bludgeoned a client to death from a chair over the pit

paragraphs: Beesway Group of School — Ojikutu, on the outskirts of Lagos; director Mr Egi Meko; Bepo served as senior English teacher; the name fight: “Group of School” → “Group of Schools”; Meko refused — “the name was divinely inspired; it has a spiritual undertone; CAC-registered; Ministry of Education backs it; you are not a kid.”

The Ogo episode — Mr Ogo, a parent; offered to sprinkle corn grains round the school for ₦35,000 to “multiply” enrolment; Bepo refused; ten years later the news: Ogo murdered a client who paid ₦29 million for a fertility ritual; the spiritualist sat atop a chair over a grave-sized pit; accomplices clubbed the client to death.

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 7
paragraphs: Chapter 7’s JAMB questions split three ways: the name fight (plot/detail), the 2:30 a.m. discovery (plot/detail), and Bepo’s moral position (theme). The theme item is the dangerous one: “why does Bepo leave Beesway” — options offering anger, fear, poverty, promotion are all wrong; the answer is his refusal to be silent about or complicit in the ritual — he simply packs and goes.

Symbol questions: the live cow — the price of enrolment, worship of numbers over souls; the grave-sized pit — the shortcut’s true destination. The “handle him gently” line is the tell of the whole scene: even the crime is run like a tired family business.

Technique questions: dramatic irony — Bepo suspects before he knows; the reader learns with him at the same pace the dark allows. The 200-metre lit houses are the image of ordinary life continuing while a ritual runs behind the fence.

Watch the option that offers “Meko reformed the school after Bepo left” — false. The text deliberately leaves Meko unchanged and unpunished, which is why Bepo’s departure is the only honest ending the chapter can give.
bullets: The theme is a silent refusal, not a loud one
A live cow — the price of enrolment
Meko stays unpunished — that is the whole point

content.heading: Go deeper: The vocabulary of the ritual scene
paragraphs: Read the ritual with its words. “Divinely inspired” — Meko’s licence to keep the wrong name; “spiritual undertone” — the alibi for refusing correction; “CAC-registered” and “Ministry of Education” — paperwork as moral armour; “too-know” — the insult that shuts a critic up; the vegetable-seller proverb — “these are not dumpsite vegetables” — the guilt-deflector: the one protesting too much becomes the criminal.

The 2:30 a.m. scene is written in hard, few verbs: failed, lies awake, shadows move, he investigates, men bury, a man clubs, two others beat, he is forced, he recovers, he says nothing. That flat rhythm is the dread — nothing about it is romantic, nothing is excused.

“Handle him gently” — the director’s order, the euphemism of a practised criminal who still believes he can stay a decent man in a disgusting hour. The euphemism is the scariest line in the chapter — worse than the cow, worse than the club.

Why a live cow? The novel never says. What it says is worse: the school wanted enrolment the way the cult wanted fertility — ritually, without work. Every incident of Beesway’s sickness in one gesture: a school eating its own soul for bodies at the gate.
bullets: Remember “divinely inspired”, “spiritual undertone” and “too-know”
The dread is told flat — few verbs, no romance
“Handle him gently” is a practised sinner being polite

lessons.title: Chapter 8 — Missions Unaccomplished
lessons.objective: Describe the Stardom prefect election economy, the Banky–Tosh Dancer 3–2 origin, and the Breath Project — the smartphone Bepo cannot bear to leave behind.

content.heading: Chapter 8 — Missions Unaccomplished
paragraphs: The prefect election heats the school, a 3–2 dance result splits two families, and Bepo’s smartphone project hangs over everything. Recall Chapter 8 as the chapter where the school’s future and Bepo’s unfinished one collide.

content.heading: The prefect machine
paragraphs: The price of nomination forms scales by post. Head Boy and Head Girl candidates pay ₦50,000 each; their deputies ₦40,000; other posts — Chapel, Health, Social, Labour, Punctuality — ₦25,000. Aspirants face a five-member screening panel of teachers, non-academics and two alumni observers; candidates with clean records and good grades sit an informal interview — each speaks for three minutes.
Names go up on the board, voters choose — and the old order is suspended because of a legal dispute. Everything in the election happens inside a courtroom’s shadow.
bullets: Head Boy and Head Girl pay ₦50,000, deputies ₦40,000, other posts ₦25,000
Five panellists hear you for three minutes
The old order is suspended — a legal dispute hangs over everything
content.takeaway: Even student power at Stardom is priced and screened

check.question: How much do Head Boy/Head Girl nomination forms cost?
check.why: The top posts are priced highest — ₦50,000 each, against ₦25,000 for ordinary posts

content.heading: The Dancer 3–2 and the two mothers
paragraphs: The dispute centres on Banky (SS2, Social Prefect hope) attacking Tosh (SS2) at Speech Day — “the son of an ex-convict”. Tosh walks out, pundits rage, family honour explodes.

The parents are politicians of the two leading parties — APC and PDP, progressive and liberal. Banky’s mother had beaten Tosh’s for the PTA treasurer’s seat. Their sons were finalists in the JSS 3 Best Dancer hip-hop final that judges gave Banky 3–2; Tosh’s mother complained bitterly.

Chief Didi Ogba — Tosh’s father, senior lawyer — did thirty-six months in detention over a ₦2.5 billion misappropriation claim; acquitted after his company refunded it; never directly guilty. He demands published apologies. Banky’s parents refuse.
bullets: Banky called Tosh “the son of an ex-convict” at Speech Day — and Tosh walked out
The parents are APC and PDP politicians — their mothers fought for the PTA treasurer seat
Banky won the JSS 3 dance final 3–2 — and Ogba demanded an apology
content.takeaway: A dance trophy, two parties and one insult — the feud was ready to explode

They were cast as rivals in a school play

content.heading: The Breath Project — the phone he can’t abandon
paragraphs: Beyond the prefect storm, Bepo worries about the Breath Project — the massive invention-club initiative he heads. It is developing a locally manufactured smartphone from recycled materials, funded externally with an NGO, Life Grid.

The school will announce the phone at his leaving. Bepo promises to return from London to be part of the launch — a pledge JAMB could quote back at you. The project is the novel’s proof that Stardom’s future is in its children’s hands.
bullets: The Breath Project is a recycled-materials smartphone powered by Life Grid
It’s externally funded and Bepo leads it in the invention club
He promises to fly home from London for the unveiling
content.takeaway: It’s the last thing he made at Stardom — his promise to come back

A locally manufactured smartphone from recycled materials

check.why: An invention club project — recycled-material smartphone, NGO-funded, unveiled at his leaving

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 8
paragraphs: Chapter 8 splits cleanly: the election economy (figures) and the Banky–Tosh feud (history). JAMB mixes the two so candidates flunk on one while passing the other. Drill the fees separately from the feud until both are automatic.

Same rule for figures — ₦50,000, ₦40,000, ₦25,000. Wrong options will shuffle them — ₦25,000 for Head Boy or Head Girl is the classic. The three-minute interview is also exam fodder: it is three minutes of informal assessment before names go up, not a formal board exam.

The feud trap: options that cast Tosh’s mother as the aggressor at Speech Day, or Banky as the calm one. The insult comes from Banky’s mouth toward Tosh’s father’s detention; Tosh is the one who walks out. Direction matters.

Theme angle: Chapter 8 is about inherited rivalry — two families exporting a political contest into a school, and schoolboys exporting it into an assembly speech. The correct option for “what drives the dispute” always names the parents, not the students.
bullets: Watch the shuffle — ₦50,000 is the top posts, ₦25,000 is the ordinary ones
Banky threw the insult — Tosh walked out
The feud is parent-driven, not student-driven

content.heading: Go deeper: The prefect election, step by step
paragraphs: Walk the election like a candidate. Step 1: a student collects a nomination form — Head Boy/Head Girl ₦50,000 each; deputies ₦40,000; every other post — Chapel, Health, Social, Labour, Punctuality — ₦25,000. Step 2: a five-member screening panel meets — teachers, non-academics, and two alumni observers from outside the school.

Step 3: candidates with clean records and good grades sit an informal interview — each speaks for three minutes. Step 4: names go up on the board. Step 5: voters choose. Step 6: the old order is suspended — the school contests a defamatory prefect speech, and the election hangs in legal uncertainty.

Notice the economics: ₦50,000 for two posts, ₦40,000 for two deputies, ₦25,000 for five ordinary posts — the tickets alone can raise ₦100,000 + ₦80,000 + ₦125,000 = ₦305,000 before a single vote is counted. The school’s democracy is priced like a market stall.

Notice the design: clean record plus good grades is the screening filter — talent in, cash-for-forms out. The old order’s suspension shows the court of procedure can stop even a priced democracy — and that power at Stardom is never more than one injunction from embarrassment.
bullets: ₦305,000 in forms before a single vote
The screen checks your record and your grades; the interview is three minutes
A court suspension can halt even a priced democracy

lessons.title: Chapter 9 — Laughing Waterfalls
lessons.objective: List the excursion destinations and their discovery facts, and explain how the Badagry visit breaks Bepo’s japa arithmetic.

content.heading: Chapter 9 — Laughing Waterfalls
paragraphs: Stardom runs about three excursions a year — the waterfalls are beautiful, the Badagry beach is not. Recall Chapter 9 as the chapter where history at the jetty undoes two years of japa arithmetic.

content.heading: The excursion calendar
paragraphs: Three trips a year — domestic each term, international yearly, ~70% kept. The catalogue: Ikogosi Warm Springs (Ekiti) — 1852, Rev. John S. McGee, from his Igede-Ekiti mission base, for a youth camp of converted king’s children.

Erin-Ijesa (Olumirin), Osun — found by a daughter of Oduduwa, or Akinla, its founder, in 1140 AD. Owu Waterfalls (Kwara) — the highest in West Africa, ~120 m above water, a 330-foot escarpment. Gurara (Niger) — a Gwari hunter named Buba, ~1748, nearly two centuries before Europeans in 1925.

Other stops: Yankari Game Reserve (Bauchi), the National War Museum (Umuahia), Ado Awaye’s Hanging Lake (Oyo), the Kano Palace, the Ooni’s palace and Obafemi Awolowo University — Mrs Gloss’s alma mater.
bullets: Ikogosi was found in 1852 by McGee, Erin-Ijesa in 1140, Gurara around 1748
Owu in Kwara is the highest — about 120 metres, a 330-foot drop
Obafemi Awolowo University is Mrs Gloss’s alma mater, and Sungbo’s Eredo is older than both
content.takeaway: Every waterfall has a discoverer — Badagry has none; it belongs to us

check.question: Who discovered Gurara Falls, and when?
options: A Gwari hunter named Buba around 1748
check.why: Buba the hunter — nearly two centuries before Europeans reached Gurara in 1925

content.heading: The Badagry leg
paragraphs: Forty SSS 1–3 students, led by Bepo, visit the palace of the Akran of Badagry — the latest First Port where slavery landed on this coast. The monarch tells them that bad guys sold their own kin — the event of the late 1720s, when Popo refugees came to the shore.

They pass the First Storey Building (Henry Townsend, 1846), where Ajayi Crowther — the first African Anglican bishop — stayed and produced the first translation of the Yoruba Bible; the Anglican Nursery and Primary School (ex-Nursery of the Infant Church, established 1843), the first church school in Nigeria; and the Black Heritage Museum — the trans-Atlantic slave museum at Badagry.
bullets: Forty SSS students saw — the Akran’s palace, and the Popo refugee landing of the late 1720s
The First Storey Building is where Ajayi Crowther made the first Yoruba Bible translation, 1846
The Black Heritage Museum is the trans-Atlantic slave museum
content.takeaway: Badagry gives them two centuries of history and one jetty of chains

check.question: What is the First Storey Building at Badagry remembered for?
options: It was the residence of the first Governor-General
Henry Townsend’s mission house; Crowther produced the first Yoruba Bible translation there
It was the first post office in Nigeria
It is the gate of the Black Heritage Museum
check.why: 1846 — Henry Townsend’s storey building housed Crowther’s first Yoruba Bible translation work

content.heading: The Point of No Return
paragraphs: Nothing touches them like the slave trade. At the Black Heritage Museum, the exhibit collapses the present into the past. Bepo, emotionally undone, realises: the same japa movement today is Africans voluntarily trading themselves for dollars and pounds to former masters who looted them — chains on the economy, just not on the wrists.

The visit ends at the Point of No Return — the jetty from which slaves were shipped. He stands there and the arithmetic of ₦1,700 a pound and ₦6 million a month quietly dies. What remains is a question he has never dared ask.
bullets: japa is voluntary self-trade to the former masters
The chains sit on the economy now — not on anyone’s wrists
The jetty kills the arithmetic — the question of staying remains
content.takeaway: One jetty turned the ₦6 million dream to dust

check.question: What does the Point of No Return change in Bepo?
options: He decides to buy a boat for the school
His japa arithmetic collapses — he sees the slave-trade parallel
He refuses to teach history again
check.why: The jetty is where the “chains on the economy” realisation lands

Erin-Ijesa: 1140 AD, a daughter of Oduduwa or Akinla.

content.heading: Go deeper: Recall cards — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The excursion plan — about three per year: a domestic trip each term; an international one each year (~70% reliability). National sights: Yankari Game Reserve (Bauchi); National War Museum (Umuahia, Abia); Hanging Lake (Ado Awaye, Oyo); Kano Palace; the Ooni of Ife’s palace; Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife (Mrs Ibidun Gloss’s alma mater); Sungbo’s Eredo in Ijebu (800–1,000 AD defensive ditch). Lagos sights: National Theatre (Iganmu), Iganmu; Lagos Mall; Epe.

The waterfalls — Ikogosi Warm Springs (Ekiti): 1852, Rev. John S. McGee, from his mission base at Igede-Ekiti; the myth: he defied warnings the springs were supernatural. Erin-Ijesa (Olumirin, Osun): discovered by a daughter of Oduduwa — or by Akinla, the founder of Erin-Ijesa — in 1140 AD. Owu (Kwara): highest in West Africa, ~120 m above water, 330-foot escarpment. Gurara (Niger State): Gwari hunter Buba, ≈1748; Europeans arrived 1925.

Badagry — 40 SSS 1–3 students; Bepo leads; palace of the Akran of Badagry; late 1720s Popo-refugees event; First Storey Building — Henry Townsend, 1846; Ajayi Crowther, first African Anglican bishop, produced the first Yoruba Bible translation there; Anglican Nursery and Primary School (ex-Nursery of the Infant Church), established 1843 — the first church school in Nigeria; Black Heritage Museum — the trans-Atlantic slave museum.

The Point of No Return — the jetty from which slaves were shipped; Bepo is undone; the parallel: modern japa = voluntary self-trading to former masters; “chains on the economy, just not on the wrists.”
bullets: Ikogosi is 1852 and McGee, Erin-Ijesa is 1140, Owu is highest, Gurara is Buba
In Badagry, it runs palace, storey building, museum, jetty
The Point of No Return — chains on the economy

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 9
paragraphs: Ikogosi/Erin-Ijesa/Gurara confusions are JAMB’s favourite Chapter 9 trap. Learn this triangle and you are safe: 1852 McGee = Ikogosi; 1140 AD daughter of Oduduwa = Erin-Ijesa; ≈1748 Buba = Gurara. Owu has no discoverer to memorise — it is the “highest in West Africa” answer, roughly 120 m / 330 ft.

Badagry ordering matters: palace of the Akran → First Storey Building (1846) → Nursery and Primary (1843) → Black Heritage Museum → Point of No Return. JAMB shuffles these four in options; the jetty is always last.

The Crowther question appears in three costumes: first African Anglican bishop, the first Yoruba Bible translation, or Townsend’s 1846 storey building. All three name the same man — Olu Ajayi Crowther — and JAMB expects you to connect any two of them.

The theme question of the chapter is certain: “what does the Badagry visit change”. The wrong options mention sadness, prayer, repentance, or cancelling excursions. The true option keeps the parallel: japa = voluntary slavery to former masters — chains on the economy, not on the wrists.
bullets: McGee 1852, Oduduwa 1140, Buba 1748
In Badagry it runs museum, jetty — the jetty is always last
The parallel is this — chains on the economy, not on wrists

content.heading: Go deeper: Why Badagry — and not the waterfalls
paragraphs: The waterfalls are in Chapter 9 for a reason — they are the school’s smiling face: Owu’s escarpment, Ikogosi’s warm water, Olumirin’s Oduduwa myth. Bepo sells excursions to parents; parents buy safety, culture, Nigeria packaged well. But the chapter hides its payload inside the easy tourism.

Badagry is where the package breaks open. The palace of the Akran, the late 1720s Popo refugees, the First Storey Building (Townsend, 1846), Crowther’s Yoruba Bible, the Anglican Nursery ex-Infant-Church school of 1843 — each site is ordinary history until the jetty. Then slavery’s machinery stands in front of forty children.

Bepo’s breakdown here is not decorative. The same book that showed him crying at assembly tears open again at the fence line between Nigeria’s past and its present. The Badagry Beach gives him the sentence the novel needed:japa is slavery’s grandchild — the masters’ looted wealth still pulling migrants across the ocean, chains swapped for economic ones.

JAMB will ask you to distinguish the smiles from the wound. The smiles: highest West African waterfall, warm springs, the 1140 AD Oduduwa myth. The wound: the Point of No Return — the only sight on the trip that rewrites a man.
bullets: The waterfalls are the school’s smiling face
Badagry is the payload — the jetty and the chains on the economy
This is the second breakdown — Badagry breaks the japa arithmetic

lessons.title: Chapter 10 — Passport Pains
lessons.objective: Trace Bepo’s two-year passport lapse from COVID to the Ibadan agent Tai, and quote the fees — ₦100,000, ₦20,000, ₦2,000.

content.heading: Chapter 10 — Passport Pains
paragraphs: Two years of procrastination, one pandemic, and a journey to Ibadan at dawn. Recall Chapter 10 as the chapter where Nigeria’s official queues met one man’s desperation.

content.heading: The two-year lapse
paragraphs: Bepo is a procrastinator. For two years his passport lies lapsed. COVID-19 makes renewal impossible; post-pandemic tales of new rules, hassles and booklet non-availability spook him. By the first quarter of 2022, renewal is an emergency.

He cannot bear the maddening crowding at the Lagos office, so he explores the Ibadan option. On a Tuesday afternoon he sets off — not in his car (Lagos–Ibadan roads, security issues) but in a shared Toyota Sienna. Everyone aboard appears destined for the world beyond. The expressway astonishes him — miles of open highway where once he agonised on his Ile-Ife excursions — and almost nobody observes the toll-gate discipline.
bullets: Two years of lapsed time, a pandemic, and the first quarter of 2022
The Lagos crowds became unbearable — that’s what pushed him to Ibadan
He rides a shared Sienna where everyone looks bound for abroad
content.takeaway: The passport has been dead for two years — the queue can’t wait any longer

check.question: By when had Bepo’s passport become an emergency?
options: After the UK appointment was signed
check.why: Two years of procrastination plus COVID forced the renewal — by the first quarter of 2022

content.heading: Ibadan, Agodi-Gate, 6 a.m.
paragraphs: He is up by 6 a.m. the next day at the Agodi-Gate Passport Office in Ibadan, as the law demands. The route is surprisingly orderly compared to Lagos — queues and procedure are civil.

A friend-of-a-friend in the Ibadan office — an unofficial agent, Tai, a business-centre operator — arranges a direct line. Tai acts as the process man: collects the passport, verifies the NIN (National Identity Number), pushes the booklet for data capture within three weeks, pointing out the hall full of people who have spent “forever” there.
bullets: He’s at Agodi Gate by 6 a.m. — civil queues, unlike Lagos
Tai is a business-centre operator — not an office agent, the unofficial kind
The NIN is verified — capture within three weeks — and Tai shows him the hall of the “forever” people
content.takeaway: It’s six o’clock, the queues are civil, and one agent gets it done

check.question: Who is Tai, in the passport episode?
options: A passport officer officially assigned to Bepo
An unofficial agent and business-centre operator in Ibadan
The driver of the Toyota Sienna
check.why: Inside the system from outside — Tai is the Ibadan fixer with the direct line

content.heading: Tai’s price, and the ₦2,000 tip
paragraphs: Tai charges ₦100,000 for a 10-year (64-page) passport, and a further ₦20,000 to expedite capture — though the same service is promised at a fraction of the cost officially. He hints his prices reflect “the rules”, not real corruption — the polite fiction that smooths the transaction.

When the officials offer to expedite things, Bepo parts with an extra ₦2,000 as courtesy — learning the waiting game can be unbearable, and that courtesy buys speed where procedure does not. The smallest payment of the saga is the one that feels most like a confession.
bullets: ₦100,000 buys the 64-page, 10-year booklet
₦20,000 more gets the capture expedited
₦2,000 as courtesy to the officials at the desk
content.takeaway: A Nigerian passport really costs ₦100,000 for the booklet, ₦20,000 to push it, and ₦2,000 as a courtesy

check.why: ₦100,000 + ₦20,000 = ₦120,000, plus the ₦2,000 courtesy at the desk

content.body: If your options shuffle the three figures, keep them separate — ₦100,000 for the booklet, ₦20,000 to expedite, ₦2,000 as courtesy — never treat them as one payment

paragraphs: The lapse — two years; COVID-19; new rules, hassles and booklet non-availability tales; by the first quarter of 2022 renewal is an emergency; he will not use the maddening Lagos office; Tuesday afternoon departure; not his car (road + security); shared Toyota Sienna; everyone aboard bound for the world beyond; the expressway astonishes him — open highway versus the agony of his Ile-Ife excursions; almost nobody observes the toll-gate discipline.

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 10
paragraphs: Chapter 10’s exam fodder is procedural — JAMB loves to test how Nigerians renew passports: procrastinate → COVID kills renewal → first quarter 2022 → Ibadan because Lagos is chaos → 6 a.m. Agodi-Gate → Tai → ₦100,000 + ₦20,000 → NIN → three weeks → ₦2,000 courtesy tip. Every step is a testable fact.

Figure traps again: ₦100,000, ₦20,000, ₦2,000. The official tariff is “a fraction” of Tai’s fees — options claiming “free” or “₦5,000” are wrong. And Tai is an unofficial agent doing official work — no option may call him a police officer or a doctor.

Theme language: the novel uses the passport as the emblem of the japa dream itself — expensive, exhausting, full of waiting, never explained honestly. If JAMB asks what the passport pain symbolises, the answer grows from that simile: the price of escape.
The courtesy question: “what extra did Bepo pay at the desk”. The distractor ₦20,000 is the capture fee, already counted; the true extra is ₦2,000 — the last and smallest payment of the whole saga.

The passport is the emblem of japa’s price

content.heading: Go deeper: The passport as the novel’s engine
paragraphs: The passport is the whole plot in one document. It expired two years before Bepo was ready — exactly like his courage in Chapter 1. COVID-19 is the outer world stalling the inner one: borders shut, offices full, booklets scarce; Nigeria itself procrastinating in a global post-pandemic jam.

Why the expressway detail? The road is clear where it used to agonise; drivers don’t keep toll discipline — a nation hurrying without rules. Bepo rides a Sienna with fellow travellers all destined for “the world beyond”. The passport queue is beaten only by queuing smarter, not by playing fairer.

Why Ibadan? Because Lagos is beyond endurance — the wait has outlived his patience; the form has outlived his courage. Ibadan is the compromise Nigeria forces on its citizens: a semi-official agent, a sixth-morning queue, a NIN check, a three-week wait, ₦100,000 + ₦20,000 + ₦2,000 — the true price of believing in the system just enough to survive it.

Theme unlocked: the passport is the novel’s thesis artefact — it holds the whole “japa” question in one green booklet: who may leave, how much it costs, what must be sold and survived to board the Saturday flight.
bullets: The dead passport is his postponed courage
Ibadan is the compromise Nigeria forces on its people
The ₦2,000 courtesy is the system’s smallest toll

lessons.title: Chapter 11 — Point of No Return
lessons.objective: Describe the three-day farewell — banner, novelty match, debate, canoe dance and the $10,000 envelope — and how the school said goodbye to its principal.

content.heading: Chapter 11 — Point of No Return
paragraphs: Three days of farewell, one banner that revealed a full name, one dance that broke him, and one envelope that said everything. Recall Chapter 11 as the chapter where the school finally knew what it was losing.

content.heading: Three days of farewell
paragraphs: The programme runs three days. A banner stretches across the main hall: “To our most committed principal…” — revealing for the first time that “Bepo” is short for Adebepo Adewale. He shifts his Emirates flight by a week; the airline charges $100; Stardom pays it.

Wednesday: a novelty match — students versus staff. The referee (later identified as Audu) rejects goals, awards penalties five times, and the game ends in stalemate. Friday: a debate on whether Nigeria gains most from art/culture or science/technology — the arts team wins, citing film, music and culture as Nigeria’s strongest exports. Bepo watches his seed pay off.
bullets: The banner reveals the name — Adebepo Adewale, “our most committed principal”
The flight shifts a week — the $100 change fee is paid by the school
Wednesday is the stalemate — Audu, five penalties — and Friday is the arts debate winning
content.takeaway: Three days packed into one banner and one goalless goodbye football match

check.question: What full name does the banner reveal?
check.why: The banner’s quiet reveal — “Bepo” was always Adebepo Adewale

content.heading: The canoe dance — and the envelope
paragraphs: A skit imitates Bepo assembly-style — voice, palms in pockets, the correction catchphrase, “PrinciPL not Principè” — to excitement and laughter. The cultural programme runs Bata, Atilogwu, Koroso, then the Canoe dance — revived from the October show he took the students to see at the National Theatre.
Deep in the trance of the Canoe dance, he cries out “Nooo!” — recalling Badagry. He collects himself, apologises jokingly; the audience applauds anyway.

The MD rises: she gives him the largest leave fee in Stardom’s history — a flat envelope. The crowd expects something absurd; it turns out at least $10,000 in a domiciliary cheque — “the highest Stardom has ever presented any disengaging member of staff”.
bullets: The skit hits all the old notes — voice, palms, “PrinciPL” — and the room roars
The Canoe dance breaks with his “Nooo!” — Badagry returns inside the trance
The envelope holds at least $10,000 in a domiciliary cheque — a Stardom first
content.takeaway: One scream broke the dance — and one envelope held the thanks

check.question: What does the MD give Bepo?
options: At least $10,000 in a domiciliary cheque — a Stardom first
check.why: The envelope held at least $10,000 — the highest disengagement gift in school history

content.heading: Chief David Aje’s eight days
paragraphs: She tells the hall how her father — the late Chief David Aje — hired Bepo. He had applied and never shown up at the interview — having only had a chat — and Aje waited eight days for him to come, earning his trust on the spot and binding him to Stardom for life.

She praises his pillar-qualities — skill, drive, empathy and morals — and calls him a blessing to Stardom. Bepo weeps at the podium — the man who never breaks, breaking at last in thanksgiving, not in grief.
bullets: He applied, never showed, gave only a chat — and Aje waited eight days
The pillars are skill, drive, empathy and morals
Bepo weeps at the podium
content.takeaway: Eight days of waiting bought Stardom twenty-four years

paragraphs: The banner — “To our most committed principal…” stretched across the main hall; reveals for the first time that “Bepo” is short for Adebepo Adewale; displayed publicly as “Adebepo Adewale”. Emirates flight shifted by a week; the airline charges $100 change fee; Stardom pays it.

He collects himself, apologises jokingly; the audience applauds anyway.

The envelope — the MD gives him the largest leave fee in Stardom’s history; a flat envelope; the crowd expects something absurd; it turns out at least $10,000 in a domiciliary cheque — “the highest Stardom has ever presented any disengaging member of staff”. content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 11
paragraphs: Three figure-traps anchor this chapter: $100 (flight-change, school-paid), $10,000 (the cheque, minimum), eight days (Aje’s wait). JAMB combines them in options freely — “$100,000”, “$1,000”, “ten days” — so chant all three until automatic, and keep the currencies straight: dollars only, never naira.

Sequence questions: banner → Wednesday match → Friday debate → canoe dance → MD’s envelope → Aje’s story → tears. JAMB asks “which comes first” and “which comes last”; practising the chain covers both.

Symbol questions: the canoe dance as trance — the body remembering Badagry before the mind does; “Nooo!” is the single syllable of refusal the novel has been building toward. The envelope signifies the institution finally speaking its gratitude in the only language it cannot fumble.

The meaning question: “what does the farewell reveal about Stardom’s culture”. The correct option keeps two halves — gratitude to long-serving educators, and an institution that publicly celebrates what it nearly lost. Options that say “Stardom forgives itself” or “Stardom finally understands teachers” both miss the twin halves.
bullets: The $100, the $10,000 and the eight days are three separate facts
The order runs banner, match, debate, dance, envelope
The farewell is gratitude — and an institution almost losing itself

content.heading: Go deeper: The farewell as a political act
paragraphs: Read the three days as politics. The banner is corporate gratitude — but it is also branding: “our most committed principal” teaches every family in the school that Stardom loves its staff completely and publicly. The banner reveals the name “Adebepo Adewale” only after two decades of “Bepo” — the institution reclaims him formally, officially, almost posthumously.

The novelty match is theatre: Audu’s five penalties, the goalless stalemate — the school’s playful honesty about its own favouritism: nobody wins fairly, and everybody is loved anyway. The Friday arts debate is the curriculum speaking — culture beats science at the farewell of the artsiest headmaster a school ever had.

The canoe dance is the farewell’s buried bomb: the one moment the carefully staged gratitude cracks, and the body screams what the mind refuses to say — “Nooo!” — Badagry revisited inside a cultural celebration. Stardom survives by swallowing the scream whole; applause at the wrong moment is its ritual.

The envelope completes the transaction: gratitude paid in USD 10,000 — the highest Stardom ever gave a disengaging head — as the institution buys back the morning it almost lost. It is the farewell of an elite school finally fluent in the only language it truly is: money, affection, and timing.
bullets: The banner is branding and reclaiming the name at once
The match is playful honesty about favouritism
The envelope is affection paid in USD

lessons.title: Chapter 12 — Dawn
lessons.objective: Narrate the Saturday flight, the slave-camp dream, and the Monday eruption — and state what Bepo’s choice means for the novel’s theme.

content.heading: Chapter 12 — Dawn
paragraphs: One Saturday at 10:45 p.m., a plane takes off London-bound — and one man’s body refuses to leave Nigeria. Recall Chapter 12 as the chapter where Dawn finally outshone Dusk.

content.heading: The Saturday flight
paragraphs: Bepo’s flight is headed for London, planned at 10:00 p.m. on a Saturday; check-in at 5:30 p.m. — an ominously-sober farewell from the halls. The VP, Apeh, drives him with Oyelana and Audu to the airport; the two vehicles are escorted through Ikeja underflow; traffic is normal.

At check-in a female official checks his ticket and smiles; alarms; his phone is in his pocket — he cannot find Seri’s call to convey he is on the way. Departures; his seat is 56, window-side, Gate 2A. He boards. The plane takes off at 10:45 p.m.
bullets: The flight is the 10 p.m. to London — checking in at 5:30, with Apeh, Oyelana and Audu
Seat 56 by the window, Gate 2A — the smile and the alarms
The plane takes off at 10:45 p.m.
content.takeaway: It’s seat 56 at Gate 2A, 10:45 p.m. — the flight he never wanted

check.question: What time did the plane take off?
check.why: 10:00 was the planned departure; 10:45 p.m. was actual takeoff

content.heading: The dream that opened the door
paragraphs: Some time later he is groggy — and violently jolted awake by a dream in which a white man stands over him screaming “Enter!” in a slave camp. Bepo cries out “No!” — leaping out of his seat as if the body had been waiting all flight to refuse its own ticket.

Airline officials are startled and curious; he is gently calmed down; the plane flies London-bound. The body that refused the flight had just told the whole plane why — the slave camp was never behind him.
bullets: He’s groggy in a slave camp, and a white man screams “Enter!” over him
“No!” — and he leaps out of his seat
The officials are startled, and he’s gently calmed
content.takeaway: The dream said “Enter!” — and Bepo said “No!”

check.question: What happens in the dream that wakes Bepo?
options: A white man screams “Enter!” in a slave camp
Seri pulls him off the plane by the arm
check.why: The slave-camp image revisits Badagry one last time — the dream votes

content.heading: Monday — “I’m back! I didn’t go!”
paragraphs: Monday at Stardom is jarring. The whole school turns down. He isn’t there. The classroom absentee trend dramatically warns students that something is wrong. Apeh visits the assembly, and her flat-toned welcome fails to replicate Bepo’s.

At the gate, staff are shocked — SHOUTS echo that he is back: “I’m back! I’m back! I didn’t go!” The school erupts with him returning — tears, dancing, singing Stardom’s school anthem: “We’re Stars, we’re Stars! We’re Stars of Stardom! We’re Stars and we have won! No night so dark! No cloud so mean! Yet Stardom Schools will win!”
His mission is clear in his own words: he didn’t go; this is where his heart is.
bullets: Monday comes, the school turns down, and the empty classrooms warn the students
Apeh’s assembly falls flat without him
“I’m back! I didn’t go!” — the school erupts and the anthem rings out
content.takeaway: Dawn is not on a plane — it is Monday assembly

content.heading: Go deeper: How JAMB words Chapter 12
paragraphs: Chapter 12 has its figures to chant — 5:30 p.m. check-in, 10:45 p.m. takeoff, seat 56, Gate 2A, 10:00 p.m. planned, Apeh picking you up at 5:30. Options will scramble them — you chant them until they’re automatic, evening to evening, Dusk to Dawn.

The dream question: “what happens in the dream”. Wrong options: “the plane crashes”, “Seri begs him to return”, “he sees Stardom’s empty hall”. Correct option: the slave-camp scene — the white man, “Enter!”, “No!”. The image is Badagry’s jetty revisited — the whole novel’s indictment of japa in one room.
The Monday question: what the students notice is the absence — not the return. JAMB inverts the order of events; the correct option names the warning, not the announcement.

Theme closure: decision-making versus loyalty resolved — home beats money, self beats comfort, service beats salary. The correct theme option always names the resolved tension, not the feeling: “he chooses Stardom over London”, not “he feels nostalgic”.
bullets: Chant them — 5:30, 10:45, seat 56, Gate 2A, and the planned 10 p.m.

content.heading: Go deeper: How the ending works — mirrors and refusals
paragraphs: The last chapter is built on mirrors. Dusk inverted: the book opens with tears at a podium, it closes with tears at a gate; Chapter 1 is public collapse, Chapter 12 public restoration; the first anthem stanza is the morning, the final anthem the return. Dawn is Dusk’s reflection in an unbroken lake.

The dream rhymes across two chapters. In Chapter 11, the Canoe dance cracks him — “Nooo!” In Chapter 12, the slave-camp dream repeats it — “No!”. Two screams, one refusal: the body learning before the mind does, twice, exactly what the jetty first taught.

The officials’ calm matters. The plane does not panic; the airline does not seize him; the world absorbs the scream the way Stardom absorbed the Canoe-dance tear. The ending dramatises a truth about institutions: they survive your rebellion by carrying on around it — the tragedy is that carrying on is also the mercy.

JAMB’s favourite closer: “why does he call it his heart” — because “I didn’t go!” is the simplest sentence in the novel, and the only one with nothing left to prove. The examination wants candidates who can hold that sentence still, without explanation, long enough to know it is true.
bullets: Dusk mirrors itself — tears at the podium answer the tears at the gate
The two “No!”s — the dance scene in Chapter 11 and the dream in Chapter 12
“I didn’t go!” — his own words, and no more proof is needed
